title: Penn State women’s soccer continues to climb in the United Soccer Coaches Poll
author: Daniel Almash | For The Collegian
description:
Penn State continued its winning ways on Friday with a 4-0 victory against Indiana at Jeffery Field. This brought their overall record to 9-3-5 on the season, and their conference play to 7-2-3.

In the recent poll rankings, the blue and white were ranked No. 21 in the United Soccer Coaches Poll, 14th on the TDS poll, and No. 20 on the NCAA RPI poll as of Nov. 3.

The Nittany Lions see this as no surprise as they have been dominant on all fronts this season.

Within the season, they have gotten outstanding freshman production with nine goals, 10 assists and 28 points. While also getting major offensive contributions coming from junior forward Aubrey Kulpa who has scored eight goals and senior Paige Kalal who has notched six assists on the season.

With the Big Ten Tournament looming on Thursday, Penn State travels to St. Louis to play No. 16 Purdue at 8 p.m. Coach Erica Dambach’s team is looking to make a deep run for a Big Ten Championship, coming off a season where she recorded her 300th coaching victory. The Nittany Lions look to carry their regular-season momentum into the postseason.

MORE SOCCER CONTENT

title: Three Penn State women’s hockey players win AHA awards for October performance
author: Brady Welsh | For The Collegian
description:
Atlantic Hockey America announced the winners of monthly awards Tuesday, with three Penn State women’s hockey players being recognized.

Abby Stonehouse won Forward of the Month as she led the conference in points per game with 14 in 10 games played. Her point total is second in the conference behind teammate Sofia Ismael and her seven goals are tied for second behind teammate Grace Outwater. Stonehouse was also awarded AHA player of the week after tallying her first collegiate hat trick Saturday at RIT.

Moving to the blue line, Sophie Morrow was named AHA Defender of the Month. The sophomore tallied one goal and 12 assists in 12 games played in October, leading the conference in assists and assists per game. She won defender of the week twice in October and had four assists Saturday, including one on each goal Stonehouse scored for her hat trick.

Finally, goaltender Morgan Stickney is the AHA Rookie of the Month. After a rough two games to start October where she allowed seven goals on 29 shots against Robert Morris and Syracuse, Stickney bounced back in a huge way, allowing a combined two goals through her final four games and achieving the first two shutouts of her collegiate career. The freshman earned three weekly awards in that span, which included two Rookie of the Week honors and a Goaltender of the Week.

The Nittany Lions are currently in first place in the AHA with a 7-1 conference record. They stayed at seven in the latest USCHO ranking. The team is off this week, but will return to action on Nov. 13 when they go to Erie, Pennsylvania, for two conference matchups against Mercyhurst.

title: Penn State notebook | Matt Campbell shares cross-country travel plans
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Days after Penn State’s first Big Ten victory of the season, Matt Campbell met with the media in the Beaver Stadium media room.

Campbell discussed Koby Howard and Chase Sowell’s availability ahead of Washington, travel plans for Saturday’s game and more.

Here’s a look at what Campbell talked about on Tuesday.

Wide receiver updates

In the absence of Howard and Sowell, Penn State had to turn to freshman receiver Amarion Jackson against Purdue. Jackson had two catches for 31 yards, showcasing his potential as a young threat.

“I thought he did a great job in terms of his opportunities,” Campbell said. “He made the most of them. I think that's a little bit of the theme of last Saturday is guys got their opportunity and they made the most of it.”

While the Nittany Lions came out with a win against the Boilermakers, it was clear that Howard and Sowell being sidelined plagued the passing game. Outside of Jackson, Brett Eskildsen and Zay Robinson were the only other receivers with a catch.

Campbell provided a positive update regarding Sowell’s availability, while uttering the same response he used for Howard a week ago.

“I think Chase is certainly probable,” Campbell said. “I think he's in a really good spot. I think Koby is still probably in the word questionable, and I think we'll have to see again where he's at.”

During last week’s press conference, Campbell said “If (Howard’s) not ready, I'm not putting him on that football field until he's 100% ready to go.” That was the same rhetoric he used this Tuesday when discussing Howard’s status.

“When he's ready, we're going to try to make sure he's on the field,” Campbell said. “But we're going to make sure he's ready to go.”

Cam Wallace’s breakout

After entering the season as the No. 4 running back on Penn State’s depth chart, Cam Wallace took a bulk of the carries against Purdue and rushed for a career-high 135 yards and a touchdown.

It was a long way to that big moment for Wallace, who broke both of his ankles against Kent State in 2024. Campbell heard about his path when the two first met in December.

“There was just a lot of frustration going on with where Cam was, and what I did appreciate, it was not b—ing and complaining,” Campbell said. “It was just some of the situations that occurred with the injury, the frustration, and then I really appreciated him telling me his story a little bit that day.”

Campbell said he distinctly remembered the conversation he had with Wallace, and even followed up with Wallace’s aunt, who played a major role in his upbringing, after the running back entered the transfer portal this offseason.

“Once I talked to his aunt, 24 hours later he called and said he wanted to come back.” Campbell said. “We're talking Sunday before the team meeting is when he decided to come back. So really grateful that he did, and really grateful to have him be a great example of what we want this program to look like and feel like on the inside.”

Following Wallace’s breakout game, Campbell again spoke with Wallace about his journey and finally having his moment, relating back to his past struggles and fighting back from his injuries.

“I had told him that Saturday night after the game how proud his mother would be, how proud his grandmother and his aunt would be, because of the resilience of how he got his opportunity,” Campbell said.

Cross-country travel

Penn State will drive an hour and a half to Harrisburg on Thursday before flying to Seattle ahead of Saturday’s game. Since the expansion of the Big Ten in 2024, cross country travel has been a major question surrounding Penn State and other East Coast teams.

“Those are things you try to do a great job in the offseason of knowing what's on your schedule, what's coming, and trying to be a great planner,” Campbell said. “Penn State has had this trip the last couple years going to the West Coast, so I think you try to take all the information, then just make the best travel plans possible.”

In the past, the size of the State College runway has been brought up as a limitation forcing the Nittany Lions to travel to Pennsylvania’s capital.

While Campbell didn’t bring that up, he talked about the time of the game being the major factor in travel. Penn State will face off against the Huskies at 3:35 p.m. ET, which translates to 12:35 p.m. PT.

“I felt like if we got in Friday, you're going to be really pushing it,” Campbell said. “If it was a day game, we tried to go on Thursday to get ourselves there, get settled in, and try to, from a sleep standpoint, try to get on the best rhythm that we possibly can, and not lose sleep.”

title: Penn State notebook | OC Taylor Mouser discusses the offense's success against Purdue
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Offensive coordinator Taylor Mouser met with the media on Tuesday after Penn State snapped a four-game losing streak, beating Purdue 31-17 on Saturday.

Mouser talked about seeing offensive success, his happiness with a more aggressive fourth-down philosophy and how the scheme differs with wide receivers Koby Howard and Chase Sowell injured.

Here’s more on what Mouser said.

Offensive success, playing to the standard

When Mouser was asked about what it meant to him for the offense to succeed after the four-game skid, he said he was "desperate" to get things going after putting blame on himself for the offensive struggles during those losses.

“When you're not winning here and you're not living up to the standard, you feel like you're letting a lot more people down than just the players, the coaches, like the alumni,” Mouser said. “Those people built the standard here that you have to live up to, and when you don't do it, you feel like you're letting everybody down, and we're not playing. We weren't playing with the standard that I had set or envisioned for the offense.”

However, the Nittany Lions found success both in the pass game and in the run game on Saturday, and Mouser said it was because the team stuck together, never pointed fingers and continued to practice hard.

Mouser said his focus was on simplifying the offensive scheme to allow the team to “play fast” in the run game. It contributed to 269 rushing yards and three rushing touchdowns.

“For me, it was just about like those guys going out there and be able to play with a level of physicality and a level of balance, a level of conviction with each other, and be able to see real chemistry at the line of scrimmage and real communication,” Mouser said. “We looked like a real football team at times in the game.”

Fourth-down decisions

Mouser said he was happy with how Matt Campbell was more aggressive with his decision-making on fourth down, as the Nittany Lions went three-for-three when Campbell kept the offense on the field.

He added how he always calls a play regardless of whether Campbell intends on keeping the offense on the field to prove how confident he is in his players to move the chains. Mouser said he “always wants to go for it.”

“I hate kicking field goals always, even though it's good to put points on the board,” Mouser said. “But it's something that I'm pretty passionate about.”

The fourth-down aggression directly led to two touchdowns, and kept the defense fresh in the second half of the game. It also helped Penn State dominate the time of possession, having the ball for 43:27 compared to Purdue’s 16:33.

“I was probably more proud of anything from our guys who had the ball for 43 minutes and really were able to play complementary football at a high level,” Mouser said.

The scheme with, without Howard and Sowell

Mouser said the offensive scheme changes depending on who’s in the game, especially if it’s Howard and Sowell, who’ve been the engine of the offense when healthy.

He noted how Campbell has always been about tailor-making his game plan to the personnel available.

“As long as I've been with coach Campbell, his thing's always been players, formations, plays, and we cater it around the people that we have,” Mouser said. “And for us, you have to find a way to create explosive plays, and when you don't have some of your most explosive athletes, like you didn't really have Chase, and we didn’t have Koby, it makes things hard.”

Without Howard and Sowell, the team spread the ball around more evenly, but also relied on the run game to get the job done. Tight end Benjamin Brahmer was the top receiver with 58 yards on four catches, while tight end Andrew Rappleyea had the only receiving touchdown.

Mouser said it was the same with the running back room, which saw Cam Wallace be the top rusher and James Peoples not get a carry.

“They know their number is going to get called,” Mouser said. “No different than you know it is with the running back situation. You might have a carry or two carries, and you have to take advantage of the opportunity that you have because (Howard and Sowell) are going to come back, and you don't know if your opportunity is going to be there or not if you don't take advantage of it now.”

title: Penn State field hockey jumps two spots to No. 12 in latest NFHCA Poll
author: Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian
description:
Hannah Prince earned her signature win Friday night by upsetting then-No. 1 Northwestern, and the Nittany Lions were rewarded with a two-spot jump in the NFHCA rankings.

Penn State sits at No. 12 after ending the Wildcats’ 35-game Big Ten winning streak. In the 2-0 victory, Cooper Cutchins netted the first goal, and Lilly Holmes notched her first goal of the season.

Aby Deverka made seven saves, good for her eighth shutout of the season. The third-year goalkeeper earned Big Ten Defensive Player of the Week honors for her troubles.

Now, the Nittany Lions will face Iowa in the Big Ten Tournament at 5 p.m. on Wednesday.

title: Penn State field hockey’s Aby Deverka earns Big Ten defensive player of the week
author: Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian
description:
After shutting out then-No. 1 and two-time reigning national champion Northwestern, Aby Deverka earned Big Ten defensive player of the week honors, the conference announced Monday.

The third-year goalkeeper made seven saves and stuffed three Northwestern penalty corners. The victory ended the Wildcats’ 35-game unbeaten streak in conference play. As she secured the victory, Deverka also notched her 200th career save.

So far this season, the Houston native has put up a career low in goals-against average, at 1.114, and a career high in save percentage, at 0.779.

The Nittany Lions travel to the Big Ten Tournament this week and will open the event at 5 p.m. on Wednesday against Iowa.

title: Preview | No. 12 Penn State field hockey faces No. 10 Iowa in Big Ten Tournament opener
author: Gianna Dowling | Sports Editor
description:
Penn State is 9-1 since Sept. 28, with the lone loss being a 1-0 defeat to Iowa on Oct. 25. Well, the Big Ten field hockey gods have emerged, and now coach Hannah Prince and her squad have a chance to avenge the Hawkeyes.

This was one of just two conference defeats for the Nittany Lions, with the other coming against Maryland on Sept. 17.

The near-undefeated October earned the blue and white the No. 3 seed in the Big Ten Tournament. Iowa earned the No. 6 seed after finishing 4-4 in conference play.

This matchup marks Penn State’s first Big Ten Tournament appearance since 2023.

Penn State’s momentum

After defeating No. 1 Northwestern on Friday, the Nittany Lions have arguably more momentum than any other team in the country. This was the first win over a No. 1 team in program history, and it put the cherry on top of an amazing debut season for Prince.

Junior goalkeeper Aby Deverka recorded seven saves for her eighth shutout of the season, putting the Houston native first in the Big Ten in this category. Due to this performance, Deverka was named the Big Ten Defensive Player of the Week.

The Nittany Lions' late-season push has been led offensively by junior forward Ella Gaitan. The Belvidere, New Jersey, native is in the midst of a career season, owning 11 goals and 25 points on the 2026 campaign. However, Gaitan is scoreless in her last three games, which is her longest streak of the season without a goal.

Gaitan’s success has come thanks to the help of graduate midfielder Sienna Dunn. The Peel, Isle of Man, native owns 14 assists on the season with .82 per game, ranking second in the Big Ten and seventh nationally in this regard.

Scouting the Hawkeyes

Iowa enters the Big Ten Tournament after ending the regular season with a lopsided 5-1 loss to now No. 1 Maryland.

Offensively, the Hawkeyes are led by the dominant Dutch duo of Frederique van Cleef and Dionne van Aaslum, who are tied for the Big Ten lead in goals with 17 each. Additionally, van Cleef is tied for a team-high eight assists, and her 2.62 points per game rank second nationally. Her counterpart isn’t to far behind in points per game, as van Aaslum’s 2.31 average ranks eighth in Division I.

Time in the cage, Iowa has been largely split between freshman Julia Classens and junior Abby Johnson, with both appearing in nine games this season. Classens leads the two netminders with 41 saves compared to Johnson’s 19. The duo hasn’t stopped the ball from reaching the net to many times this season, combining for just three shutouts on the season.

Both goalkeepers appeared in the loss against the Terrapins. Classens started the game, but allowed three goals in the first quarter, calling for Johnson to replace the first year. Johnson eased the pain a little, recording two saves, but still allowed Maryland to find the back of the net twice.

Last time they met

When the Nittany Lions took a road trip to Iowa City on Oct. 25, they were in the midst of an eight-game win streak, but the Hawkeyes snapped it in a close battle.

Iowa took the win after van Aaslum scored a goal in the third period. The Hawkeyes outshot Penn State 15-7, and five of the blue and white’s shots were game-winners in the final frame.

Deverka recorded four saves for the Nittany Lions, and Classens had three of her own. This meeting marked Classens' lone shutout of the season.

Penn State did anything but fall after this defeat, winning its last two games of the season to help secure a top-three seed in Prince’s first Big Ten Tournament.

The Nittany Lions and Hawkeyes will face off at 5 p.m. Wednesday in Columbus, Ohio.

title: Nittany Lions in the NFL | S Zakee Wheatley has career milestone, TE Mike Gesicki continues touchdown streak
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Many former Penn Staters took the field over the weekend in the NFL, with some continuing strong campaigns through Week 8.

From a pair of Carolina Panthers safeties to tight end Mike Gesicki extending his touchdown streak, there was a lot that went down for former Nittany Lions as the season hit the halfway point.

Here’s who stood out in Week 8 of the NFL season.

Zakee Wheatley, Nick Scott, safeties, Carolina Panthers

The Panthers have a pair of former Penn Staters in the back end of the secondary, and both of them made an impact in Carolina’s loss to the Green Bay Packers.

Safety Zakee Wheatley made his presence known with his first interception of the year. On a deep pass attempt, Wheatley picked off Green Bay quarterback Jordan Love, marking his second forced turnover of his rookie season.

Nick Scott has also played a hand in some major plays for the Panthers this year. Scott forced a fumble in the second quarter to end a Packers drive that entered Carolina territory.

While both players had big plays on Thursday, it wasn’t enough to propel the Panthers to a victory, with Carolina losing, 27-19.

Mike Gesicki, tight end, Cincinnati Bengals

Gesicki has continued his impressive year as one of Joe Burrow’s favorite targets.

In the Bengals’ win over the Tennessee Titans, Gesicki caught four passes for 76 yards and a touchdown. His 25-yard touchdown reception marked the fifth straight game where he found the end zone.

Gesicki now leads the league in touchdown receptions by a tight end with six, while amounting 241 receiving yards. He’s provided additional threats for the Bengals’ offense, alongside wide receivers Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins.

Kaytron Allen, running back, Miami Dolphins

Running back Kaytron Allen made his presence felt on special teams on Sunday. He totaled two tackles with the Miami Dolphins, both of which came on punt coverage to take down one of the more explosive return men in New England Patriots’ Marcus Jones.

Allen has yet to record any rushing yards with the Dolphins after they acquired him off waivers from the Washington Commanders on Oct. 9. He has totaled 41 rushing yards on the season, all with Washington.

Pat Freiermuth, tight end, Pittsburgh Steelers

Another tight end who’s found his footing in the AFC North, Pat Freiermuth reached the end zone once again, this time in a unique way.

As time was expiring before the half, the Pittsburgh Steelers lined up in the tush push formation, with Freiermuth taking the snap. He was pushed into the end zone by fellow tight end Darnell Washington, recording his fifth total touchdown of the year.

Freiermuth was limited through the air, catching two passes for 35 yards, but his 28-yard reception was vital to his eventual rushing touchdown to end the half, giving the Steelers a comfortable 20-6 lead.

Jahan Dotson, wide receiver, Atlanta Falcons

Wide receiver Jahan Dotson was the recipient of a massive completion in the Atlanta Falcons’ rainy game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

Dotson was one of two players in the game to have more than one reception, and his 76-yard catch pushed him to 95 yards on the game on two catches.

The former Nittany Lion’s 337 yards on the season is second on the Falcons behind wide receiver Drake London. His two receiving touchdowns are also second on the team, proving to be a reliable threat for quarterback Michael Penix Jr.

Odafe Oweh, outside linebacker, Washington Commanders

Outside linebacker Odafe Oweh has settled in nicely with his new team. Oweh signed a 4-year, $100 million contract with the Commanders in the offseason, and he’s picked up his production as of late.

In the Commanders’ victory over the Philadelphia Eagles, Oweh recorded a sack and two tackles as the Eagles’ offense couldn’t get much going with backup quarterback Tanner McKee.

On the season, Oweh has notched four sacks, including one in each of his last two games.

Chop Robinson, edge rusher, Miami Dolphins

Another former Penn State pass rusher had himself a strong day against the Patriots.

Edge rusher Chop Robinson was constantly pressuring quarterback Drake Maye on Sunday. In the loss to the Patriots, Robinson totaled two sacks and three tackles, doubling his sack total on the season.

Additionally, Robinson recorded eight pressures with a 47.1% pressure rate, which was the second highest pressure rate of any NFL defender this season. The former Nittany Lion has started to find more consistency rushing the passer in the past couple weeks after a slower start to the season.

title: Penn State’s Beatlemania club invites people to ‘Come Together’
author: Emily Nowikowski | For the Collegian
description:
When The Beatles’ popularity swept the United States in the 60s, it came with screaming crowds, mobbed airports and sold out record stores. This craze, the blueprint for modern day fandom, had a name: Beatlemania.

Today’s students weren’t around to witness The Beatles on a rooftop, line up when ‘A Hard Day’s Night’ hit theaters or catch one of the band’s packed concerts. However, Penn State’ first official Beatles fan club, called Beatlemania, evidently, is keeping the buzz alive.

Winding down from a long day of classes by discussing their favorite aspects of the band is what the club’s all about, Zoe DePaul, its president and founder, said. DePaul became interested in the band after she watched their musical comedy film “A Hard Day’s Night.”

Beatlemania has already hosted several events, with more in mind for the rest of the school year.

“My favorite night has been either our show-and-tell or our pin-making night,” DePaul, 19, of Philadelphia, said. “We had a piece of John Lennon's hair at the show and tell night.”

Although the club is still in its early stages, it's already looking to grow. The executive board is hoping to bring in guest speakers to talk about the era and take a trip to the “The Fest for Beatles’ Fans” in New York City next year.

At its last meeting, members listened to the album “Rubber Soul.” After each song, the club discussed their thoughts, and executive members shared facts about the album. At another meeting, the club had a watch-party of one of The Beatles’ official films, “Help!”

“It's kind of a different crowd for each week,” DePaul, a second-year studying marketing, said. “That's definitely my favorite because I'm personally a very big fan of people.”

DePaul said that to her, The Beatles represent culture and said that this was a hard pivot for bands in this time period. She said that The Beatles represent unity — especially within the fan culture — which is why she chose to become a fan and start the club in the first place.

The club is open to both super fans and casual fans alike, something Sean Dufifie, 23, of Milford, Pennsylvania, said he enjoys about the meetings. He also enjoys meeting new members and having the opportunity to discuss The Beatles — one of his favorite bands — with others who may not know as much.

“They make it very clear that you don't have to be the biggest super fan in order to (contribute) to the discussion,” Dufifie, a third-year studying criminology, said. “Regardless of your commitment to the fabulous four, it's welcome for everyone.”

Treasurer Megan Yeckley, 18, of Quaker City, Ohio, joined the club because she’s excited about meeting new people and seeing what college has in store, she said.

“It's brought me a bunch of new friends that we could just bond over our shared likeness of the band,” Yeckley, a first-year studying music education, said.

The executive team is also working to gain more fundraising for the club in the future. They have a battle of the bands-style fundraising event coming up, Yeckley said, and they’re planning on having local bands perform Beatles covers.

Vice President Emily Ledbetter said she felt nervous coming to school at Penn State because she didn’t know what to expect. She wasn’t sure if she’d find any Beatles fans, let alone clubs, on campus. But finding a place in Beatlemania has helped settle her nerves.

“I thought it was nice to have everyone just sit, watch the movie together and have some notes on it,” Ledbetter, 18, of Fort Lauderdale, Florida, said.

The club’s advisor, Andrew Lawrence Whyte (Andy), who is an Operations Supervisor at the Bryce Jordan Center, has been a great help and support system for the club, according to Ledbetter. She said that he goes above and beyond by bringing in memorabilia and items from The Beatles era to show or give to the club.

Penn State’s Beatlemania meets every Thursday at 6 p.m. in Willard 071. Everyone is welcome, and there’s an interest form on the club’s Instagram for new members.

“It's been really great meeting all these people and becoming their friends and just seeing everyone's different backgrounds,” Ledbetter said. “But we all connect to one thing, which is The Beatles.”

title: Column | You remove your own power by not voting
author: Teresa Phelan | Opinions Editor
description:
We’re heading into midterm elections with President Donald Trump sitting at a 32% approval rating, according to a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll, and a Republican congressional trifecta. The state of the country may seem hopeless or as if change is impossible — I think most people would agree to that. In times when any hope of decent public officials feels nearly impossible, the power goes back into the hands of the people.

Maybe this prospect is even scarier: letting the fate of your state fall into the hands of people who, up until last week, didn’t even know when election day was, or the girl who told a Penn State Votes volunteer she would vote “for whoever would keep drink prices down.”

While the joke she thought would land warranted no laughs from anyone around, she represents a large microcosm of people who think their place in politics is nonexistent; that hold a belief that voting is reserved for a certain facet of the population that doesn’t include them. The same people who can’t be bothered to vote often have the most to say.

Voting on Tuesday isn’t going to rewire our political system, but if you want change, whether it be the faces in office or legislation that needs a facelift, you have to vote. You’re allowed to be frustrated with the political system, and you’re allowed to feel disappointed in the candidates available to you and you’re allowed to feel like neither party adequately represents your beliefs and values, but do not mistake your frustration for powerlessness.

Depending on where you're registered to vote, there’s a lot on the ballot, from governors to Senate seats. You don’t get a say if you aren’t participating in the system intended to help create the very change you’re hoping to see. (Remember those posters they taught you in history class that said, “No taxation without representation?”)

Half the battle is understanding what you want, what your candidate actually endorses and the viewpoints you hold on certain issues. Voting based on your friends, social media, or what you assume a party or person represents doesn’t make you an educated voter, but it does make you part of the problem.

Regardless of gender, age, race, sex, or sexuality, the ability to vote isn’t a privilege you should take lightly. Generations of Americans, especially women, have fought tirelessly for the right, an incomprehensible right to citizens of some other nations. (I know this isn’t the most empathetic country in the world, so it can be difficult for many to reconcile the sacrifices made by those before us and the apathy that surrounds civic responsibility today.)

Regardless of whether you show your face at the polling booths, you’re not removed from the consequences of an election. Instead, you’ve removed yourself from the process.

In the 2024 presidential election, 53% of eligible college students voted, according to CIRCLE's National Study of Learning, Voting, and Engagement at Tufts University, but as we know, the turnout is not going to be as dense for midterms.

Just because it’s not the president doesn’t mean it’s unimportant. In Texas, Michigan and Ohio, Democrats James Talarico, Abdul El-Sayed and Amy Acton, respectively, will battle to steal the power from their Republican counterparts, Ken Paxton, Mike Rogers and Vivek Ramaswamy.

I don’t think one election is going to fix everything. We’ll still have political division that creates nationwide animosity and, for many, dwindling faith in our current administration. But there’s one thing that remains pretty clear: Our civic duty doesn’t discriminate and voting is bipartisan.

Don’t expect change in a system you refuse to engage with. You cannot expect your interests to be prioritized if you never make an effort to represent them yourself. How are you going to complain that nobody is listening when you don’t speak up?

Our representatives only have power because we gave it to them, so the power really belongs to us. I understand it isn’t always obvious, and as we’ve seen, it certainly doesn’t guarantee the outcomes we hoped for.

It still exists. Tuesday is an opportunity to exercise it.

title: Penn State men’s soccer travels to face No. 11 Maryland in season finale
author: Luci Palacios | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State travels to College Park, Maryland, Wednesday to take on No. 11 Maryland at 8 p.m. at Ludwig Field.

The Nittany Lions are 3-8-3 overall and 0-6-3 in the Big Ten, but they will look to carry momentum from their most recent victory into a matchup against one of the nation’s top-ranked teams. Maryland is 10-4-1 overall and 4-4-1 in the Big Ten and enters the contest with a strong home record, going 7-1-1 at Ludwig Field.

Maryland holds a 25-21-9 advantage in the all-time series against Penn State. The teams last met in a 2-2 draw at Jeffrey Field, with neither side able to come away with a victory. The Nittany Lions will look to earn a road win and hold off the No. 11 Terrapins.

Maryland looks to defend home turf

Maryland is coming off a 2-1 road loss to then-No. 7 Washington on Oct. 30. The Terrapins outshot the Huskies 10-5 in the first half but conceded the opening goal in the 31st minute. Washington added another goal early in the second half before Maryland responded through Rodrigo Neri.

Neri recorded his eighth goal of the season, leading the Terrapins in scoring and ranking tied third in the Big Ten in goals. Midfielder Henry Bernstein assisted on the goal, marking his team-leading ninth assist of the season. Bernstein is tied 10th nationally in assists and leads the Big Ten in the category.

Said El Eyssami also provides an offensive threat for Maryland, ranking second on the team with five goals.

The Terrapins outshot Washington 19-15 overall, but goalkeeper Laurin Mack was kept busy, recording seven saves in the loss.

Mack has been a key presence in Maryland’s goal this season, totaling 70 saves while allowing 24 goals. His 70 saves rank atop the Big Ten and 10th nationally, while his 4.67 saves-per-game average also leads the conference. Mack was also named Big Ten Goalkeeper of the Week on Oct. 27, earning the honor for the second time this season and fifth time in his career.

Nittany Lions aim to carry momentum

Penn State enters Wednesday’s contest following a 3-1 victory over Duquesne on Oct. 28. The win marked a strong offensive performance for the Nittany Lions, who outshot the Dukes 15-8 and scored all three goals in the first half.

This improved the blue and white’s home record to 3-5-1, but its away record is 0-3-2, meaning Penn State will have to battle uphill at Maryland.

This win marked the Nittany Lions’ first win since early September against Yale, which was a 1-0 win at home.

Junior Etienne Reck opened the scoring just two minutes into the contest, finding the back of the net off an assist from Noah Förster. Reck’s goal marked his fourth of the season.

Penn State doubled its lead in the 36th minute when Joe Buckley scored off an assist from Peter Doran. It was Buckley’s second goal of the season.

The Nittany Lions added a third goal in the 42nd minute after a Duquesne player received a red card. Grant McIntosh converted the resulting penalty kick, sending the ball into the roof of the net for the first goal of his career.

Sophomore Justin Ross also made his first career appearance between the posts, recording four saves in the victory.

The blue and white will look to carry that offensive production into Wednesday’s matchup against a Maryland team that has scored consistently this season and boasts a strong home record.

Maryland also has a tough goalkeeper to get by, meaning they’ll have to finish the ball whenever possible and keep Mack busy.

title: Advisors, faculty say students can start building professional careers in class
author: Isabella Gearhart | For The Collegian
description:
Sooner or later, every student gets asked what they plan to do after graduating. At Penn State, students thinking about it have a few places to start.

While students have Penn State’s explicit resources on hand as they navigate entering the professional scene, they also have the extensive alumni network and rich variety of faculty members that also serves as a guide. Several Penn State faculty and staff members said networking is a large part of building professional careers, but more goes into it too.

Malia Brown, an academic advisor at Penn State, said developing a professional identity takes time and practice, especially for students entering unfamiliar environments.

“The best thing that you can do is just practice,” Brown, 25, of State College, Pennsylvania, said. “The way you communicate with your professors is just one example of how you’re going to learn how to be professional.”

Brown emphasized the importance of maintaining a consistent professional image across all settings. A student’s online presence can play a crucial role in shaping how others perceive them, both professionally and personally.

“The way that you're marketing yourself in person should reflect on your social media,” Brown said. “Does that mean you shouldn’t have fun or post things where you’re enjoying your life? No, it doesn’t mean that, but you shouldn’t have to post everything and have that digital footprint for everyone to see.”

Matt McAllister, interim head of the Department of Film Production and Media Studies at Penn State, offered a different perspective on personal branding.

“I personally am skeptical of the word ‘brand’ to describe a person because I think really what that is, is what is their personhood? That is, what makes them a unique person,” McAllister, 65, of State College, Pennsylvania, said.

McAllister said students should consider their passions, involvement and personalities when developing their identities, rather than focusing on how others perceive them. He said students who demonstrate confidence in their interests can form a stronger sense of individuality.

Brown said she originally entered college hoping to become a dentist but later discovered that her interests and professional goals were different.

When she came to Penn State, she said she was nervous everyone had figured out what they wanted to go, while she hadn’t. She said exploring opportunities in writing and news, as well as speaking with professors and advisors, could have helped her discover her interests sooner.

“Start seeing what your likes and dislikes are,” Brown said. “Then you can start building a foundation of what you want to accomplish within your college years.”

McAllister said students can begin establishing their professional reputations through everyday classroom interactions. He encouraged students to participate in classroom discussions, express interest in course materials and communicate with professors, even if they're uncomfortable speaking in front of others.

He also highlighted the value of utilizing connections that can be formed in classrooms, clubs and even off-campus settings.

“Students shouldn’t be shy about talking to professors and getting to know them because they might have a lot of insight into the things that you might want to do,” McAllister said.

McAllister said when he was younger, he wished he would have explored his passions even more and looked for opportunities to become involved in activities that interested him.

“I would say cultivate your areas of passion, and think about what excites you and how to get involved in that,” McAllister said.

Bob Martin, the assistant dean for internships and career placement at Penn State, said students should begin by identifying their career interests before pursuing internships.

“Start writing down your interests. When you see something and go, ‘That sounds intriguing, I think I’d like to explore that a little more,’ write it down,” Martin, 60, of State College, Pennsylvania, said.

Martin said experimenting with different internships and extracurricular activities can help students discover their career interests and learn from different experiences.

Students with limited professional experience, Martin said, should get involved with clubs and classroom projects to demonstrate relevant skills to potential employers.

“They do want to hire somebody who can tell that positive story of all the growth they’ve gotten from all those different experiences,” Martin said.

Martin said students need to develop career-ready skills, such as communication, leadership and critical thinking. He also said students should tailor their resumes toward specific career interests.

“If you’ve got three different interests, you should have three different resumes,” Martin said.

Martin said he wished his younger self would’ve recognized the importance of exploring interests without feeling pressured to determine an entire career path immediately. He said students should focus on communicating what they have learned, rather than dwelling on uncertainty about their futures.

“Finding what you don’t want to do is just as important as finding what you want to do,” Martin said. “Sometimes it takes multiple steps to really get where you want to go with your first destination after graduation.”

title: Recruiting roundup | 4-star CB Kei’Shjuan Telfair headlines visitors to Penn State’s first Big Ten win
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State hosted a number of recruits and a top-100 prospect in the Class of 2029 for its win over Purdue, 31-17, to claim a first victory in the Big Ten under Matt Campbell.

4-star cornerback Kei’Shjuan Telfair was the top commit present on Saturday night while a few potential flip targets got to see a losing streak snapped.

Additionally, 247Sports 4-star defensive end Tristan Alexander, the No. 2 player in Pennsylvania’s 2029 class, was in attendance, marking a big chance for Penn State to leave a good first impression on the Philadelphia native.

Here’s who was in attendance for Penn State’s first conference victory.

Commits watch first Big Ten win

Four current Penn State commits were at Beaver Stadium to witness the Nittany Lions’ beat Purdue.

Telfair headlined the list as the No. 3 player out of Ohio, No. 10 cornerback and No. 93 player nationally, per 247Sports composite. He’s the only commit to break the top-100 in Penn State’s 2027 class and hadn’t attended a game since the Nittany Lions beat Marshall in Week 1.

3-star cornerback Dhillon McGee returned to Beaver Stadium for his second-straight week while 3-star offensive lineman Jon Sassic was in Happy Valley for his third game in a row. McGee ranks as the No. 62 player out of Texas and No. 50 cornerback in the country. He transferred this year to Texas-powerhouse DeSoto High School.

Sassic suffered a season-ending injury before the start of his senior season at Pittsburgh Central Catholic. He now sits at the No. 28 spot in Pennsylvania and No. 60 spot among the nation’s offensive linemen.

3-star kicker Carter Petri was the only commit in the 2028 class to visit Beaver Stadium on Saturday. He’s the No. 2 kicker in the nation and No. 7 player out of New York, and Kohl’s Kicking ranked him a 4.5-star recruit after an impressive showing at the 2026 Kohl's Eastern Spring Showcase.

Flip targets

A pair of potential flip targets were treated to a Penn State victory on Saturday.

3-star wide receiver Arnold Mugerwa, who’s been committed to Rutgers since June 4, was at the game. Mugerwa’s a local of Johnstown, Pennsylvania, and Penn State is trending toward flipping him after Campbell offered him on Oct. 25.

Mugerwa is ranked as the No. 15 player out of Pennsylvania and No. 64 wide receiver in the nation. He has 625 receiving yards and eight touchdowns on 46 receptions in his senior year at Richland and has one rushing touchdown.

3-star defensive lineman Jayden Paulino was also at Beaver Stadium. He committed to Boston College on June 17, but Campbell hasn’t yet offered the New Jersey native.

Top-3 player in Pennsylvania tops 2029 class visitors

Alexander watched Penn State’s pass rush pressure Purdue quarterback Ryan Browne six times on Saturday. Not only is he the No. 2 player out of Pennsylvania in his class, he’s the No. 8 edge rusher and No. 67 player in the nation.

Alexander’s stats back up his national ranking, as he owns 58 tackles, 15 tackles for loss, 10 sacks, 19 quarterback hurries and a fumble recovery touchdown on the season with Imhotep Charter, the fifth-ranked team in the state.

He was offered by Penn State on Oct. 20 and has 19 total offers including Alabama, Texas, Michigan and Ole Miss.

title: Penn State men’s basketball forward Roko Prkačin is ‘kind of like LeBron James’
author: Will Horstman | The Daily Collegian
description:
Roko Prkačin was a man among boys at the Bryce Jordan Center on Monday night. The 23-year-old forward just kept making physical play after physical play to lead Penn State to a 97-57 win over Canisius.

Prkačin came close to not being able to play. Just three days before dropping 28 points in the Nittany Lions’ season opener, he was cleared to play by the NCAA after making the jump from professional basketball overseas.

“It was stressful at times,” Prkačin said. “Our focus was here on the court every day to get better, and we had an administration team do their job, and everything became great.”

That excitement was evident. Once Prkačin first came off the bench with 16:44 left in the first half, he soon gathered an offensive rebound and scored on a put-back jumper. He then blocked a layup before draining a layup of his own on the other end.

At times, Prkačin played on an entirely different level than anyone else on the court. LeBron James was mentioned in the postgame press conference because of Prkačin.

“Roko's really versatile,” forward Josh Reed said. “I think everyone saw that tonight. He can play inside and out. He can score the ball, read on the ball and also make plays for others. Kind of like LeBron James in a way. That's kind of what he added to this year's team.”

Prkačin was heavily guarded by two Canisius players on the baseline midway through the first half, but that didn’t stop him. He dribbled past them both and hit one of his highlight dunks of the night, electrifying the home fans.

The Zagreb, Croatia, native had back-to-back dunks in the second half. He was a walking highlight machine, as it felt like everything was going his way in his collegiate debut.

Prkačin shot 12-of-14 from the field with six total rebounds and a block. He had four offensive rebounds which all turned into baskets for himself, showcasing a physical playstyle in the paint. And not to mention, he did all of this in 20 minutes.

“I was very proud of him,” Mike Rhoades said. “I thought our guys did a good job of getting him the ball and sometimes just really quick opportunities to score. He has really good hands, really good feet, and he could find different ways to score. You saw that with some of his footwork and moves, and he's really good in transition in the open court as well.”

When Rhoades found out that Prkačin was cleared to play by the NCAA, he called him and said “freedom.” He said he yelled that to him “like Braveheart.” It was more than just getting the full roster available for the season opener. It was getting Prkačin, a former professional player, officially cleared to play in the NCAA.

Rhoades remembered his phone calls to Prkačin while he was recruiting him. What stuck out to him was how receptive he was.

“My conversations with him when he was back home led to more than just basketball,” Rhoades said. “It was really cool.He's a mature kid. He wants to learn about a lot of things, even outside of basketball. He was eager. He's had a really cool journey as a basketball player, but also some ups and downs.”

Prkačin played for Nanterre 92 of Pro A, the top professional league in France, before coming to Penn State. He’s been a professional player since the 2020-21 season, and he was once considered an NBA lottery pick.

When he joined the Nittany Lions this offseason, Prkačin said the coaching staff wanted him to become even more physical. He had just played 28 games in one of the best overseas professional leagues, but the staff wanted him to be tougher.

It worked, because Prkačin was the most physical player of the win with his highlight-reel dunks and tough rebounds.

“I took it personally kind of, and I think it helped me a lot,” Prkačin said. “I'll try to stay consistent on that throughout the whole year.”

title: Penn State women's volleyball earns 2 weekly Big Ten awards
author: Daniel Almash | For the Collegian
description:
Penn State ended this week with two wins over Ohio State and Purdue, extending its winning streak to five matches and earning conference accolades in the process.

On Monday, senior right side hitter Kennedy Martin, and freshman Middlem blocker Kendall Northern both took home weekly conference honors. For Martin, it’s her second straight Big Ten Player of the Week award, and fifth of her blue and white tenure.

Across eight sets Martin averaged 5.25 kills per set, hit for .337%, posted 6.50 points per set and 1.50 blocks per set.

In Penn State’s two matches this past week, Northern recorded 13 total blocks, 12 total kills, 1.63 blocks per set, all while recording her first career service ace against Purdue on Saturday.

For the blue and white, these are the third and fourth total conference accolades this season after Alexis Stucky earned Setter of the Week honors earlier this season.

title: ‘We got to be really physical’ | Hard-nosed defense propels Penn State men’s basketball in season-opener
author: Myles Hannak | The Daily Collegian
description:
All offseason, Mike Rhoades preached about the need to be physical and to have depth of talent.

In Penn State’s 97-57 season-opening win, the new-look Nittany Lions showed both in a complete rout of Canisius. Once the blue and white took a lead after just over two minutes of play, Rhoades never looked back as his squad completely shut down all the Golden Griffins threw at them.

“It’s nice to have you don't have to hide somebody on defense. That was something last year we had to do with multiple guys; that was really hard,” Rhoades said. “This year we have multiple guys that can guard multiple positions and are physical and have some length and go for the ball. We got to be more physical than we were tonight, and when we're punching up in weight class, we got to be really, really connected.”

The blue and white only returned three players this year: fifth-year forward Josh Reed, big man Ivan Jurić and guard Reggie Grodin, who redshirted last season. What was once the youngest unit in the Big Ten by far has completely changed, now with an average age of 21 and almost the entire roster having previous collegiate or international experience.

“We have a ton of versatile guys, a lot of older guys who have been in college for a long time,” Reed said. “We got a lot more size on this year's team as well, which I feel like allows us to switch one through four.”

Fifth-year newcomer Roko Prkacin led the blue and white offense with 28 points on 12-of-14 shooting, with almost all the Zagreb, Croatia, native’s points coming at the rack. Fellow Zagreb native, 7-footer Ivan Jurić snagged a career-high 15 rebounds off the glass.

“I think we are trying to be physical and be aggressive, but we also want to be smart,” Prkacin said.

The Golden Griffins were held to 39.2% from the field and 18.2% from downtown while also logging 17 turnovers, which led to 21 Penn State points off of possession changes. Despite the swarming defense and offense, the blue and white only fouled sparsely, sending its opponents to the charity stripe only nine times compared to its own 29 free throws.

“We turn them over on deflections, and some of our switching causes confusion and all that stuff,” Rhoades said. “I think we have some guys individually that can swipe at the ball and make some plays. We had a couple traps.”

Penn State dominated from inside the paint with its intensity, as over 60% of its points came from inside, with a 45-28 rebound advantage and a total of 24 second-chance points. The depth also showed through, with 14 total players appearing for the Nittany Lions and 53 total bench points.

With that depth, Rhoades deployed multiple looks against Canisius, and nearly every player contributed defensively; eight players logged a steal in the win. Miami (OH) transfer forward Brant Byers and Grodin led those efforts with a pair each.

“If you're not big and strong and physical in our league, you get bludgeoned. So we have to be flying around, and we have to play really, really hard,” Rhoades said. “... We got to be really physical and strong and knock people off their path and off their block; we have to. If not, they're going to do it to you.”

title: Shooting struggles loom large in Penn State women’s basketball season opening loss
author: Gianna Dowling | Sports Editor
description:
Penn State opened its 2026-27 campaign on Monday night, welcoming Cleveland State to the Bryce Jordan Center. While the season opener marked the start of a new chapter for the Lady Lions, it also marked the debut of first-year head coach Tanisha Wright.

“It was great to get that first one under the belt,” Wright said. “We've talked about this on and on, about the support that we're going to need from our fans through the ups, through the downs, and so it was really cool to see so many familiar faces out there in that crowd.”

Despite the long-awaited return, Penn State fell 62-61 to Cleveland State in a tight contest that featured sloppy offense.

“Who we are, who we are today, won't be who we are in December, but you know, it's better to learn your lessons from wins than it is from losses, obviously,” Wright said. “But we'll grow from this; we'll be able to get better from this.”

For the blue and white, these offensive struggles and inconsistency proved to be the biggest obstacle as Penn State struggled to find consistent rhythm and posted a poor shooting effort.

The Lady Lions finished with 31.8% from the field and connected on only six of 27 attempts from beyond the arc.

Penn State struggled to find ways to score when perimeter shots weren’t falling and Wright acknowledged that her team could’ve done a better job of moving the ball rather than settling for difficult attempts.

“I thought we could have worked the ball a little bit more, moved the ball, been patient a couple times, and maybe try to get easier shots at times, especially when our outside shots weren't falling,” Wright said. “That's a lesson for a brand new team learning, learning each other, learning themselves, and we'll grow and we'll get better in that area.”

The first-half numbers highlighted Penn State’s struggles as the Lady Lions made just eight field goals in the opening half and were 1-of-13 from three-point range.

“We just need to tighten up on little things,” sophomore guard Ava Black said. “Everything is very fixable, correctable, just little things.”

Penn State showed signs of improvement coming out of halftime, putting together its strongest stretch of the evening in the third quarter. In this frame, the Lady Lions shot 47.1% from the field.

“I feel like we definitely had good moments,” Black said. “A lot of things we practiced came to light. We also just missed a lot of easy shots."

While its field-goal percentage improved significantly after halftime, the blue and white couldn’t maintain efficiency at the foul line.

After going 8-of-9 from the charity stripe in the first half, Penn State’s accuracy dropped to 5-of-10 in the second. This drop became a key factor in a one-point win.

Although the result wasn’t what Wright envisioned for her first game at the helm of her alma mater, the opener offered an opportunity for the new-look Lady Lions to identify areas that need improvement.

“Lots and lots of growth for us and a lot of work for us to be able to do moving forward, but still confident in this group and what they're capable of doing,” Wright said. “We got to have a short-term memory, be able to bounce back and prepare for the next game.”

title: Tanisha Wright’s Happy Valley homecoming spoiled, Penn State women’s basketball drops season opener
author: Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian
description:
As the roars of Cleveland State’s celebration filled the bowels of the stadium, Tanisha Wright faced the difficult reality of dropping her first game as the head coach of her alma mater.

“Obviously disappointed with the outcome,” Wright said. “Lots, lots and lots of growth for us, and a lot of work for us to be able to do moving forward, but still confident in this group and what they're capable of doing.”

In her return to Happy Valley, Wright saw a strong contingent of fans rocking the number 33. Sitting courtside, two women showed off a “Welcome Home Tanisha Wright” sign, and a number of fans donned shirts reading “here for coach T.”

Additionally, Brad Troyan showed up in a Wright jersey from her Penn State playing days. Troyan, 41, of Philadelphia, described Wright as “one of my good friends.”

He attended Penn State with Wright and said he was “very excited” to see her back inside the Bryce Jordan Center.

“I remember her passion,” Troyan said about Wright’s collegiate career. “She loved Penn State, and she loved the game of basketball, and just her energy and her passion.”

Wright appreciated both the energy and passion of her cheering section throughout the game. She also got the loudest roar of anyone announced during the starting lineups.

“It was great,” Wright said. “It was great to get that first one under the belt and get it done. Obviously, we've talked about this on and on about the support that we're going to need from our fans through the ups, through the downs, and so it was really cool to see so many familiar faces out there in that crowd supporting. So, (I’m) excited for them and for our team.”

That excitement couldn’t translate to strong play on the floor, as the blue and white trailed in every quarter of its 62-61 loss to the Vikings and never led by more than four points.

Wright didn’t call a timeout until there were 50 seconds left in the fourth quarter, then she used every one she had and more the rest of the way. First, she called a timeout and set up Enjulina Gonzalez to get downhill off of a Petra Božan handoff, but the play stalled out, and the Lady Lions were forced to take another timeout.

“It was more just (that) we weren't as organized as we needed to be coming out of the timeout, and instead of wasting a possession, I had another timeout, so I just called another one instead of wasting the possession,” Wright said.

Later, Penn State came out of its third timeout looking for Devyn Quigley through an elevator screen or Ava Black. Gonzalez couldn’t get a pass off, and the Lady Lions were called for a five-second violation.

“I thought the opportunity was there to make that inbounds pass, and (Gonzalez) didn't feel comfortable,” Wright said. “She couldn't find what she was looking for, but we as a team just have to be more alert in those situations, and the most important thing in that situation is (to) get the ball in.”

Wright’s squad managed to set up yet another side-out-of-bounds play with a timeout with 22 seconds on the clock. With a very similar build to the first set piece, Wright schemed up a wide-open three for Quigley on the right wing, which missed long.

The rebound was deflected out of bounds, and the call went in favor of the Vikings. Without a timeout in her pocket, Wright decided to appeal the call and lost, which earned Penn State a technical foul. Cleveland State’s lead grew to five with 14 seconds to play, and the Lady Lions never regained the lead.

Ultimately, Wright chalked up the unexpected loss as a learning experience for her still-gelling team.

“I think it was a good first lesson for them to have learned, (and) for myself to have learned, not just them,” Wright said. “We got to have a short-term memory, be able to bounce back and prepare for the next game.”

That next game will come on Saturday when the Lady Lions travel to Cincinnati to take on the Bearcats at 2 p.m.

title: Penn State women's basketball falls to Cleveland State in disappointing season-opener
author: Nick Myers | For The Collegian
description:
Suiting up for their first home game in the Tanisha Wright era, the Lady Lions weren’t able to pull out a win against the Cleveland State Vikings led by Macie Taylor.

The foes spoiled the debut of the blue and white’s new coach, with a 62-61 win in Happy Valley.

Taylor, a grad student making her first appearance as a Viking after transferring from the Miami (OH) Redhawks over the offseason, led the game in points with 20, shooting 50% from the field, along with six rebounds and five assists.

Chloe Oliver and Sarah Hurley each contributed nine points, and Paula Pique led the team in rebounds with nine rebounds.

For the Nittany Lions, Ava Black led the team in both scoring and on the glass with her debut double-double, putting up 17 points and 10 rebounds.

Devyn Quigley, after getting into foul trouble and shooting just 1-for-6 to start, finished with 12 points, all in the second half.

Cristen Carter and Savannah White also dominated the glass, each contributing eight rebounds.

The Vikings, coming off a 26-10 season last year and with a chance to start their new season off strong, struggled heavily in the first half. Despite a game-opening three from Sarah Hurley to take the early lead, their offense ran dry for the rest of the half, shooting for a combined 9-of-31 from the field, with just 25% from behind the arc.

The Lady Lions were no better, shooting an abysmal 24% from the field, with just one made three across 13 attempts.

Keeping players out of foul trouble was another consistent problem for the Lady Lions offense. After two quick fouls from Quigley and Enjulina Gonzalez, they were limited for the remainder of the first half. Wright later mentioned their absence as a major factor in their early struggles.

To close the first half, after tough battles at the rim on both ends, the Vikings finished with a 27-25 lead, keeping things well within reach for the Lady Lions.

In the third quarter, it’s clear their time in the locker room paid off, as the Lady Lions went out shooting just under 50% from the field on 8-of-17 shooting. Quigley led the offensive surge with seven points after being benched due to fouls for most of the first half.

The Vikings found a surge of their own in the third, going on multiple runs throughout the quarter thanks to some tough shots from Taylor and Sarah Hurley.

Going into the fourth quarter, the score was tied 44-44 after a tough driving layup from Quigley, who showed her ability to get inside the defense and finish in the paint.

This offensive showing was far from over, though, as Sylvia Gonzalez and Sarah Hurley combined for three quick triples in the first two minutes to make it 47-44.

The game stayed close until roughly the minute mark, when the Vikings broke through for a seven-point lead with just 14 seconds left.

Despite a series of sloppy turnovers and a failed challenge resulting in a technical foul as they had used up all of their timeouts, the Lady Lions showed they wouldn’t quit that easily.

With less than 10 seconds off the clock, Quigley connected for her second three of the game, making the score 62-58. This was immediately followed by a quick turnover from Skylar Durley, now giving Penn State the ball down four with seven seconds remaining.

The Lady Lions followed up with another clutch triple from Ava Black, cutting what was a seven-point lead down to just one in four seconds.

After a quick foul on the Lady Lions, Taylor was sent to the line for the fifth time. Despite going 7-of-8 beforehand, Taylor missed both of her free throws and gave Penn State the ball in transition with four seconds remaining, and only down a point.

The Lady Lions didn’t capitalize, however, as the Vikings' defense didn’t even allow them to attempt a shot in time, finishing the game 62-61.

Despite the many problems offensively, Wright described all of their problems as “Very Fixable.”

“The team we are now is not the team we will be in December,” Wright said.

Up Next

The Penn State Lady Lions will continue their schedule with a three-game road stint, kicking off against the Cincinnati Bearcats at 2 p.m. on Saturday.

title: Debutant Roko Prkačin explodes, Penn State men’s basketball routs Canisius in season opener
author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian
description:
When Roko Prkačin failed to appear in either of Penn State’s preseason exhibitions, Mike Rhoades said that he was “honoring the process” when it came to the international prospect’s eligibility.

Monday night proved the wait was worth it.

Prkačin burst onto the scene with 28 points as the Nittany Lions cruised to a 97-57 win over Canisius in their tenth consecutive season-opening victory.

“He's not a good kid, he's an awesome kid,” Rhoades said of Prkačin. “He wants to be coached hard, he wants to get better, he's a really good teammate. You’ve got to do this against everybody, but it's a great start for him.”

After both squads missed their first three field goals, Brant Byers scored Penn State’s first points of the season on a wide-open dunk. He sank a three-pointer on the Nittany Lions’ next possession to single-handedly put the blue and white up five early.

Prkačin checked into the game as Mike Rhoades’ first man off of the bench and got to work immediately, snatching an offensive rebound and converting a layup before leaping into the air to snag an errant pass and convert another close shot.

Canisius shot one-for-six from the field in the first quarter before Clinton Efinda found nylon on a pull-up jumper from the free-throw line, and Alex Mack hit an eerily similar shot for the Golden Griffins a possession later to cut Penn State's lead to seven.

Facing a Canisius double team, Prkačin spun around the pair of Golden Griffins and drove along the baseline to deliver another highlight with an emphatic dunk that fired up the Legion of Blue.

The 6-foot-8 forward sat in the middle of the first half after picking up a pair of fouls early. Prkačin turned the ball over for an easy Canisius bucket immediately upon returning to the court, but quickly made up for it with two tough rebounds and an and-one layup.

That toughness was a consistent theme for Prkačin throughout the evening.

“(The coaches) call me out when I’m not aggressive and when I’m soft,” Prkačin said “So I took it personally kind of, and I think it helped me a lot”

Thomas Allard was named a captain early on Monday evening and earned the start in his first game as a Nittany Lion. The Suwanee, Georgia native spent the first four years of his college basketball career at the Division II level before transferring to Penn State in the offseason.

He didn’t attempt a field goal in his first 15 minutes in blue and white, but he put back a missed three-pointer by Roberts Blums and swished a long-range shot of his own on consecutive possessions to quickly pick up his first five points and force a Canisius timeout.

Nate Fouts ended a seven-point Penn State run with a shot from beyond the arc for the Golden Griffins. François Wibaut buried one in response, and Ivan Jurić converted on a close layup to give the Nittany Lions a 47-26 advantage at the half.

Jurić opened the second frame with another layup before a three-pointer from Byers and a jump shot by Reed on ensuing possessions.

Then, Prkačin took over.

In a scoring blitz, the Croatian converted back-to-back jump shots and a pair of layups. He caught a feed in transition and rose up to slam the ball home, then worked up the court after a Canisius turnover and delivered another emphatic dunk.

Prkačin hung onto the rim for a moment, then dropped to the hardwood and released a celebratory scream as Kernkraft 400 blared over the Bryce Jordan Center speakers. He’d scored 12 consecutive points for Penn State, forcing Canisius coach Jim Griffin to call a timeout.

“He can play inside and out,” Reed said of Prkačin. “He can score the ball, rebound the ball, and also make plays for others. Kind of like LeBron James in a way.”

The Nittany Lions got an and-one bucket from Wibaut, Prkačin’s fellow international newcomer, before Juric sank a pair of free throws and a smooth jumper to send the game into the under-eight media break.

Byers made his second steal in the blue and white and initiated a fast break. Prkačin ran down the court in stride with the Miami (OH) transfer and soared towards the basket for an alley-oop slam.

If Prkačin felt he hadn’t accumulated enough highlights that night, he reached up for a single-handed dunk on the next possession.

From there, Penn State cruised to its first win of Rhoades’ fourth season at the helm. He utilized his depth down the stretch, with Reggie Grodin and Andy Gemao seeing the first minutes of their collegiate careers.

Grodin, a redshirt freshman, notched his first two points on a pair of free throws in the game’s dying minutes before blocking a Golden Griffin shot and feeding Gemao for his first college score.

Walk-on guard Grant Spacciapolli and freshman forward Aleksandar Zečević checked in, meaning all 14 players on Penn State’s roster saw time in the campaign’s first game.

“We need the bench, and I've always called it our army,” Rhoades said. “We want to build an army so everybody's ready to impact the game and impact winning, so we’ve got to continue to build that. We tried to recruit that way, and we’ve got some guys that come off the bench and really help us. I think you'll see different starting lineups as well because of that.”

Up next

The blue and white close out its homestand to begin the year with a Thursday clash against Chattanooga, set for 6 p.m. at the Bryce Jordan Center.

title: Penn State men’s hockey lands commitment from Maximilian Mareš
author: Sawyer Klasnick | For The Collegian
description:
Penn State has bolstered an already strong 2027-28 recruiting class by landing a commitment from Maxmilian Mareš.

Mareš, a 6-foot-6 forward from Ostrava, Czechia, is the No. 13 prospect in the 2027 NHL Draft, according to TSN's Craig Button. Mareš currently plays for the Rimouski Océanic of the QMJHL, where he has six goals and 10 assists through 15 games.

Mareš' commitment continues a trend that Guy Gadowsky's staff has capitalized on following last year's rule change allowing players from the Canadian Hockey League (CHL) to compete in NCAA Division I. The CHL includes three major junior leagues: the QMJHL, Western Hockey League and Ontario Hockey League.

Mareš joins a growing list of players with CHL experience who have committed to or played for the Nittany Lions, including Gavin McKenna, Egor Shilov and Jackson Smith.

Penn State is back in action this weekend with games Friday and Saturday against Notre Dame.

MORE HOCKEY COVERAGE

title: Penn State men's tennis coach Bruce Lipka steps down
author: Lexie Linderman | Football Editor
description:
Another year, another head coaching job open at Penn State.

Bruce Lipka has stepped down as the head coach of the men's tennis team, effective immediately, to pursue "a professional opportunity outside of college athletics." Assistant coach Thoma Wright will serve as the interim head coach.

“We're grateful for everything Bruce has contributed to Penn State and our men's tennis program,” Vice President of Intercollegiate Athletics Pat Kraft said in the release. “We are incredibly appreciative of the time, energy and commitment he has given to our men's tennis student-athletes.

Lipka joined the Nittany Lions in June 2024, serving as the head coach for two full seasons and amassing a 28-28 record in dual-match competition.

Before arriving at Penn State, Lipka was the Director of Racquets at the Woodmont Country Club in Rockville, Maryland. He also mentored many professional tour-level athletes, including a few who won Grand Slams.

The Nittany Lions are set to compete in the ITA Sectional Championships in Charlottesville, Virginia, this weekend, Nov. 5-7.

title: Penn State women’s volleyball rises in latest AVCA poll
author: Joey Bolger | For the Collegian
description:
After another successful week, the Nittany Lions have jumped two spots in the latest AVCA poll, from No. 13 to No. 11.

Penn State, along with Washington, Minnesota, North Carolina and Vanderbilt, are the most notable risers, with all teams rising two spots.

The blue-and-white are currently on a five-game winning streak, with three of them coming against ranked opponents.

Penn State will be tested on the road this week, heading up to Minnesota on Friday to take on the No. 19 Golden Gophers, then on Sunday will take on No. 7 Wisconsin in a highly anticipated Big Ten matchup.

MORE BASKETBALL COVERAGE

title: Gov. Candidate Stacy Garrity addresses supporters during visit to Berkey creamery as midterms draw near
author: Jonathon Chiu | The Daily Collegian
description:
Republican Stacy Garrity, the state treasurer running for governor alongside Jason Richey, visited the Berkey Creamery Sunday as part of her campaign tour throughout the Commonwealth. She’s running against Democratic incumbent Gov. Josh Shapiro.

Her visit comes just days before Election Day, and a week after the Penn State College Democrats hosted an appearance by Shapiro for a “Rally in the Valley” event at Old Main.

Around 20 supporters, including members of the Penn State College Republicans and the Centre County Republican Party, came in support of Garrity and Richey, who both gave speeches promising to combat unaffordability; creating a first homeowners program; and lowering certain taxes, including the gross receipts tax, which contributes to an increase in energy bills.

In a press conference following hers and Richey’s speeches, Garrity said she would enact regulations on data center development and give local governments in the Commonwealth more control in regulating their development — a position contrasting her initial support for data centers as sources of economic growth in Pennsylvania.

She said to the media that she has plans to “unleash” the Commonwealth’s energy resources by lifting Pennsylvania’s moratorium on drilling in state parks and forests, and wants to tap into the state’s abundance of natural gas. In an interview, Richey said this would help lower taxes and energy bills and provide more in-state job opportunities, particularly for college graduates.

Centre County Republican Party Chair Michelle Schellberg, who’s running against incumbent State Rep. Scott Conklin (D-77), said hers and others’ presence at the creamery was meant to show Garrity “the love and support that she needs” ahead of Election Day.

She said the Democratic Party has left behind many of its voters, including those in Pennsylvania, “that are not socialists or believe in socialism.” The midterms, she added, are a time for all Americans to come together in support of Republican candidates to “bring back common sense” to the government.

“I'm door-knocking for my own campaign, and I heard from a Democrat today that the Democratic Party has left her and that she is not really sure what to do. And so I gave her some pointers about how we're the party that's here to support the Constitution, and I know Stacy will do that,” Schellberg, 56, of Halfmoon Township, Pennsylvania, said.

Penn State College Republicans President Tristin Kilgore, 22, of Newtown, Pennsylvania, said Garrity’s visit to campus provides students the opportunity to learn about her and her campaign.

“It's crucial to go to the polls, because as we saw in 2024, how your voice and your vote does matter and can make monumental shifts in policy, as we've seen in the Trump administration,” Kilgore, a fourth-year studying political science, said. “We can have the same thing in Pennsylvania where we can unlock the potential of this Commonwealth to be able to make sure that our students here at Penn State are able to have a great and successful life here in Pennsylvania.”

Garrity said in an interview that it’s important for more young people to vote. Pennsylvania’s role in shaping America’s past through its industries, natural resources and universities would have a renewed focus under her leadership, she said.

She added that Pennsylvania has the potential to lead the nation, not trail it, and putting families in Pennsylvania first matters.

“When you're an older person like me, you know the history of our great Commonwealth,” Garrity, 62, of Athens, Pennsylvania, said. “We built America. And so when you're a young person and we've had mediocrity in the state for so long, I think sometimes people think that that's just the way it has to be and they don't think about the fact that with all of our blessings.”

title: Penn State LB Tony Rojas named to Comeback Player of the Year midseason watch list
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State's top player has earned more recognition.

Tony Rojas was named to the Comeback Player of the Year midseason watch list on Monday.

Rojas has been all over the field this season, leading the team in tackles with 58 despite just a two-tackle performance against Purdue.

title: Penn State men's basketball announces team captains for 2026-27 season
author: Will Horstman | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State announced its team captains for the 2026-27 season Monday.

Forward Josh Reed, guard Thomas Allard and guard Dasonte Bowen are the official leaders of the Nittany Lions.

Reed is a team captain for a second straight season. He averaged 11.5 points and 4.1 rebounds per game in 2025-26. He returned for his fifth year of college basketball after getting eligible through the Ohio 5-in-5 eligibility lawsuit.

Allard and Bowen are entering their first seasons with Penn State, but they both have four years of collegiate experience. Bowen transferred in from St. Bonaventure, and Allard made the jump from Division II.
