title: Penn State women’s soccer notebook | Erica Dambach talks Big Ten Tournament
author: Zach Schroder | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State ended its season strong with a 4-0 win over Indiana last Friday. The Hoosiers scored an own goal in the 30th minute to go down 3-0 early. The offensive performance in the regular-season finale gives the Nittany Lions strong momentum as they head into the Big Ten Tournament.

The blue and white are now set to face off against Purdue for the second time this season. Its last matchup with the Boilermakers ended in a 2-2 draw at Jeffrey Field. This time the two squads will meet at a neutral site, Energizer Park, an MLS stadium, in St. Louis.

This will also be a ranked matchup this time around as Penn State ended the season ranked No. 23 while Purdue is sitting at No. 18 in the IWOSC Coaches Poll.

Coach Erica Dambach met with media over Zoom on Monday, discussing the upcoming tournament and postseason.

Injury update

Despite the dominant win over Indiana, Penn State had a couple of scares in the match. The Nittany Lions suffered two injuries against the Hoosiers, both coming in the second half of the match while the game was all but won.

Redshirt senior midfielder Molly Martin and sophomore midfielder Kennedy Ring both left the game and went immediately to the locker room. “We don’t”, said Dambach when asked if she had an update on the two injured players.

“We’re patiently waiting for some updates, hoping to get those today,” Dambach said. “(Monday) football weekends aren’t the best for the rest of us from that standpoint.”

Martin started in all 17 regular season games and ranks sixth in minutes for the squad. Ring played in 16 of the games and played valuable minutes off as a sub. Dambach will have some decisions to make regarding the starting lineup depending on what news she receives.

Familiar team, fresh environment

This will be Penn State's second time seeing the Boilermakers this season; their last matchup happened at home for the Nittany Lions at Jeffrey Field. While a neutral site doesn’t have the same advantages of home field, Dambach says it doesn’t change much for them.

“I think the team’s pretty fired up to go play in an MLS stadium. I think either way the team’s in a really good place with it, but there’s just a tremendous amount of excitement being in a big time stadium on Thursday.”

Dambach also discussed what she could take away from her first Purdue matchup.

“Certainly you’re gonna take the first match into consideration and what we were able to do. I respect the Purdue coaching staff, I know they're gonna tinker,” the skipper said.

The Nittany Lions may also have some bulletin board material to use against the Boilermakers, and this rematch is one that Dambach’s squad was hoping for.

“Honestly, I think if you ask this team who they wanted to play again, they would have said Purdue”, Dambach said. “They very much feel like there’s unfinished business.”

Ever evolving

Dambach discussed becoming stagnant for the postseason and how her team has grown over the course of the season and what it will look like as it enters into the next phase.

“This team’s continuing to evolve game after game, and we’ve gotta make sure we keep studying what this team’s doing well and the challenges that we're facing to evolve with them,” Dambach said. “For us it’s about trying to figure out who our best 11 are to start the game, but also I think a huge part of this Penn State 2026 team is the depth that we’ve been able to roll out there and how can we get at them when we hit the 25-minute mark in the first half.”

Dambach has talked a couple of times about her freshmen this season and how they aren’t really freshmen anymore with the experience they’ve gained this year.

“I think with each passing week you’ve seen them step into more and more significant roles, not just minutes but roles,” Dambach said. “I think you’re starting to hear them; they’re asking for the ball, they want the ball.”

Additionally, she added that they understand they’re part of a team heading into the postseason, and they need to be more than themselves.

title: Penn State women’s hockey’s Abby Stonehouse earns AHA Forward of the Week honors
author: Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian

A pair of road victories over the weekend led to an individual honor for Penn State. The conference announced Monday that Abby Stonehouse was named Atlantic Hockey America Forward of the Week.

title: Recap | Nittany Lion Wrestling Club members shine at Senior World Championships
author: Gavin Leonard | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State and the NLWC showed why they’re consistently at the top over the weekend.

Current and former Penn State wrestlers took home hardware on the international stage, competing at the 2026 Senior World Championships this week.

Nittany Lion Wrestling Club representatives claimed championships in their respective weight classes, solidifying their status as legends. If the NLWC was its own country, it would’ve finished fourth in the world in points.

Here’s how those members fared in their respective weight classes.

Roman Bravo Young - 57 kilograms

Roman Bravo Young represented Mexico well, advancing to the championship match of the 57-kilogram weight class. His path through the bracket was nothing short of dominant.

Bravo-Young defeated Kazakhstan’s Meirambek Kartbay 5-2 during the qualifying round, Mauritius’ John Leopold 10-0 in the Round of 16, Mongolia’s Munkh Batkhuyag 4-3 in the quarterfinals and DPR Korea’s Chong Han 4-1 during the semifinals.

His run came to an end at the final stage of the bracket, where he suffered a 10-0 defeat against the United States’ Spencer Lee and settled with second place in the tournament. Lee improved from his last outing, as he placed fourth in the 2025 Senior World Championships at 57 kilograms.

Marcus Blaze - 61 kilograms

While Marcus Blaze’s run ended during the semifinals, the sophomore persevered through a loss to reach third in the bracket.

Blaze won his first two matches convincingly, winning 7-2 against Turkey’s Emrah Ormanoglu and 10-0 against Moldova’s Leomid Colesnic. Blaze’s quarterfinal match went down to the wire, losing 3-2 after Iran’s Ahmad Mohammadnezhadjavan scored the winning point in the last few seconds.

Blaze’s competition did not end there, as he won his repechage match 9-1 against India’s Nikhil Nikhil to earn a spot back in the bracket and a chance to win third place. Blaze took full advantage of the opportunity and defeated Kazakhstan’s Assyl Aitakyn 4-2 to secure a spot on the podium.

Zain Retherford - 70 kilograms

Zain Retherford reached the semifinals in his fourth appearance at the Senior World Championships, an impressive feat for the former Nittany Lion.

He cruised through his first three matches of bracket play, winning by fall against Belgium’s Muhammad Abdurachmanov, defeating Hungary’s Iszmail Muszukajev by fall and 7-0 against Azerbaijan’s Kanan Heybatov.

Ultimately, Retherford couldn’t get past the semifinals after coming up short against Kyrgyzstan’s Ernazar Akmataliev and took home a bronze medal.

Levi Haines - 79 kilograms

Levi Haines added another first-place medal to his long list of achievements in his first appearance at the Senior World Championships.

Haines won his first three matches against Morocco’s Mohammed Bouazouni, Poland’s Szymon Wojtkowski and Russia’s Ismail Khaniev by a combined 18-1, including a fall, as well.

Haines’ following matches in the semifinal and championship matches remained close contests throughout. Haines defeated Mongolia’s Suldkhuu Olonbayar 3-3 on criteria, and followed by outlasting Iran’s Mohammad Nokhodilarimi 4-3 to earn first place in the 79 kilogram bracket.

Kyle Dake - 86 kilograms

A member of the NLWC, Kyle Dake solidified himself as one of the greatest wrestlers in American wrestling after becoming the oldest American wrestler to win a world title. Dake’s win marks his fifth career gold medal and makes him the first wrestler to win world titles across three different weight classes: 74 kilograms, 79 kilograms and 86 kilograms.

Dake defeated Kazakhstan's Bolat Sakayev, Kyrgyzstan’s Malik Shavaev, Russia’s Ibragim Kadiev and Azerbaijan’s Arsenii Dzhioev en route to his historical accomplishment. The 35-year-old wrestler held on in the final two minutes after being up by three points, taking the gold medal, 3-2.

Kyle Snyder - 97 kilograms

Kyle Snyder was the third NLWC member to take home gold at the World Championships. His journey through the bracket was both nail-biting and overpowering at times.

His opening match in the tournament against Turkey’s Alperen Tokgoz was his biggest win with a score of 10-0. Snyder defeated Russia’s Abdulrashid Sadulaev 4-4 by criteria in the quarterfinal and outclassed Poland’s Zbigniew Baranowski 5-0 in the semifinal.

The Nittany Lion Wrestling Club member ended his run with a hard-fought 4-4 win by criteria against Japan’s Arash Yoshida to become a back-to-back champion.

MORE WRESTLING CONTENT

title: Staff predictions | Predicting Penn State women’s basketball’s 2026-27 record
author: The Daily Collegian women's basketball staff
description:
The wait is over, and hoops in Happy Valley are back.

Penn State is coming off two subpar seasons, and Pat Kraft called for change in the offseason by bringing in Tanisha Wright as head coach.

In a team full of new faces to the blue and white faithful, will the Lady Lions prevail in Year 1 under Wright, or will the new era get off to a slow start?

Here are our staff predictions.

Jimmy Blair: 15-15

The Lady Lions have a chance to jump out to a solid start early in their schedule. Early home games against Cleveland State and Bowling Green are matchups the blue and white can look ahead to.

The squad will be tested in many away games early in the year, including against opponents Cincinnati, Arizona State and Baylor. After the opening stretch, the blue and white will travel to East Lansing for its first conference matchup against rival Michigan State. A win here could give the team massive momentum heading into the conference schedule.

A three-game road stretch against UCLA, USC and Michigan followed by a home matchup against Ohio State may prove to be the toughest stretch of the campaign. The Lady Lions have the opportunity to play many conference games at home, which will hopefully put them in a good position in the conference standings going into the Big Ten tournament.

The Nittany Lions could be much more dangerous than in recent years. I think they’ll finish 15-15 on the year.

Gianna Dowling: 11-19

While there’s plenty of reason for fans to be excited about Lady Lion-legend Tanisha Wright as the program's new leader, it’ll still be a work-in-progress season for the new-look Penn State squad.

I think the blue and white will start off strong by winning its first three non-conference games, but will drop its first game of the season to Arizona State on Nov. 15. The Lady Lions will bounce back against Bowling Green and Saint Joseph’s, but will have a winless trip to the Bahamas over Thanksgiving break.

In Big Ten play, I think Penn State will snag early wins over Purdue and Rutgers, but will skid in January — a month that features five preseason top-25 opponents. The Lady Lions will bounce back with their second win over Rutgers on Feb. 8, and will round out conference play with a win against Wisconsin on Feb. 28.

Ultimately, I see the blue and white winning just four games in the Big Ten gauntlet and falling just short of making the conference tournament in Wright's first season.

Noah Radio: 12-18

It’s going to be a tough year; there’s no way around it. Tanisha Wright’s return to Happy Valley is inspiring plenty of optimism, and she even found herself in five-star recruit Jordyn Palmer’s top four schools.

However, that excitement might not breed victories in year one. The Nittany Lions have a few tantalizing transfers with multiple years of eligibility, like Devyn Quigley and Petra Božan, but the pieces are going to take time to gel.

Early in the year, Penn State has a solid mix of layup matchups and big tests. Cleveland State and Bowling Green offer quality opportunities to get in the win column, while Cincinnati and Dayton serve as measuring sticks for Wright’s first team.

Arizona State, Baylor and defending Big 12 champion TCU are the highlights of the nonconference slate, and I think the only victories the blue and white can hope to pick up are moral victories.

In Big Ten play, Michigan State’s five-star recruit Lilly Williams will prove too much to handle early and spell a bad message for the rest of the season. I’m confident in Penn State’s ability to beat Rutgers on Jan. 8, but I’m only counting on two more victories.

To win those additional conference games, Penn State will have to beat a fellow bottom-dweller like Purdue or Northwestern twice, or pull an upset, perhaps against one of the Big Ten’s nine preseason-ranked teams.

Throughout the year, I believe the Lady Lions will show signs of promise and start peeking out the windows of the Big Ten’s basement.

Sienna Pearce: 13-17

So far, Penn State hasn’t had a good track record with teams entering their “rebuilding season.” For that reason, I think the Lady Lions will struggle in their transition. With a brand new coach and transfers, blue and white has a lot of work to do.

However, under the leadership of Penn State alum coach Wright, the Lady Lions have the unique opportunity to learn from a coach who was once in their shoes. Wright’s impressive 21-year career in the WNBA as a player and coach may give blue and white a fighting chance to be competitive.

If the new players and coach can get in sync, I think they have the opportunity to surprise teams they fell to last year, like Maryland or Oregon.

However, I predict that the Lady Lions will have a rough January. I think they will inevitably fall to powerhouse teams like UCLA or USC on the road. Despite these losses, I still believe that blue and white has the ability to improve their 4-14 conference record from last season.

Nick Myers: 12-18

As the Lady Lions enter an entirely new era of basketball, no matter how much excitement there is, growing pains are bound to show up one way or another.

Despite their season starting relatively light, the unfamiliarity between new players and coaches, mixed with the early-season sloppiness every team faces, I wouldn’t be surprised if some of these highly winnable matchups become more competitive than anticipated.

As the season goes on, the Lady Lions will enter another highly competitive year in the Big Ten, despite coming in last place a year ago with a 4-14 conference record. They also lost two of their strongest players this offseason to transfers: Gracie Merkle and Kiyomi McMiller, who averaged 40 points per game combined.

Disregarding the negatives, I still think that this team will come out of this season stronger than ever. I have unbelievable trust in Wright, as both a former athlete and Penn State alum, to re-establish the winning culture and set this program up for future success, even if it isn’t immediate.

title: Staff predictions | What will Penn State men’s basketball’s regular-season record be in 2026-27?
author: The Daily Collegian men's basketball staff
description:
Penn State returns today.

After a bottom-barrel Big Ten finish saw Mike Rhoades’ unit lose all but three players, he and his staff retooled their squad with a completely new identity. With all the offseason work soon about to show, it’ll soon be time to see what sticks.

Here are our basketball staff’s record predictions for the Nittany Lions in 2026-27.

Myles Hannak: 18-14 (7-13 Big Ten)

There’s a real chance that their roster is the best Rhoades had at his disposal in his entire Happy Valley tenure.

It needed to happen; Penn State was too weak and young to compete in the Big Ten, and the current group’s makeup addresses that directly. I do have doubts about how long it takes this roster to fully gel, but I think the versatility and depth of talent allow a lot of flexibility before you find what clicks. Last year’s team didn’t have that.

The pieces, the mentality and the love for the blue and white are all there. With a veteran core, Penn State won’t make the same rookie mistakes as it did a year prior. My eyes are turned fully to the Palestra game against in-state rival Pittsburgh.

Last season the Panthers blew out the Nittany Lions, and Jeff Capel has brought his squad a similar level of roster building this summer. If you can put up a result there, you can genuinely argue that this year’s Penn State squad is not only different, but competitive.

I think navigating the Big Ten slate might be a bit less bumpy than expected. Everything we’ve seen at open practices and from players so far suggests this team is tough and wants to be known as gritty.

Will Horstman: 16-16 (6-14 Big Ten)

Penn State is objectively a better team than last season: It has the age and the experience needed to be more competitive in the Big Ten.

I still think it’s going to be a tough climb out of the basement of the Big Ten standings, so this season could still only have minimal conference wins. The main issue is the lack of depth, which will likely show up at some point this season.

The frontcourt duo of center Ivan Jurić and power forward Roko Prkačin could be really special. Pairing them with shooters Brant Byers and Roberts Blums and having a new facilitator in Dasonte Bowen could give this team a good offense.

But I’m not sure if this team improved enough defensively to truly stack up some more Big Ten wins. Prkačin will help with rebounding, but he’s going to need some help on the glass, and that’s where Jurić has to make a Year 2 leap in.

We’ll see what happens Monday, but there’s no real test on the schedule until Pitt next weekend and Thanksgiving week in the Bahamas. Even then, it’s very possible the Nittany Lions will have only one or two losses by the time Big Ten play starts because the non-conference slate is so easy.

This team should have improved from last season, so Rhoades should have some better results. It might still remain in the bottom half of the Big Ten standings, but Penn State will finish closer to 10 conference wins than zero.

Elliott Inscho: 17-15 (7-13 Big Ten)

It would be hard for the 2026-27 campaign to not be better than the Nittany Lions’ showing last year. While I don’t think this is a team that has any realistic possibility of making a significant impact in the postseason, Rhoades has seemed to do a good job at building a roster that will win more than three conference games.

Josh Reed and Ivan Juric, the only returners who played significant roles last season, should be more than capable of consistently delivering for Rhoades. Brant Byers was a key piece of Miami (OH)’s magical run last season and Dasonte Bowen showed flashes against Drexel.

Shooters like Roberts Blums and Thomas Allard have led Rhoades to describe this group as some of the best three-point squads he’s ever had at Penn State. It’s also an older, more experienced team, which will matter in Big Ten play.

As my fellow reporters mentioned above, the game against Pitt at the Palestra looks like the first true measuring stick on the schedule. The Panthers certainly aren’t a shoo-in for March Madness either, but playing an in-state Power 4 rival early in the year will tell us a lot about Penn State.

I think it’s one of the only games in the nonconference that could be an excusable loss, and I fully expect the blue and white to handle business in the rest of the early slate. A loss or two in the Battle 4 Atlantis tournament is also realistic.

The veteran presence will help Penn State be more competitive in Big Ten play, but I still don’t think that it’s fleshed out or skilled enough to come close to contending. It should absolutely be better than last year, though, and will help Rhoades’ seat from warming up too much.

title: Film, film, more film | Here’s what’s happening in the valley
author: Sarah Price | The Daily Collegian
description:
Editor's Note: Penn State men's basketball made students tickets for the home opener on Monday free. The original version of this article stated that students had to purchase tickets.

It’s time to say goodbye to Halloween and hello to a new month. Happy November, Penn State!

Hopefully, you spent Sunday recovering from the busy weekend. If you still have an itch to scratch, here’s what’s happening in the valley this week.

Monday, Nov. 2

Double Header at the BJC: Lady Lion’s and Men’s Basketball

On Monday night, the Lady Lion’s and men’s basketball teams will host their home opener in a double header at the Bryce Jordan Center. The Lady Lions start at 5 p.m. against Cleveland State, while the men’s team starts at 7:30 p.m. against Canisius.

Students can attend the both games for free, with the first students in attendance at the Lady Lion's game on Monday night to receive a home opener shirt while supplies last. And, if you stay in the BJC until 7:30 p.m. for the men’s basketball game, you could receive a second free student T-shirt while supplies last.

Centre Film Festival

The Centre Film Festival is a weeklong celebration of film and conversation connecting local voices with global ones through media arts, workshops and masterclasses. The festival starts Monday morning with multiple movie screenings happening all across the valley.

For those of you stuck on campus Monday, you can catch “Tipping Point PA” and “Like Father” at 12 p.m. in the Foster Auditorium. “La Bola Negra” and “Kiloran Bay” will be at 6 p.m. at The State Theatre.

Student tickets are free, but be sure to grab your pass on its website.

Tuesday, Nov. 3

Nature Sketching at The Arboretum

After Halloweekend, some Penn State students may need to reconnect with nature.

Penn State’s Arboretum invites adults of all skill levels to this free, drop-in class. Attendees are able to bring their own materials or use those provided by the arboretum.

The class starts at 10 a.m. and lasts until 11:30 a.m., which makes it the perfect way to relax after a, perhaps, questionable weekend.

Sports Trivia at Doggie’s Pub

If you’re over the age of 21, and looking to test your knowledge of sports after Penn State’s first BIG 10 win against Purdue, look no further than Doggie’s Pub. On Tuesday night, from 7 to 9 p.m., make sure to bring two to six of your best friends who “know ball” to secure a win.

Wednesday, Nov. 4

The State Theatre: Arrival – Screening and Expert Q&A

The Penn State Eberly College of Science and Department of Astronomy and Astrophysics is hosting a free movie screening at The State Theatre of the 2016 film, “Arrival,” starring Amy Adams, Jeremy Renner and Forest Whitaker. The movie screening is a part of Eberly’s Science Matters Spotlight Sessions.

The movie will begin at 6:30 p.m., with the Q&A session immediately following the film, sponsored by the Penn State Extraterrestrial Intelligence (PSETI) Center. The panel will feature Sheri Wells-Jensen, a professor of linguistics at Bowling Green University, science journalist Nadia Drake and Jason Wright, director of the PSETI Center.

Be sure to register for the free event ahead of time on The State Theatre’s website.

Thursday, Nov. 5

Folded Flowers: The Art of Kusudama

If you’re looking to relax after a stressful, and quite frankly busy, Halloweekend, make your way to the Palmer Museum of Art to learn the art of Kusudama, a traditional Japanese paper craft that uses simple, modular origami elements to create colorful paper bouquets and balls. The event will take place in the Palmer Museum Studio Classroom from 6-7:30 p.m.

Don’t worry, no prior experience is required as they will guide you step-by-step through each fold to create a beautiful handmade piece that can be used as decoration. Registration is required for this event on the Arboretum's website. Students and Arboretum volunteers pay $10, while standard adults pay $15.

Friday, Nov. 6

No Refund Theatre: “The Rocky Horror Picture Show”

No Refund Theatre is a student-run organization at Penn State that performs numerous theatrical productions each semester, free of charge. The purpose of the organization is “to give all students, regardless of major, the opportunity to perform, direct, and produce all types of theatre.”

On Friday, the No Refund Theatre will perform “The Rocky Horror Picture Show.” The NRF performs their productions on campus in Forum 111, with Friday’s show starting at 8 p.m.

Saturday, Nov. 7

The Rivet Winter Market

If you’d like to start purchasing your holiday gifts early, The Rivet at Discovery Space is hosting a two-day winter market, where you can find one-of-a-kind handmade gifts while supporting local artists, makers and businesses.

If you need a break from shopping, the winter market will offer various food trucks throughout the weekend, with beverages and bites galore.

The winter market is on Saturday, Nov. 7, and Sunday, Nov. 8, from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m.

Sunday, Nov. 8

Centre Film Festival: Closing Night Ceremony

To commemorate the week-long celebration of film in the valley, The Roland Theatre will host actor Delroy Lindo and his wife Nashormeh Lindo, artist and educator, in a closing night ceremony.

title: Big Ten roundup | Lincoln Riley earns signature win, 2 top 25 teams get upset in Week 9
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
The college football chaos continued across the country this week, with this season having the most parody across the board in recent years.

In the Big Ten, that continued with an upset win by USC, while the conference’s second-highest ranked team, Indiana, survived for a second straight week. Two teams ranked just inside the top 25 dropped their Week 9 games to keep the middle of the conference jam packed.

Here’s what happened around the Big Ten.

USC upsets No. 2 Ohio State

Saturday marked another opportunity for Lincoln Riley to get a signature win at USC, and he did just that. While Ohio State was deploying a backup quarterback in true freshman Luke Fahey, the Buckeyes’ defense had no answer for the Trojans’ offense.

USC got out of the gates quick, with a 69-yard touchdown pass from Jayden Maiava to wide receiver Trent Mosley on the second play from scrimmage.

While Ohio State’s offense couldn’t generate touchdowns, kicker Connor Hawkins went four-for-four, but the defense couldn’t get stops when it needed to. The Trojans led 20-9 at the half, and it was all they needed to pull off the upset.

With a 30-18 win, USC is right back into College Football Playoff conversations. It’s been a whirlwind of a season for Riley, who at one point was very much on the hot seat. Now, he has the Trojans in a better spot to get over the hump in 2026.

Northwestern, Wisconsin lose, fall out of rankings

Northwestern and Wisconsin entered the week ranked, but both of them had to go on the road on Saturday.

The Wildcats made the trip to Eugene, Oregon, to take on an Oregon team that’s a shell of what it was supposed to be this season.

However, behind a strong game from Dylan Raiola, who totaled 336 passing yards and three touchdowns, the Ducks pulled off the upset.

Oregon led 27-26 with just over 10 minutes left in the game, and Raiola launched a dagger to wide receiver Dakorien Moore, who caught it in stride and took it 75 yards for a touchdown. The one-play touchdown was the final score of the game, as Oregon defeated Northwestern 34-26.

Wisconsin traveled to the ever dangerous Kinnick Stadium, and the environment that has witnessed many upsets saw another one Saturday.

Iowa remained with Hank Brown at quarterback, and he played a flawless game for a Hawkeyes offense that took a jump in production compared to their typical outings.

It was all Iowa throughout the game, as Brown’s 222 yards and two touchdowns led the Hawkeyes to another ranked victory. On the defensive side of the ball, Iowa limited Wisconsin to 235 total yards and no points on the scoreboard.

The 30-0 blowout in Kinnick moved Iowa to 6-2 on the season and it jumped back into the rankings at No. 21 in the AP Poll.

Late game chaos

Indiana and Washington were the beneficiaries of late-game chaos, with both coming out victorious at the end of their matchups.

Indiana and Minnesota were knotted at 10 entering the fourth quarter, and the field goal kickers got a lot of work. Tied at 13, Minnesota kicker Luke Drzewiecki drilled a 60-yard field goal with 13 seconds remaining.

The Hoosiers’ backup quarterback, Grant Wilson, then led a quick drive to get them to the same spot that Minnesota was on its field goal attempt. Indiana kicker Paddy McAteer hit his own 60-yard field goal as time expired to send the game to overtime.

On the first play of overtime, Wilson found Charlie Becker in the end zone to immediately take a 23-16 lead. Minnesota quarterback Drake Lindsey had his chance to tie it back up, completing a 17-yard pass to wide receiver Noah Jennings to move the sticks, but the Hoosiers defense put the stop there.

Lindsey was sacked on back-to-back plays to end the game, and Indiana survived for the second consecutive week, defeating the Golden Gophers 23-16

Later in the day, Washington traveled to Nebraska for a primetime matchup with the Cornhuskers.

It was a low-scoring affair, as Nebraska led the Huskies 7-3 with under two minutes left in the game. Washington quarterback Demond Williams Jr. found receiver Chris Lawson for a short completion before he ran it into the end zone to take the lead.

The Cornhuskers had an opportunity to retake the lead, but on the second play of the drive, Nebraska quarterback Anthony Colandrea threw a pick six. In the matter of 30 seconds, Washington went from trailing 7-3 to leading 17-7.

The Huskies went on to defeat Nebraska, 17-10, ahead of their matchup with Penn State in Week 10.

title: Hear from The Daily Collegian alumni as they reflect on their years in the newsroom
author: Teresa Phelan | Opinions Editor
description:
For nearly 140 years, The Daily Collegian has churned out talented reporters who went on to work for national news outlets, win prestigious awards and take their journalism skills to various fields, even outside of communications.

We asked alumni to look back on their experience in our newsroom. Here’s what they have to say.

Samantha Ruland

The Daily Collegian gave me an education in journalism that went far beyond anything I could have learned in a classroom. As a student reporter, I covered the criminal cases involving Graham Spanier, Tim Curley, and Gary Schultz, and the death of Tim Piazza, competing with some of the biggest news organizations in the country and often beating them to stories. Those experiences prepared me for the difficult, sensitive reporting I would do early in my career with the USA Today Network, including covering the Pittsburgh synagogue shooting, and gave me confidence well beyond my years. As editor-in-chief my senior year, I got an equally valuable, if sometimes sobering, education in the business of journalism, including navigating the decision to cut our print publication from five days a week to two our spring semester. Now, as the planning and coverage editor for features at The Philadelphia Inquirer, I find myself drawing on so many of the skills I developed at the Collegian, from leading a newsroom and planning ambitious coverage to navigating an ever-changing industry. I wouldn't be the journalist or editor I am today without the experiences, instincts, and confidence the Collegian gave me.

Kailee Warner

I was with the Collegian from 2020-2024 where I wrote for the sports section covering women's volleyball and field hockey my freshman year, and then continued with field hockey the next three years. I learned so much during my time at the Collegian and it prepared me for my current side job where I run and write for the sports section of my three local newspapers: Perry County Times, the News Sun and Duncannon Record. I met so many people through the Collegian, including my alumni mentor whom I still communicate with and even some Olympians! I had many memorable experiences and I greatly appreciate everything I learned and gained during my time at the Collegian.

Daniella Carbone

My experience with The Daily Collegian had a big part in developing the skills that have shaped my career today. As a senior videographer from 2021-2024, I gained hands-on experience filming, editing, conducting interviews, and telling meaningful stories through video. The opportunities I had at TDC allowed me to build confidence as a storyteller, collaborate with a team, and learn how to bring stories to life from start to finish. Today, working in video production and corporate communications, I continue to draw on the technical skills and storytelling foundation I developed at The Collegian. I’m grateful for the experience and the role it played in preparing me for my career.

Darian Somers

The Collegian quickly became my home at Penn State and that isn't just because I spent several nights sleeping on the sports couch. No part of my college education was as valuable as the Collegian but that isn't as valuable as the memories and the lasting life lessons, not just journalism ones, that I learned there. I am forever grateful for my time at The Collegian because it taught me so much.

Emily Muniz

Before joining the Daily Collegian, I had no experience at all with journalism besides an undying passion for it. The Collegian fueled, nurtured, and raised that passion. Now, each time I edit an article for my freelancing job, I am reminded of reading my articles out loud with my editors at that long white desk in the Willard Building and I think about what changes they would make.

Mercedes Hamilton

My time at the Collegian has truly prepared me for anything. From juggling enterprise stories and breaking news to building a brand new beat about an underrepresented community, my time at the Collegian has already shown up in so many ways at my first job — and I haven’t even been here a month! I’m eternally grateful for the foundation the Collegian has given me and the friendships I’ve been lucky enough to carry with me.

Ritamarie Montagna

During my three years at The Daily Collegian, I had the opportunity to be a part of lifestyle, news, multi, socials and BOE, which taught me countless journalistic skills that I’ve been able to carry with me even in my current career as a teacher. I currently work as a preschool teacher’s assistant, and one of the biggest parts of that job is conversation — whether with students, parents, or co-teachers — conversation is one of the main keys to my job. Every day, I thank the Collegian for the conversational skills that were instilled in me during my time as a reporter and an editor through communicating with my sources and my TDC colleagues. More than an educational resource for me, TDC was my home while I was at Penn State. I also thank the Collegian every day for the friends I made and the people I met during my time there, whom I still talk to nearly a year and a half after my graduation.

Caitlin Concannon

My time at the Collegian was important to my growth, both personally and professionally. Early on in my TDC career as a reporter and a member of the digital and social team, I began to understand the importance of community and advocating for your peers. My experience communicating with students, faculty, and community members during my time on campus helped to shape the way I view advocacy and the responsibility to tell somebody’s story. Today I’m a paralegal in capital mitigation and sentencing advocacy as I prepare for law school. On a daily basis, I draw on the skills I developed while at the TDC and am grateful for the tools it gave me in interviewing, research and giving a voice to those who don’t always have one. I don’t know where I would be today without my TDC family — they found me when I needed them most.

Emma Lessick

Being a member of the Collegian transformed my hobby of photography into a purpose. I was able to work on deadlines and see my photos in a print and on the website, which was incredibly rewarding. My experience at the TDC allowed me to travel for women’s basketball and shoot a Penn State football game, all things I wouldn’t have been able to do without the Collegian.

title: Degrees you can surprisingly study at Penn State
author: Rebecca Fein | The Daily Collegian
description:
Everyone knows a “finance bro,” a stressed engineering comrade or even a communications diva. But what about the students who take the road less traveled?

Here’s a look into Penn State’s programs that are so small the amount of people pursuing it could fit into a school bus.

Forest Technology Major

Remember when you were a kid and your mom told you to put the phone down and play outside more? If you were a rebellious child, this one is for you.

Penn State offers forest technology as a major. Forest technology trains individuals in all technical aspects of forestry, including evaluating, managing and protecting forest resources.

Students with this degree can end up in a multitude of careers, the most common being public agencies, utility companies, pulp and paper manufacturers and landscaping firms.

Mining Engineering Major

Heigh-ho, heigh-ho! For anybody who’s interested in mining or the process of extracting minerals, mining engineering could be the right fit for you.

Mining engineering focuses on the fundamental principles necessary to perform mineral extraction, development, recovery and processing.

Possible career options with this degree include working for private and public sectors as mining engineers or pursuing advanced education to possibly go into academia.

After all, mining engineers would never take these skills for “granite.”

Professional Photography Major

Professional photography is a “picture perfect” major.

It's common to hear of the popular photojournalism major, offered by the Donald P. Bellisario College of Communications, but this major is actually a part of the College of Arts and Architecture.

The professional photography degree is intended for students to develop the craft of photography to the most advanced level. This degree focuses on giving students the necessary skills to be a successful professional photographer.

Wildlife and Fisheries Science Major

You give a man a fish, you feed him for a day. You teach a man to fish, you feed him for a lifetime.

Penn State offers a major entitled wildlife and fisheries science. This major has two distinct tracks you can embark on, either wildlife or fisheries, and focuses on the study of the conservation of wildlife ecosystems and the identifications of different wildlife species.

Pursuing this major prepares students for science careers in natural resource companies.

Equine Science Minor

Penn State has an equine science minor for all horse lovers, in addition to the Penn State Equestrian team led by Kristin Gretok.

The equine science minor is dedicated to developing a foundation in horse exercise physiology and training principles, farm management, animal genetics and even using horses for human therapy.

Minoring in this gives off some serious “mane” character energy.

Poultry and Avian Science Minor

Don’t be “chicken,” give it a try!

The poultry and avian science minor allows for students to center their education around ensuring continued health for birds, gaining hands-on experience in caring for birds and tutorials on the live production management of broilers, turkeys, laying hens and ducks.

Popular Music Minor

Grab a microphone and belt it out!

At Penn State, you can minor in popular music. This minor provides both music and non-music majoring students with an advanced knowledge of famous songs from multiple genres and the ability to analyze and criticize all different forms of popular music.

Game Development Minor

For those still purchasing new skins in Fortnite and those waiting anxiously for Grand Theft Auto VI, Penn State’s game development minor might be the right fit for you.

From learning about what makes video games fun to actually planning out levels of different games, coding and making up storylines, this minor has it all.

Penn State really offers all students a chance to find their passions. Whatever you choose to study, “we are” the place that can provide the right opportunities.

title: Preview | Penn State men’s basketball hosts Canisius, Chattanooga to open season
author: Myles Hannak | The Daily Collegian
description:
The roars of the Legion of Blue are almost back.

Penn State will soon break in the Bryce Jordan Center for the first time this season, welcoming a pair of nonconference opponents for a tuneup slate. With Mike Rhoades soon about to lead his fourth season in Happy Valley, the blue and white look to start the season strong on its home hardwood.

Here’s the outlook for the Nittany Lions’ first two games this season.

Lights, camera, action

The Nittany Lions begin their season hosting a Golden Griffins squad that finished 10-21 last season and struggled to 3-13 away from home. Canisius finished second to last in the Metro Conference, while Penn State finished at the bottom of the Big Ten.

Leading Canisius is longtime college coach Jim Christian, who is in his third season in Buffalo, New York after previous stops with Kent State, TCU, Ohio and Boston College.

It doesn’t appear to be a much different fate for Canisius this season, as KenPom has them ranked as a bottom-20 team in the nation, while statistician Evan Miyakawa doubles down, placing the Golden Griffins as the seventh-worst team in the country.

The lone bright spot for Canisius has been guard Michael Wilson Jr., who transferred in from Bellarmine after a previous stop at DII, North Greenville. Wilson scored 30 points in the Golden Griffins’ exhibition win over Robert Morris, in which he went an efficient 11-of-13 from the field.

Wilson is just one of 12 newcomers for Canisius in what was a busy offseason of recruiting from the transfer portal, as the Golden Griffins only have three true freshmen.

Tipoff for the season opener is set for Monday at 7:30 p.m.

Welcome back

The blue and white conclude its homestand by welcoming back a familiar face, as the Mocs are led by coach Dan Earl. The 1997 alum of Penn State is top-15 in program history in points, assists and 3-pointers.

Earl also had experience on the sideline in Happy Valley, serving as an assistant from 2006-11, helping the Nittany Lions set a program record of 27 wins in 2009, claiming the NIT Championship that same year and helping mold current Penn State assistant Taylor Battle.

The fifth-year Chattanooga coach had a remarkable 2024-25, winning the NIT Championship in his new home, but hit a real wall last season, finishing under .500 for the first time in his entire Golden Griffins tenure.

6-foot-4 guard Tate Darner returns for his sophomore season as Earl’s primary offensive threat. After finishing third on the Golden Griffins in scoring, the Lakeland, Florida, native likely sees an uptick in production after the two leading scorers departed. Darner was also named to the Preseason All-Southern Conference Team.

Chattanooga opens its season on Monday against No. 11 Louisville before its clash at the BJC with Penn State.

With both squads utilizing strong guard play, Mike Rhoades’ new-look backcourt will have its hands full defensively. Lucky for the blue and white, the only 7-footer it’ll face is Chattanooga true freshman John Fleeman, which could give returning Penn State big man Ivan Jurić a big stretch of the season.

Tipoff against Chattanooga is set for 6 p.m. on Thursday.

title: Position preview | Penn State men’s basketball to feature sharpshooting frontcourt
author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian
description:
With Halloween in the rearview mirror and the temperature in State College creeping lower by the day, it’s almost time for students, fans and alumni to sweat with Penn State.

Mike Rhoades’ roster has seen a major overhaul since it last took to the court, though the fourth-year coach’s backcourt group features one of only three remaining faces from last season. The rest of the guards will be donning the blue and white for the first time on Monday.

Rhoades has already described this season’s Nittany Lions as the “best shooting team I’ve had since I’ve been here,” and the guard group is largely the reason.

Here’s a look at the ones and twos that will suit up for Penn State in the 2026-27 season.

Transfers

Dasonte Bowen’s name was floated by several members of the squad on local media day as a potential impact player for Penn State in his return to the Big Ten.

The Boston, Massachusetts, native began his college career at Iowa, playing two seasons for the Hawkeyes before transferring to St. Bonaventure ahead of his junior year. An injury in his debut campaign in Iowa City forced a redshirt and allowed him to be eligible for Penn State this season.

Bowen didn’t play in the Nittany Lions’ exhibition win over the Bonnies, but showed flashes in a 12- point performance against Drexel. He also led the team with seven rebounds.

Starting alongside Bowen, Roberts Blums had a quieter night in Philadelphia with five points while shooting 2-for-3 from the field. A Riga, Latvia, native, Blums spent his first two years at Davidson. He led the squad with 12.4 points per game last season before transferring to Penn State.

Blums won the 2024 Latvian League championship before moving stateside, and also claimed a gold medal at the 2023 FIBA U18 European Championships with his country.

After four years at Central Connecticut State, Jay Rodgers will finish his college basketball career in Happy Valley.

The Pickerington, Ohio, native will give Rhoades significant playmaking. He ranked No. 8 in Division I with 6.9 assists per game.

Rodgers is yet to make a field goal with Penn State in just over a half hour of time on the court. He shot 0-for-2 against St. Bonaventure and didn’t attempt a shot against Drexel, though he converted on two free throws against the Dragons.

Not many of Penn State’s transfers have a story as interesting as Thomas Allard’s. The 6-foot-7 guard played for Lincoln Memorial and Alabama-Huntsville, both Division II institutions, before jumping to the Power 4 level this season.

Last season, he averaged 13.7 points per game as the Chargers soared to an appearance in the NCAA Division II Sweet 16.

Allard is a slick shooter from beyond the arc. All five of his shots against St. Bonaventure came from long range, and he made four. It was a tougher task against Drexel, though, as he missed all four three-pointers.

Backcourt freshmen

Andy Gemao is part of a significant international contingent among this year’s Nittany Lions, but is the only traditional freshman recruit of the cycle.

An Iligan City, Lanao del Norte, Philippines native, Gemao played high school basketball in Canada before Rhoades recruited him. He was a team captain at Royal Crown School in Toronto, Ontario, and was named a first-team NPA All-Star and second-team OSBA as a senior.

He’s also represented the Philippines at the U19 and U16 level, appearing at the 2026 adidas Eurocamp and adidas Nations Tokyo U-19 camp.

Walk-on Grant Spacciapolli was a two-time captain at Pine Richland High School, averaging 16.1 points, 5.4 rebounds and 2.7 assists as a senior. Spacciapolli holds the Rams’ record for career three-pointers.

Return of Reggie

Reggie Grodin is Rhoades’ only backcourt returner. He saw no game action last season and redshirted, but averaged 12 points and 6.6 rebounds per game as a senior at The Newman School in Boston.

He’s seen the roster change drastically around him, and is joined by roommate Josh Reed and neighbor Ivan Juric as the only continuity with last season’s roster. At local media day, he noted that it’s been interesting to see the squad shift to an older team this year.

“I've never been in a situation with that, but I guess that's the norm in college basketball now,” Grodin said. “It's been great. I don't want to say you can't win, but it's definitely difficult to win with a bunch of young guys in the Big Ten versus (having) more experience.”

title: Stock up, stock down | RB Cam Wallace breaks out, WRs sit back in Penn State’s first Big Ten win
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State finally won a Big Ten game under Matt Campbell, as the Nittany Lions beat Purdue, 31-17, at Beaver Stadium on Saturday.

Without wide receivers Koby Howard and Chase Sowell, Penn State looked to the run game and aggressive decision-making to beat the Boilermakers. However, there were still some concerns the Nittany Lions must address.

Here’s whose stock rose and whose stock fell in Penn State’s first Big Ten win of the season.

Stock up: Cam Wallace

Because Carson Hansen was announced as the starting running back, it came as a surprise to see Cam Wallace receive the first carry.

Wallace hadn’t touched the football since getting two carries in Week 4 against Wisconsin, but he looked like a completely different player and finished with a career-best 135 rushing yards against Purdue.

“He has continued to stay the course,” Campbell said postgame. “How he's practiced has earned the right to go in and not just play, but honestly take advantage of his opportunity. That's what I'm really excited about.”

Wallace’s explosive 48-yard rush late in the first quarter helped set up Penn State’s second touchdown, and he finished the game as the Nittany Lions’ top running back, tallying 135 rushing yards and a touchdown, averaging 6.1 yards per carry.

Hansen wasn’t too far behind, accumulating 96 rushing yards and a touchdown, averaging 5.6 yards per carry.

Wallace didn’t get into the end zone until 9:23 remaining in the fourth quarter, a 2-yard rush up the middle — a reward from the coaching staff for his career-best performance.

Stock down: Wide receivers without Koby Howard or Chase Sowell

It wasn’t a surprise to see the wide receivers take a backseat role when Koby Howard and Chase Sowell were listed out before the game. Howard was the core of the offense through the first three weeks of the season before his injury, and Sowell later adopted that role.

Without either, Rocco Becht found the tight ends more often and even worked the running backs into the passing game while still looking for big plays out of wide receiver Brett Eskildsen.

Eskildsen was the most-targeted wide receiver with four opportunities, but he only had one catch. Becht tried to find him in the end zone, but the ball was underthrown and cornerback Don Saunders ran right into him. No flag was thrown.

Meanwhile, true freshman Amarion Jackson’s two catches for 31 receiving yards were the most by a wide receiver Saturday. Zay Robinson had a catch for seven yards.

Tight end Benjamin Brahmer was the top receiver overall with four catches for 58 yards on seven targets, closely followed by Andrew Rappleyea’s 45 yards.

Stock up: Pass rush

Although the Nittany Lions didn’t record a sack until defensive end Yvan Kemajou’s late in the fourth quarter, the pass rush was much improved.

Penn State hurried quarterback Ryan Browne six times, leading to Browne going 10-for-29 with two interceptions. Defensive end Alexander McPherson — someone who’s earned more playing time as of late — had two quarterback hurries in the first quarter.

Defensive end Caleb Bacon also hurried the quarterback twice, while linebacker Tony Rojas and defensive lineman Keanu Williams had the others. Kemajou would’ve had one of his own, but he was called for roughing the passer despite Browne still holding the football when contact was made.

Even when Browne got the ball out on his lone touchdown pass of the game, McPherson applied heavy pressure and Bacon whiffed on a sack, and the throw was made in desperation while falling to the ground.

Stock down: James Peoples

Running back James Peoples has been a regular in the backfield, averaging 8.14 carries per game with a high of 14 against Wisconsin. He’s been trending down since his 67-yard performance against the Badgers, with 20 yards on seven carries against USC being his best performance since Week 4.

Peoples stock plummeted again, as he didn’t get a single carry against Purdue. Wallace took Peoples’ spot in the depth chart Saturday and forced the coaching staff to keep him on the field, leaving the Ohio State transfer out of the equation.

Campbell called Hansen and Wallace an “elite one-two punch” after the game, and said the pair looked closer to how he wants Penn State’s run game to be for the rest of the season.

However, Campbell also said the same thing about Hansen and Peoples after the USC game, but Peoples has seemingly been eclipsed by Wallace. If that’s the case, there’ll be no room for Peoples to make an impact should Wallace win the long-term position battle.

Stock up: Aggressive decision-making on offense

Campbell has been known for his passive decision-making earlier in the season, drawing boos from the home crowd any time he sent Nathan Tiyce on the field to punt.

That all changed against the Boilermakers, as he routinely kept the offense on the field on fourth down. It worked splendidly for the Nittany Lions, who went three-for-three on fourth-down conversions.

Tiyce was seen working on rugby-style throws in warmups, and got to show his Australian roots on a fake field goal play. He threw the ball underhanded to Brahmer on fourth-and-7 for 13 yards, getting down to Purdue’s 7-yard line and setting up Rapplyea's touchdown to take a 7-0 lead.

Hansen’s 1-yard rushing touchdown later in the contest was scored on fourth-and-goal, and it was the eventual game-winning score.

Gutsy decision-making like this was a major factor in Penn State’s victory, and who knows what would’ve happened if Campbell was this aggressive against Wisconsin or Northwestern.

title: Iowa State professor gives lecture on AI’s potential to both protect, harm energy infrastructure
author: Jonathon Chiu | The Daily Collegian
description:
Around 20 students and faculty took their seats in 108 Chambers Building Friday to listen to a lecture by award-winning Iowa State University Professor Manimaran Govindarasu on finding new ways to protect power grids and energy infrastructure as cyberattacks using artificial intelligence (AI) increase.

Despite technical difficulties delaying the lecture’s start time by several minutes, Govindarasu, an Iowa State University Anson Marston Distinguished Professor in Engineering and Murray J. and the Ruth M. Harpole Professor in Electrical and Computer Engineering, surged past the obstacle and gave an hourlong talk on AI’s impact on cybersecurity, from cybercrimes to espionage.

Govindarasu said cybersecurity professionals are using AI to find vulnerabilities even in the foundations of the internet, such as PHP, the language behind up to 70% of websites.

During the lecture, he said this proliferation of AI and growing cyberthreats create a need for more investigations into how AI can help prevent attacks on power grids, including those improved on or created by the technology.

Govindarasu also said the protection of energy infrastructure in the face of increasing AI-based cyberthreats could potentially be achieved by enacting stricter security measures; like a “zero-trust” architecture, which would install stricter authorization and access controls within a system, making successful cyberattacks harder.

Govindarasu, who has conducted years of research into improving the cybersecurity capabilities of power grids, often with funding from several academic organizations and federal agencies like the U.S. Department of Energy and Department of Defense, said in an interview that there needs to be a more "adversarial" way of thinking among cybersecurity professionals to fully leverage the benefits of AI to better protect from energy infrastructure threats.

“The whole national security and economic security is centered around the security and resiliency of the grid infrastructure. If AI-based adversarial models are going to be leveraged by adversaries, could be hackers or terrorist groups, they can target our critical infrastructure,” Govindasaru said. “The first thing for a defender to understand is what adversaries can do so that we can stay ahead of the game in terms of using those same solutions for developing the most advanced security solutions.”

Nilanjan Chaudhuri, a professor in the College of Engineering whose research and interest areas include AI and energy systems, said he shares similar views to Govindarasu on how AI is currently being used both constructively and destructively.

He said harnessing the potential cybersecurity applications of AI will require the cooperation of multiple disciplines and backgrounds, such as engineering and computer science.

“One of the challenges in today’s world, so far as the cybersecurity risks are concerned to our critical infrastructure, is power systems,” Chaudhuri said. “You look at the opportunities as to how you mitigate those challenges, it's not just electrical engineering. It's a cross-disciplinary sweet spot where you can apply your talents and you can grow and be part of the workforce in future.”

Steve Zukley said that despite being required to attend lectures to further study for his master’s degree in electrical engineering, he found the intersection of AI and cybersecurity in Govindarasu’s talk to be particularly interesting, since it was something he “really hadn't considered.”

Since much of the U.S. power grid, including its computer systems, is several decades old, he said, there's an increasing need to find ways to keep pace with modern threats.

“If the power grid goes down during a blizzard or during a heat wave, people will pass away,” Zukley said. “Quantum computing is still kind of on the horizon but everyone has access to AI, the good guys and the bad guys, so I think that's the main reason that this is such an important talk to have.”

title: Preview | Penn State women’s basketball opens Tanisha Wright era against Cleveland State
author: Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian
description:
Basketball season has arrived. At 5 p.m. on Monday, Devyn Quigley and Co. will lace up their sneakers, Joe Putnam’s voice will hit the airwaves, and the Tanisha Wright era will officially tip off against Cleveland State inside the Bryce Jordan Center.

“We're ready to get started,” Wright said at local media day. “It's been a long time coming. We started this journey with zero players, so to be able to field the roster of 11 and the caliber of people that they are, we're ready to get started, so excited.”

The Lady Lions got started in the form of an exhibition against the University of Pittsburgh at Johnstown on Oct. 27. Penn State blew out the Division II Mountain Cats, 84-47.

In the lopsided matchup, Petra Božan played like a seasoned Big Ten opponent against a Division II team. The Split, Croatia, native scored the first four points of the game and finished with 20 points. She made nine of her 12 shots and physically dominated inside.

Božan was often spelled by Cristen Carter, who racked up eight rebounds, including six offensive snags. The two forwards did spend time on the floor together, a possibility that Wright addressed at local media day.

“Everybody knows that we have 11 players, and so we're going to take advantage and take the opportunities that present themselves,” Wright said. “There might be opportunities that present that they need to play together, and so we're going to take advantage of our full bench and use it to the best of our ability.”

It remains to be seen how much time the 6-foot-4 pair will spend on the court together in the regular season, but Wright previewed the strategy in the exhibition.

Another preseason theme is the reliance on Quigley and Enjulina Gonzalez in the backcourt. The duo played 33 and 35 minutes, respectively, against Pitt-Johnstown.

Quigley scored 16 points, Gonzalez led the team in assists, and perhaps most importantly, Gonzalez didn’t turn the ball over. The team totaled 18 giveaways, including four by Božan and three apiece by young guards Ava Black and Kamrah Banks. Carter and Savannah White also added three each, and Quigley turned it over twice.

Wright’s squad will need to rein that in as they enter the regular season. Out of the Horizon League, Cleveland State represents a solid opportunity for a fast start.

The Vikings were picked seventh in the Horizon League preseason coaches poll and have no projected all-league player. Last year, Cleveland State went 26-10 and made a run to the WNIT quarterfinals. However, none of its returning players averaged more than 4.1 points.

Like Penn State, the Vikings are also under a first-year head coach, and it’s a familiar face. Bob Dunn spent last season on Carolyn Kieger’s staff in Happy Valley after stints as an assistant at Miami, Cleveland State, George Mason and Wager.

At Penn State, one of the Cleveland-area native’s specialties was coaching the post, where he guided Gracie Merkle to the best field goal percentage in the country. Now, Dunn is trying to leverage his high major experience into success at his hometown school.

When Dunn returns to the BJC on Monday, it should be a fresh slate in blue and white. The lone returning player, Vitória Santana, didn’t appear in the exhibition game, so barring a surprise, the season opener will focus on introducing the new-look Lady Lions.

title: Projecting Penn State men’s basketball’s starting lineup ahead of 2026-27 season
author: Will Horstman | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State received big news Friday ahead of its season opener on Monday night against Canisius. Forward Roko Prkačin was cleared to play by the NCAA, making him on track to be available after missing the team’s two exhibition games.

Prkačin was a part of Mike Rhoades’ remake of the Nittany Lions’ roster this offseason. Rhoades added 11 new players to the team, which means the starting five will look very different this upcoming season as compared to last.

Here’s a projection of what the starting five will look like for the Nittany Lions once the season opens in just a couple of days.

Point guard: Dasonte Bowen

Dasonte Bowen seems to be the clear favorite to start at point guard. He missed the first exhibition game against St. Bonaventure, but returned when Penn State faced Drexel last Monday, starting at point guard.

Bowen brings experience, having played two seasons at St. Bonaventure and two years at Iowa. He averaged 10.9 points, 3.0 rebounds and 4.8 assists per game with the Bonnies last season.

He has a fifth year of eligibility because an injury cut his 2024-25 season short. Bowen was a late add in the transfer portal by Penn State not because no one wanted him, but because he’s not sure many people were aware he had an extra year.

“That could be why it took a little bit longer than most,” Bowen said. “But what stood out to me about here was just the honesty that coach came with instantly. He instantly told me nothing would be promised, but there'd be a great opportunity, and I'd have to come here and work and go from there. That stood out to me just because I'm big on those types of values.”

Shooting guard: Brant Byers

Brant Byers grew up a Penn State fan. He attended some Nittany Lions basketball games as a kid, and now he gets to play for them after transferring in from Miami (Ohio).

Byers brings a level of shooting Penn State hasn’t seen in a while. Byers shot 3-pointers at a 39.2% clip last season, which makes him a good fit at shooting guard in the starting five. He’s also 6-foot-8, so he’ll have a size advantage here.

Byers is brought in after Rhoades gave him a chance to build a basketball program at Penn State. He’ll get to help make it happen as a projected starter.

“A big part of why I came here is obviously I'm from Pennsylvania, so Penn State basketball has always been kind of personal to me growing up,” Byers said. “I've always been a fan, and then coach Rhoades and the staff also just made a pitch that I couldn't turn down.”

Small forward: Josh Reed

Due to injuries and other personnel decisions, Josh Reed played more at power forward last season than the team expected. Now, Penn State has the ability to keep him at small forward more often, which is his best fit in this starting five.

Reed is currently eligible to play and recently received good news from the Ohio eligibility lawsuit, in which he is a plaintiff, as he looked to play another year of college basketball after the 5-in-5 rule changes. The Ohio Supreme Court reversed a decision that made Reed and the other plaintiffs ineligible, so he’s good to go to play for Penn State.

It’s important to note that his status might change in the future as the legal process continues to play out. But Reed will certainly be a main contributor again after averaging 11.5 points and 4.1 rebounds per game last season.

“I’m just focusing on basketball, keeping that the main thing and controlling what I can control,” Reed said. “There's a lot of things right now that are out of my hands.”

Power forward: Roko Prkačin

It really can’t be overstated how important it was for Penn State to get Prkačin eligible for the 2026-27 season. He’s classified as a fifth-year player who has just one season of eligibility, but he’ll be a key player this season.

Prkačin is a true power forward for the Nittany Lions, who haven’t really had a player like this recently. He averaged 10 points and 4.3 rebounds per game with Nanterre 92 last season in France’s top professional league in France.

Prkačin said it was a straightforward decision to play for Penn State, and he wasn’t really considering other college teams.

“I spoke to coach Rhodes, and I really love his idea and program about everything, and really enjoy the culture he's building here,” Prkačin said. “I saw myself in that situation.”

Center: Ivan Jurić

Ivan Jurić is back for Year 2 as Penn State’s center. He really flashed his potential in his freshman year, so he could be primed for another step forward in his development this season. He’s ready to apply what he learned going through a Big Ten schedule last season.

“It's the little things that win games,” Jurić said. “Every team can beat every other team. I would say, like getting the 50-50 balls, just diving on the floor. It's those little things that literally separate the difference.”

Jurić averaged 10.2 points and 5.3 rebounds per game last season. He’s still the youngest player on a team that got much older this offseason, but he’s going to be one of the leaders on the court.

Projected top rotational players

Penn State doesn’t have as much depth as Rhoades would like, but it still has some key pieces who can come off the bench. Notably, guard Roberts Blums offers high-scoring potential off the bench.

Guard Thomas Allard has impressed during the offseason after making the jump from Division II. He could push for a starting spot, as Rhoades likes his mistake-free play, but it’s hard to see where with the roster fully available.

Forward François Wibaut will also play sizable minutes off the bench with his defense. Expect him to be relied on in late-game defensive situations.

Forward Tim Oboh will back up Jurić at center and guard Jay Rodgers will spell Bowen at point guard. It’s a 10-man rotation for Rhoades and the Nittany Lions, who look to improve from a 12-20 record last year.

title: Week 9 report card | Penn State offense bounces back, defense holds steady in win over Purdue
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s first Big Ten win in the Matt Campbell era is finally here after the Nittany Lions defeated Purdue 31-17 on Saturday.

They had success on both sides of the ball with a dominant running attack from Cam Wallace and a pair of interceptions from safeties Jamison Patton and Jeremiah Cooper.

Here’s how I’d grade Penn State in its win over the Boilermakers.

Overall: B+

Coaching staff: A

Campbell made a handful of aggressive decisions on fourth down, including electing for a fake field goal where punter Nathan Tiyce threw the ball rugby-style to tight end Benjamin Brahmer for a first down.

Offense: A-

While the Nittany Lions moved the ball via the running game and through the air, the lack of wide receiver contribution was somewhat alarming.

Penn State was without star receivers Chase Sowell and Koby Howard, so Brett Eskildsen and Amarion Jackson were the starters. The two, along with Zay Robinson, had just four catches for 55 yards.

Pass game: B+

Becht played some of his best Big Ten football against the Boilermakers, throwing with 67% accuracy for 175 yards and a touchdown.

He was able to get tight ends Andrew Rappleyea and Benjamin Brahmer involved, finishing the day with a combined eight catches for 106 yards.

Run game: A

While Purdue has the worst passing defense in the Big Ten, Penn State relied on the ground game without Sowell and Howard.

Wallace ran for 135 yards, averaging 6.1 yards per carry with a touchdown. Carson Hansen also had his best performance of the season with 96 yards on 17 attempts while also finding the end zone.

Offensive line: A-

For the first time in Big Ten play, Penn State's offensive line generated big gaps for the run game to develop. However, they were worse in pass coverage, giving up two sacks.

Defense: A-

Penn State’s defense performed well enough to come out with a win over the Boilermakers. However, it gave up two big passing plays in the first quarter that led to Purdue's only offensive touchdown of the day.

Pass rush: B

The fact that someone other than Rojas was able to generate a sack warrants celebration for the Nittany Lions. Defensive end Yvan Kemajou recorded his second sack of the season, while the rest of the defense recorded six quarterback hits.

Secondary: A-

It’s no secret that Penn State boasts one of the best secondaries in the Big Ten, if not in all of college football, led by cornerbacks Audavion Collins and Daryus Dixson.

Quarterback Ryan Browne, who averaged the fourth-most yards per game in the conference coming into Saturday, was held to just 142 yards against the Nittany Lions, but had passes of 38 yards and 32 yards in the same drive, leading to a touchdown.

Linebackers: B-

There was nothing special about Penn State’s linebacker play against Purdue, as Kooper Ebel had the best performance with three tackles and a pass breakup.

Special teams: F

Penn State's special teams had its worst performance of the season on Saturday.

Kicker Ryan Barker missed two of his three field goal attempts, while one of Nathan Tiyce’s two punt attempts was blocked and returned for a touchdown.

title: ‘Our fans make the difference’ | Despite sparse crowd, fans at Beaver Stadium make presence felt
author: Lexie Linderman | Football Editor
description:
The Beaver Stadium crowd was bleak on Saturday. Penn State’s run out of the tunnel was one of the quietest in recent years. There were loads of empty seats in the upper bowl, and the student section was never even close to filling up.

But late in the game, it didn’t feel like that, even with the student section emptying out as the night waned on Halloween. The crowd made its voice heard on a few flags, or lack thereof, and brought momentum back to the Nittany Lions when they needed it most.

“We have the most loyal fanbase in all of college football,” offensive lineman Cooper Cousins said postgame. “I know there's a lot of people out there that might like to degrade our fanbase and say a lot of nasty stuff about our university and our fanbase, but you look at our fanbase every Saturday, and it's people not only from around the state that are taking off work, are leaving their home, getting a hotel, and parking in an RV two days before the game.”

Cousins added, “I say it all the time, our fans are 12th man, and our fans make the difference. The more the merrier, and they showed up tonight and they packed Beaver, and we're nothing without them, so I appreciate them.”

It was expected that Saturday’s matchup against Purdue, which resulted in a 31-17 win for Penn State, wasn’t going to come close to reaching Beaver Stadium’s capacity. Tickets were available for as low as $3 before kickoff. A chicken basket inside costs $17.25

But Penn State was holding firm, with the athletic department’s verified tickets not dropping below $50. The announced attendance on Saturday was 102,041, which seemed like a stretch.

There were a lot of different factors contributing to a lack of fans in the stadium. For starters, both the Nittany Lions and the Boilermakers entered the contest at 3-4. Penn State had yet to win a Big Ten game, with a lot of the fanbase severely unhappy with the football program and Vice President for Intercollegiate Athletics Pat Kraft.

It was also Halloween, and a 4:15 p.m. kick is a bit late for some students who had their eyes set on a night out.

Regardless, those who came stuck around. And Campbell was impressed with the showing, taking the time to thank the fans in an opening statement postgame.

“To our fans that were here today, I thought we had the energy in that stadium,” Campbell said. “What they gave our football team was awesome, and I really just can't thank them enough. So I wanted to start off and certainly say that they were incredible.”

Linebacker Kooper Ebel said he didn’t even notice the crowd wasn’t as full Saturday considering how loud it got at some moments. Beaver Stadium was specifically rocking in the third quarter after defensive end Yvan Kemajou was called for roughing the passer, even though he made contact with Purdue quarterback Ryan Browne when the ball was still in his hand.

The crowd was booing nonstop in the minutes after and absolutely erupted after safety Jamison Patton picked off Browne just two plays later.

“It sounded just as full as normal, especially when you're at home and you're playing defense,” Ebel said. “We felt their support all the way throughout the entire game. I know, especially late in the game.”

But the lack of fan attendance on Saturday is concerning if it becomes a consistent trend. The Wisconsin game in Week 4 also had lots of empty chairs, and fans aren’t going to want to spend hard-earned money on a Penn State game if the product on the field isn’t what they expect.

There are only two home games left for the Nittany Lions, with one on the Saturday before the university’s Thanksgiving Break, so it’s foregone conclusion the student section will be thin.

The rest of the stadium might fill up, though, if Campbell and company can build off this win against Purdue.

“We love the fans out there,” cornerback Daryus Dixson said. “Win or lose, they always cheering for us. So it's always grateful to have fans out there.”
