title: Preview | No. 7 Penn State women's hockey to face RIT in road test
author: Rafael Rivera | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State heads to Rochester, New York, for a two-game set against RIT, Friday at 6 p.m. and Saturday at 2 p.m. at Gene Polisseni Center.

The Nittany Lions are 7-3 overall and atop the Atlantic Hockey America standings at 5-1. They’ve won five straight since an overtime loss to Syracuse almost three weeks ago. They’re ranked No. 7 and coming off sweeps of Lindenwood and St. Lawrence.

Grace Outwater scored the overtime winner in Saturday’s 2-1 win over the Saints, her 12th game-winner and the most among active AHA players. Abby Stonehouse scored twice in Friday’s 3-1 win, including the game-winner.

Penn State leads the AHA at 3.22 goals per game, and first-year forward Sofia Ismael leads the team with 12 points, tied for the league lead. Half of the team’s 32 goals this season have come in the third period.

RIT has struggled. The Tigers are 2-8 but unbeaten in AHA play after sweeping Delaware, and they’ve lost four in a row since. Last weekend, No. 4 Northeastern beat the Tigers 5-0 and 8-1, and RIT is averaging 1.9 goals per game while allowing 4.9.

The goaltending is the biggest gap between the teams, and Penn State’s own crease is still sorting itself out as both Maddy Campbell and Morgan Stickney have been posting strong performances.

Coach Jeff Kampersal says the staff is deciding day to day based on practice. Both goalies, he said, are “neck and neck in terms of ownership of the net.” He also said Stickney’s skill at playing the puck behind the net is like having an extra defenseman.

Campbell is 3-2 with a 1.88 goals-against average and a .918 save percentage, second and fourth in the AHA in those categories. Stickney is 4-1 with a 2.08 GAA and a .912 save percentage.

Stickney won both starts at St. Lawrence, posting a .953 save percentage across the two games, and earned AHA Goaltender of the Week honors.

RIT has used three goalies. First-year Oceanne Thiffault is 1-5 with a 4.28 GAA and an .868 save percentage.

Junior Brenna McNamara is 1-3 with a 5.17 GAA and an .828 save percentage, and sophomore Tahlia Vasseur has a 5.98 GAA. Thiffault made a career-high 35 saves against Northeastern on Friday.

McNamara has beaten Penn State before. She made 34 saves in RIT’s 3-2 overtime win last February, the Tigers’ only win in four games against the Nittany Lions last season.

The Tigers do have some scoring. Junior forward Zoe Ziotas leads the team with seven goals and nine points and has two short-handed goals. Junior Brac Kelley and sophomore Kailey Favro each have six points. Penn State leads the all-time series 42-20-7.

The teams met in a Sept. 18 exhibition that Penn State lost in a shootout, but this is a different team now. Kampersal says it will have to handle RIT’s physical play. “RIT is very physical. We need to be ready,” he said.

Kampersal also wants a better start. The Nittany Lions have played well when trailing, and he wants them to carry that underdog mentality for the full 60 minutes instead of waiting until they’re down.

That matters against a young roster. Seven freshmen have joined the team this season and all of them play regularly. Kampersal says mistakes are expected, but he wants to see them improve, especially on repeated ones.

Special teams could matter too. Kampersal said RIT has historically had a good power play, so Penn State can’t afford to take penalties. This year the Tigers are just 4-for-32 (12.5%) with the extra skater.

Penn State will also be missing a forward. Nicole Hall is away with Sweden’s national team. She has four goals and an assist this season, including a two-goal game against Syracuse. Kampersal said the staff would use practice to decide who moves onto her wing.

Outwater, Stonehouse, Ismael and fellow first-year Kylie Amelkovich will need to carry the offense.

title: ‘It was really good for us’ | Penn State made most of bye week, evaluating its play
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Following Penn State’s loss to Michigan, running back Carson Hansen said he thought the bye week was coming at the right time given the four game skid the team is on.

Now with the bye week behind the Nittany Lions, the players felt the extra time was good for them to try to get back on track with just under half the season still left.

“When you take the bye week, it's a complete evaluation period,” tight end Andrew Rappleyea said Wednesday. “Honestly, we put a cut up together of this is bad and this is good, and a lot of things you watch it’s like, ‘Damn, I didn't know it looked that bad,’ but it didn't. So then you see the things that are good, like, ‘Hey, we need more of that,’ and that's the reality of this week.”

Rappleyea felt that although the tapes can be hard to watch, it was something necessary for Penn State to work out of the skid.

On the other side of the ball, defensive end Alexander McPherson recognized the same thing with their evaluations. McPherson’s part of a pass rush that has generated minimal pressure in the first seven games, recording nine total sacks as a defense.

“It was very good for us because we could really self-evaluate and figure out what we needed to work on,” McPherson said.

The players felt the time they were able to take to look themselves in the mirror was very good for the team. It allowed them to see everything they’ve put on the field thus far, and what specifically should be worked on.

“You got to look back at it,” wide receiver Chase Sowell said. “You got to see what we did well and what we did bad, and hammer on the things that we did really well, and then also get the things that we did poorly, get corrected, get minor tweaks. Whether that's us meeting with the coaches or meeting as a unit and just watching old film, what was working in this offense before.”

One of the aspects that Rappleyea knows there’s not much tape on is a successful running game. While the pass game has allowed the offense to build some sort of identity, Rappleyea knows a complementary offense is necessary to have sustained success.

Rappleyea said the Nittany Lions “need to just run the ball down people’s throats,” but also they haven’t done so at any point this year. He also recognizes that to find more success in the run game, the offense needs to simplify things.

However, Purdue’s defense ranks No. 118 in the country against the pass, so the run game may not be a focal point given the success Penn State’s passing game has had at times.

Off the field, the team used it as a week to reflect on everything, but on the practice field it was still treated like a game week. Even without full preparation for a game on Saturday, Penn State had a strong week of practice.

“I think the the biggest piece that I saw from the bye week is our football teams' demand to come out and have great practices and want to fix the problems equally from the coach's standpoint of collectively trying to fix the problem, so I think that gives me a lot of confidence, and I think we're really excited about continuing to move this thing forward from that perspective for sure,” Matt Campbell said.

title: Penn State LB Tony Rojas named Butkus Award semifinalist
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State's star linebacker has been promoted to an award semifinalist.

Tony Rojas was named a semifinalist for the Butkus Award on Thursday, given annually to the nation's top linebacker.

After returning from a season-ending knee injury sustained early last season, Rojas has been Penn State's top defender, leading the team with 56 tackles, five sacks and 10.5 tackles for loss.

He also has two interceptions, two pass breakups, two quarterback hurries and a forced fumble.

Rojas has already been named an AP Midseason All-America second team member as well and was added to the Chuck Bednarik Award watch list on Wednesday.

title: Preview | No. 14 Penn State field hockey hosts No. 1 Northwestern, concluding season
author: Annie Alberts | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State is about to have a long but entertaining week.

The Nittany Lions start the Halloween weekend with a match against No. 1 Northwestern. The last time the Nittany Lions faced the Wildcats, they lost 4-0. However, Penn State is entering the game at No. 14 in the NFHCA Poll, its best national ranking it's had all season.

After Friday’s game, the Nittany Lions are advancing to the Big Ten quarterfinals. This is the first time they’ve participated in the postseason tournament since 2023, when they lost to Ohio State in the opening round.

This year’s postseason is taking place at Ohio State’s Buckeye Varsity Field; however, the Buckeyes aren’t participating in the tournament.

As of now, Penn State is 11-5, which is the best record it has had since it last made the tournament. Last week, they faced Indiana and Iowa, earning a win and a loss. Both were conference games, resulting in their conference record being 5-2.

The Wildcats have had an unbelievable season so far. They come into the game with a 16-1 record, only having lost to No. 8 Princeton, who earlier this season beat Penn State.

Northwestern has beaten every conference team its played, including top-ranked teams such as the Maryland Terrapins and Iowa Hawkeyes.

The purple and white have scored 56 goals this season, while its opponents have only hit the net 13 times. This statistic is thanks to Ashley Sessa and Ilse Tromp, who’ve scored 24 goals combined, split evenly between the pair.

Sessa also has 10 assists, giving her 34 points overall. She has the most points on the team and the third most in the entire NCAA.

Northwestern has an impressive offense. They also have Olivia Bent-Cole, a talented senior for the Wildcats. She has 25 points this season, including seven this past weekend. She averages 1.67 points per game, making her the fifth-ranked scorer in the Big Ten.

Northwestern’s goalie is Juliana Boon, one of the most well known goaltenders in NCAA field hockey. Her save percentage is at an outstanding .838, stopping approximately 84% of shots on goal. She’s had 62 saves so far this season and received the NCAA’s Goaltender of the Year award in 2025.

Aby Deverka, Penn State’s goaltender, ranks slightly below her in saves, with an impressive 60. Deverka ranks No. 2 in saves in the Big Ten, with Boon the only one above her.

Northwestern last lost to Penn State in 2021. It was a fierce matchup that went into double overtime, with the Nittany Lions winning 2-1 at home.

Penn State finished the 2021 season with statistics very similar to what they have now. Their ranking was No. 14 on the NFHCA poll and their record was 11-5. That’s the exact ranking and record they had going into their game against Northwestern this year.

The Northwestern team gets a lot of praise from fans and spectators, especially for their offensive strengths.

The Wildcats average 17.882 shots per game, while their opponents average only 8.353. Northwestern made 304 shots and 175 shots on goal this season.

Due to its near-undefeated record and statistics, Northwestern is tied with UMass Amherst for the highest winning percentage, winning 94% of the matches they’ve played in.

In addition to that, their Big Ten record is unbeatable at 7-0, trumping the rest of the conference.

In the upcoming Big Ten tournament, Northwestern clinched the No. 1 seed, even though matchups haven’t been released yet. It’s favored to win the tournament due to its winning percentage and other factors.

Penn State has played exceptionally well in comparison to its recent seasons. To beat Northwestern, it must give its all, offensively and defensively, in a game on Friday in Happy Valley.

title: Confident offense leads to major victory for Penn State men’s soccer
author: Henry Bustin | For The Collegian
description:
On Wednesday night, Penn State showed what “We Are” means in its final home game against the Duquesne Dukes, with the blue and white’s offense playing expertly, scoring three goals in the first half that would lead to its victory by the end of the match

Following a major 5-0 loss to Rutgers on Oct. 20 and a 2-2 tie to Wisconsin on Oct. 24, Penn State had nearly nothing to lose going into this game with a shaky record consisting of eight losses throughout the season. Regardless of that record, the Nittany Lions’ offense worked together this game to demonstrate how teamwork and strategy can benefit a team, allowing them to win their Senior Night match.

The squad kicked off the first half with a banger. Early on in the third minute, junior forward Etienne Reck scored a bicycle kick goal with an assist from Noah Förster. This immediately set the tone for a game that would be dominated by the Nittany Lions, who would score additional goals later in the half.

“I think it was important because it was an early goal, and they kept pushing us, and we were all positive and wanted to win the game,” Reck said post-game. “It was the whole team, and I would say the pressure was so good. We deserved this game.”

After Reck’s goal, the Nittany Lions continued applying pressure for the entire half. They displayed their strength and aggression when they blocked two punts from Duquesne goalie Sam Coss, both within the same minute of the game. The energy from Penn State was unmatched on Jeffrey Field, as they were determined to win to honor their seniors.

Later in the 36th minute, after the ball had advanced to the Dukes’ and Coss had failed to save it, sophomore Joe Buckley scored the second goal on the open net after an assist pass was handed straight to him from Peter Doran, furthering the score and spirit of the Nittany Lions.

When asked about the team’s performance, coach Rob Dow credited their strategy.

“I thought Beckham Brown did a fantastic job turning the corner, creating those 2-versus-1s, and once we did, we created set piece after set piece, and we knew we had a big advantage over the match,” the skipper said.

With morale and performance high, the blue and white were relentless on the field, continuing to make attempts on the net. The final goal was a spectacle to be remembered in itself. In the 42nd minute, midfielder Grant McIntosh nailed a free-kick, bar-down goal, giving one last point to the blue and white’s score, making the first half a major success.

In the second half, the Dukes landed a goal on the Nittany Lions, making the score 3-1. Despite this, Penn State continued to prevail. Sophomore goalkeeper Justin Ross made two saves, both within the sixth minute of the game, and he continued to make more saves throughout the half.

The Dukes managed greater possession time in the second half compared to the first, but the blue and white continuously displayed their skills by stealing and applying the same pressure back, reserving their net and keeping Duquesne on their feet, eventually finishing the final home game with a score of 3-1; Nittany Lions as victor.

The superior performance of Penn State and its overall win by the end of the game wouldn’t be possible if not for the offensive scorers who earned points for the team. Through Reck’s goal early in the first half, combined with the open-net goal by Buckley and the bar-down goal from McIntosh, the Nittany Lions played great in this game. Their teamwork and technique allowed them to secure a final home game victory that will serve as a memorable triumph for the Nittany Lions for seasons to come.

title: Penn State men's soccer sees turnaround on Senior Night against Duquesne
author: Daniel Almash | For The Collegian
description:
Penn State took on Duquesne on Wednesday evening and went home happy. Going into this matchup, the Nittany Lions only had two wins on the year and are 0-6-3 in Conference play. However, on Senior Night, the Nittany Lions came to play.

Junior forward Etienne Reck from Marl, Germany rocketed a bicycle kick within two minutes of the opening kickoff. The nine-win Duquesne Dukes were stunned throughout the first half. They were building solid possession, but Penn State’s backline seemed extra fortified on a night of such magnitude for not only the players but for the coaching staff as well.

Approaching the 36th minute in the first half, Penn State gained possession. Freshman midfielder Peter Doran dribbled past Duquesne’s senior goalie Sam Coss and laid it off to sophomore defender Joe Buckley, who placed the ball perfectly into the net, for Penn State to take a 2-0 lead.

Approaching the end of the half, the Nittany Lions were riding their two-goal lead and Grant McIntosh received a through ball and was hit in the back by Duquesne’s freshman centerback Steel Bayer. Penn State was awarded a free kick on the red card by Bayer, and McIntosh drilled a 25-yard bar down goal to give the Nittany Lions a commanding 3-0 going into the half.

Going into the second half, Penn State had amazing control of possession, and thingslooked effortless. In the 51st minute, Duquesne called for VAR after a player was pushed down in the box. The Dukes were rewarded a penalty kick, and sophomore midfielder Hákon Dagur cut the deficit to 3-1.

The Nittany Lions ended up taking the Wednesday evening matchup by a score of 3-1 in regulation. One of many noticeable performances came from sophomore goalkeeper Justin Ross, who notched four saves in this outing.

The Dukes earned a lot of corner kicks throughout the match, and it was Ross commanding his backline to mark in the box to avoid conceding the lead and momentum. After the match coach Rob Dow was asked about his message to his players pregame to win their last home game of the year.

“Yeah, it was all about the guys who were gonna play their last game on Jeffrey Field and honoring them,” Dow said. "They deserve to be honored. They deserved our best game.”

Additionally, the skipper was asked about the team's momentum going into next season and the potential of the program.

“Yeah, it means that the Big Ten ain’t no joke. And for us to play teams, to have a lot of confidence this time of the year, not everyone loves the timing it’s taking for us to excite our fans consistently, and for us to carry some swagger, but we are building and moving as we go,” Dow said.

The Nittany Lions travel on the road next week to play the Maryland Terrapins, who are 10-3-1 overall on the season, while Duquesne looks to defend its home turf against La Salle and try to notch double digits in the win column.

title: UPUA passes resolution opposing on-campus Flock cameras
author: Jonathon Chiu | The Daily Collegian
description:
The University Park Undergraduate Association (UPUA) voted unanimously during their general assembly meeting Wednesday to ratify a resolution establishing its official “course of action” to address the presence and use of Flock Safety cameras on campus. It’s expected to be delivered to the University Police & Public Safety (UPPS) and Penn State’s administration.

The presence of Flock cameras at University Park has been called out by community members as implementations of mass surveillance that threaten peoples’ privacy both on and off campus. On Oct. 14, university police and Penn State Chief Financial Officer Sara Thorndike confirmed all on-campus Flock cameras will be taken down after reviewing the operational value and cost of continuing their usage.

The resolution, designated #06-21, is based off of a Sept. 30 informational report written by two UPUA representatives — James Dugery and John Wozniak — planning out how the organization will address ongoing concerns about the presence of over 20 Flock ALPR cameras in University Park.

The cameras, which were installed in August 2025 for UPPS’ use as part of a one-year pilot, represent a fraction of a nationwide network of between 120,000 and 170,000 Flock cameras, according to the American Civil Liberties Union and Cybersecurity Researcher Joshua Michael.

The resolution asserts UPUA will not support any future attempts to implement ALPR cameras from another company at Penn State, which neither Thorndike nor UPPS have ruled out. It also affirms its push to “increase transparency and build trust” between UPPS and UPUA by having UPUA President Kat Hogan sit on the university police advisory board.

Dugery, one of the resolution’s three head sponsors, along with Wozniak and Campus Operations Committee Chair David Washabaugh, said seeing it passed by a unanimous vote presents a “united front” on ALPRs on campus.

“There are never ending cycles here. We will have a new assembly in April, but if something were to come up in the spring, we can use this as a springboard to continue working on public safety and transparency is a broader issue,” Duggery, 22, a fourth-year studying political science, said.

Washabaugh, 21, a fourth-year studying community, environment and development, said having this relationship between UPUA and UPPS will ensure they acknowledge the resolution.

“Now that Kat Hogan sits on that board to work with them, I think we're gonna have a similar relationship now of they're going to come to us first before those things happen, especially because of legislation like this,” Washabaugh said.

title: Learn to Flourish Design Hub places students at center of mental health research
author: Neel Ved | The Daily Collegian
description:
In November 2025, Penn State created the Learn to Flourish Design Hub after university alumni Julie and Jason Borrelli gifted $2 million for its creation. The hub is an on-site research and learning space located within the Edna Bennett Pierce Prevention Research Center of the College of Health and Human Development.

The hub allows for partnerships between faculty experts and engaged students as they work together to co-design, test and spread interventive measures to prevent adverse mental health outcomes and promote flourishing among college students.

The human flourishing work was started with a course called “The Art and Science of Human Flourishing,” developed in 2017 by a group of “contemplative scholars” from three universities, Blake Colaianne, director of Learn to Flourish Design Hub, said.

At the time, Colaianne was in graduate school and part of the research team on the course when they started to recognize the value of human flourishing in education.

“My own research began to progress in terms of understanding how much human flourishing needs to be done collectively… and also recognizing the power of the student voice,” Colaianne, 38, of Latrobe, Pennsylvania, said.

One of the areas the hub has been targeting at Penn State is student-athletes. For Erik Borgia, 21, of Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, this was one of the main reasons he joined the hub.

“I took the class HDFS 108, ‘The Art and Science of Human Flourishing,’ last fall semester and immediately loved it,” Borgia, a fourth-year studying psychology, said.

Borgia, who’s currently a research assistant for the hub, said when Colaianne told him about the hub’s creation, he knew he wanted to be part of it, since he’s an athlete himself, participating in club basketball.

Through the hub, Borgia has researched and interviewed the NCAA and professional athletes about mental health. He said it’s very powerful when people share their story, as it can be an effective way to help others.

“There are always people that think they are alone in what they are going through, if they are struggling, even if they are not struggling they might feel a sense of isolation,” Borgia said. “When you tell your story, the whole point of the class is to educate people.”

When conducting experiments with student-athletes, there are many metrics and outcomes the hub looks for to determine if a mental resource is working or not — like if depression and anxiety symptoms are declining.

Borgia added that some other ways to test a resource is working is through survey items, self-reports and physiological measures that show mindfulness and compassion. Through self-reports people can see the results.

Outside of the Penn State community, the hub has been working with high schools in the Pittsburgh area. The design hub is tailoring its class to a younger audience, according to Elise Mitchell, 23, of Lancaster, Pennsylvania.

“Every high schooler in those high schools will have to take the course, and they are going to get some feedback and data to see if the course is helpful in lowering rates of depression, anxiety and increasing certain components including mindfulness and human flourishing,” Mitchell, the hub’s research director, said.

Mitchell also said that it has developed a series for middle school students on human flourishing.

The most challenging, but rewarding, part of Mitchell’s role has been managing the teams. Some weeks can be slow while other weeks are very busy, she said, so she has to adjust based on how research and project development is going.

“It definitely makes it worth it, and it is nice to see in real time how the work we are doing is affecting people. And how it is reaching students, and how they are resonating with it,” Mitchell said.

She said during her first month at the hub she helped run a workshop for female engineering students, something she described as a “little stressful,” as she wasn’t sure if the content was resonating. However, the feedback from the workshop was positive and very helpful, she added.

Though the hub is fairly new, Mitchell said she expects the hub will continue the same work over years to come, including addressing issues in the student community for creating tools that will promote skill cultivation and, ultimately, help students flourish.

“Research definitely takes time, and it is definitely a long term thing,” Mitchell said. “You have to be the turtle in the race and not the rabbit, but it is definitely rewarding. I am excited to see where we are in three to five years.”

title: Staff predictions | Can Penn State bounce back coming off its bye week against Purdue?
author: The Daily Collegian football staff
description:
The most critical stretch of Penn State’s season begins Saturday, as there are just five more chances for the Nittany Lions to win three games and reach bowl eligibility.

Purdue is one of the teams left on Penn State’s schedule it likely needs to beat if it wants to play in December, as the Boilermakers also sit at 3-4, losing their most recent matchup to Washington at home.

Both teams are coming off a bye week, giving them ample time to prepare for this bout and work to fix their struggles. The real question is whether the Nittany Lions’ preparation paid off more.

Here’s who we think will come out on top in this battle of 3-4 programs.

Andrew Deal: Penn State 27, Purdue 10

Purdue is a weird team. It’s lost to Washington, but has beaten teams like Purdue and Illinois.

This game could go one of two ways. In Purdue’s win against Minnesota, running back Fame Ijeboi ran for 195 and three touchdowns. However, the Boilermakers rank No. 109 in the country in rushing yards per game at 128.43.

I think Penn State’s run defense will do enough to limit Purdue on the ground, something it’s yet to do this season.

On the offensive side of the ball, the Nittany Lions will continue to have to rely on the pass game. The Boilermakers struggle in the pass game, ranking No. 118 in the country in passing yards allowed per game.

Rocco Becht has had moments where he’s looked like the passer that Penn State was expecting to have throughout the year. I expect Becht to showcase that talent whether Koby Howard is available to play or not, and wide receiver Chase Sowell will continue to be the team’s top receiving threat.

The game will be close early on as the Nittany Lions shake off some rust from not playing last week. I see Penn State pulling away as the game continues, earning its first win in the Big Ten of the Matt Campbell era.

Andrew Mercer: Penn State 27, Purdue 20

It can’t be overlooked how Purdue crushed a Minnesota team, 41-13, that took down Michigan, Washington and Iowa this season.

But if I were to point out one thing Purdue absolutely doesn’t have, it’s a pass defense. The Boilermakers will enter Beaver Stadium allowing 251.6 passing yards per game, while Penn State’s entire offense comes through the air.

Honestly, I don’t think it’ll matter whether Howard plays or not, as the Nittany Lions are due for a conference victory, and Becht is due for a solid performance against a Big Ten opponent. Becht has wide receiver Chase Sowell, so there’ll be at least somebody downfield who can capitalize on a weak defense.

I have Penn State scoring three touchdowns and kicker Ryan Barker converting on two field goals for a seven-point win, putting the Nittany Lions at .500 on the year.

Purdue has a strong pass offense of its own with quarterback Ryan Browne who averages 266.3 passing yards per game, one step above Becht’s 228.3 yards per game. But Penn State has the better pass defense, and if cornerbacks Audavion Collins and Daryus Dixson play like they did against Michigan, the Nittany Lions will be just fine there.

I can’t say the same about the run defense, as I believe both Boilermaker touchdowns will come from Ijeboi. Two field goals later, and Purdue will come within a score, but fall short of upsetting Penn State.

Lexie Linderman: Penn State 28, Purdue 14

The Nittany Lions are facing a Purdue team this weekend that’s a bit hard to get a read on. But the Boilermakers provide Penn State with a good opportunity to get its first conference win out of its bye week.

It would also be really hard for the Happy Valley faithful to swallow a loss to Purdue, which is notoriously a bottom-tier Big Ten program that Penn State consistently beats up on — the Boilermakers haven’t defeated the Nittany Lions since 2004 and only have three wins against them all-time.

If Campbell wants to start really proving he can be the guy for Penn State, a win over Purdue at home would be a big help.

Becht has a chance to really right his season with a stellar performance against the Boilermakers’ pass defense, which ranks last in the conference with 251.6 passing yards allowed per game.

Howard might also be returning this weekend, which provides another weapon for Becht, albeit him likely being on a pitch count. Even if Howard doesn’t play, Sowell has shown he can perform against conference opponents.

Penn State’s offense needs a good showing in the red zone this weekend after weeks of struggling to convert, and I think Taylor Mouser will get that with four touchdowns and a 14-point win over the Boilermakers.

Noah Aberegg: Penn State 24, Purdue 17

Since losing 34-13 to Northwestern, Penn State has steadily improved in its last two games. Coming out of the bye week, I think the Nittany Lions will have enough to pull out their first victory since Sept. 19.

Aside from the lack of pass rush, each aspect of Penn State’s game has grown.

Becht’s confidence has increased, but his turnovers have been the plaguing issue. If he can play a turnover-free game, I think the Nittany Lions’ offense can be consistent.

Purdue’s defense gives up the third-most rushing yards and the most passing yards per game in the Big Ten. While the Nittany Lions haven't been able to establish a run game, I think Becht and his receivers will run wild through the air.

Offensively, the Boilermakers have the fourth-best passing attack behind Browne. But Penn State has the best secondary in the conference and will lock down Purdue's receivers.

I think Becht will lead the Nittany Lions to three touchdowns and a field goal with a strong air attack, while Ijenoi will succeed on the ground for Purdue. However, Penn State will outperform and earn its first win in Big Ten play.

title: Penn State men’s hockey opens Big Ten play against No. 18 Minnesota
author: Maggie Hardy | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Big Ten is a notoriously tough division in college hockey, but this year, the competition is stronger than ever. Out of the seven-team conference, four are ranked top-20 nationally, with Michigan, Wisconsin and Michigan State all within the top five.

After a slate of nonconference games, Penn State opens Big Ten play this weekend against No. 18 Minnesota.

The Nittany Lions travel to Minneapolis, Minnesota, for an 8 p.m. puck drop Friday and a 7 p.m. puck drop Saturday at 3M Arena at Mariucci.

About Penn State

Penn State had a rocky start to the season, dropping its first four games before finally moving into the win column with a series sweep over Canisius.

“We have a lot of work to do,” coach Guy Gadowsky said. “I think we took the step. I don’t think it was a big step…we’re not close to where we have to be.”

Sophomore defenseman Jackson Smith has been one of the leaders for the blue and white, tallying two goals and five assists on the season. The 2025 first-round NHL Draft pick had a career-high three-point effort in Friday’s win, then scored the overtime winner on Saturday to earn Big Ten Third Star of the Week honors.

“Smith is an awesome hockey player, and we need him to be awesome for us to win,” Gadowsky said. “I think his feet are what make him elite, and when he’s playing with his feet and not just his hands, he’s extremely difficult to stop.”

Transfer sophomore Justin Poirier has also been key for the Nittany Lions this season, leading the team with eight points — three goals and five assists — through six games.

Goaltenders Josh Fleming and Ryder Fetterolf have been splitting time in net, and both have been solid for the blue and white.

Fleming returns following a strong freshman season in which he earned All-Big Ten Honorable Mentions, and has posted a .904 save percentage through three starts.

Fetterolf began his collegiate career this season after being named both the CHL and OHL Goaltender of the Year last season. The freshman registered his first win on Saturday after stopping 26 of 28 shots faced.

Scouting Minnesota

Minnesota struggled last season, finishing sixth in the Big Ten and ending with an 11-22-3 record.

What followed was a transformative offseason that replaced its coach of eight years, saw seven skaters depart for the transfer portal, and added a 13-person new class.

“There’s a different approach because we don’t know what to expect from them,” Gadowsky said. “We knew in the past, everybody tweaks a little bit, but they were very consistent with what they’ve done, and this year, with the new coaching staff, it’s obviously very different.”

So far, the new Golden Gophers squad has turned some heads.

After being swept by then-No. 19 Michigan Tech to open the season, Minnesota went on to split its series with then No. 9 Minnesota Duluth and, most notably, swept then-No. 3 North Dakota this past weekend.

Forwards Brodie Ziemer and Wyatt Cullen lead the Golden Gophers, each with five points.

Ziemer returns to Minnesota — this time as a captain — for his junior year after being the driving force behind the team’s offensive production last season. The forward is coming off a 36-point campaign that paced all Golden Gophers, earning him a spot on this year’s Preseason All-Big Ten First Team.

Cullen is one of Minnesota’s most highly-touted new additions, after being selected 10th overall in this year’s NHL Draft by the Nashville Predators. The freshman earned the Big Ten First Star of the Week after registering a hat trick and an assist in the Golden Gophers’ win over North Dakota Friday night.

title: With pride decor past their doors, downtown shops aim to make ‘people feel a little less alone’
author: Hadley Louisa-mae Milhomme | For the Collegian
description:
In downtown State College, there are many local businesses that showcase their support for the LGBTQ+ community.

Whether students or residents need a safe corner of Happy Valley to enjoy a bite, study or escape from campus and feel welcomed and supported, shops like Elixr Coffee Roasters, Uncle Eli’s and Webster’s Bookstore Cafe, all have pride decor hanging in their windows or just past their opened doors.

Sadie Robinson, 20, of State College, who recently started working at Elixr, said local businesses have more influence than most people might think. She’s grown to love her morning regulars, she said, who are typically an older crowd.

When regulars ask her questions about what her modern graphic t-shirts mean, or why she chooses to wear her makeup a certain way, she said she takes it as their efforts to bridge the generational gap and create a welcoming space.

“Seeing older people specifically show up to places that fully support queer people is important,” Robinson, a third-year studying art history, said.

Robinson said customers never question the pride flag hanging in the cafe, and she believes that passive form of representation lends to making a space feel more comforting. And she said that because many employees, alongside herself, are a part of the LGBTQ+ community, no one has to fear shying away from expressing themselves due to fear of judgement.

Another place that cultivates a welcoming environment is Uncle Eli’s, a locally owned, long-standing art store in the downtown area. Natalie Pearson, 21, of State College and one of Uncle Eli’s employee’s, said it’s a place where she felt she was able to express herself.

“This was the first place that the people here and just the environment was somewhere that I felt really safe being myself and being open to talking about things, showing my art and not feeling embarrassed,” Pearson said.

It’s very important that everybody gets to find a place where they belong at some point in their life, Pearson said. Feeling accepted as a teenager and having somewhere to turn to really helped her grow into an adult, she added.

Since State College is a college town, Pearson said the stereotypical student culture still remains prevalent and influential.

“Everyone is in a frat, or they’re in a sorority,” Pearson said. “That’s totally fine, but I think it also makes people who dress differently or have a different opinion stand out very dramatically.”

Penn State’s sports programs and Greek life organizations tend to soak up a lot of the spotlight. They’re two of the biggest appeals to the university, which can make students in other extracurriculars within the arts or liberal studies feel forgotten, Pearson said. She said having accepting places around campus that appreciate artists, theatre and other diverse interests, can help students feel appreciated.

Webster's Bookstore Cafe, a bookseller and coffeehouse, has been a proud ally toward the LGBTQ+ community for years. Employee Devin Charles, 23, of Toledo, Ohio, wanted to work somewhere quiet and calm, so their friends recommended Webster's because they knew it’s “a good place to be.”

“I’ve had my own fair share of experiences getting called racial slurs in the street, homophobic slurs and things of the sort in this very town,” Charles said. “So it’s 100% important for this place to exist, and other places like it.”

Charles said they see the importance in shops displaying their allyship, as people can maintain some optimism and know that it’s truly not wholly bad. These safe spaces, like Webster's, are especially for students and faculty who are from out of state, they added.

“They come from all over the world just to further their education,” Charles said. “It’s so important to know that these places exist because it helps people feel a little less alone.”

title: No. 23 Penn State women’s soccer is set to host Indiana for final regular-season match
author: Sara Castrovinci | The Daily Collegian
description:
No. 23 Penn State returns to Jeffrey Field for its final regular season game before heading into Big Ten Tournament play after defeating then-No. 5 Michigan State 2-1 and drawing Michigan 2-2.

The Nittany Lions are set to host Indiana on Friday at 7 p.m. for their Kick or Treat match.

The two programs last met on Oct. 19 of the 2025 season. The Hoosiers took a 2-1 win on their home turf at Yeagley Field over the blue and white, their first win against Penn State in 30 years.

The Nittany Lions dominate the all-time series record at 30-2-3, while Indiana has never beaten the blue and white in Happy Valley, standing at 0-19.

What to expect for Indiana

The Hoosiers have had a rough season so far, standing at 4-11-2 overall and 1-9-1 in conference play. Indiana looks to get back in the win column as it is currently on a three-game losing streak.

Maggie Ledwith leads the Hoosier pack with 12 points on the season, including five goals and two assists. The junior midfielder has played and started in all 17 matches, serving as the primary offensive facilitator and tallying 33 shots.

Behind Ledwith are Bella Haggerty and Kennedy Neighbors, both tallying seven points in the regular season. Haggerty has notched three goals and one assist while Neighbors owns two goals and three assists.

On the defensive end, Dani Jacobson has been the main goalkeeper this season, allowing 36 goals over 17 matches. The fifth-year player has a low save percentage of 0.471 in comparison to opponents' 0.767, showcasing how the Hoosiers have continuously struggled to keep rival attacks at bay.

Indiana has already been eliminated from Big Ten Tournament contention, being outscored 19-3 at Bill Armstrong Stadium. Friday’s matchup is the Hoosiers’ one last chance to leave their 2026 run on a positive note.

What to expect for Penn State

Unlike Indiana, the Nittany Lions have a winning record, sitting at 8-3-5 with a home record at Jeffrey Field of 5-0-3.

The blue and white are coming off of a gritty win against then-No. 5 Michigan State that boosted them into the top-25 rankings, now sitting at No. 23. This momentum will be dangerous for Indiana, as it already struggles against mid-tier teams, let alone ranked programs.

Aubrey Kulpa has led Penn State in points all season, with 20 points from eight goals and four assists. The junior forward was recently ranked No. 64 in the list of the nation’s top players according to Top Drawer Soccer and was in the Week 11 selection pool for the IWSOC “National Player of the Week”.

The Cromwell, Connecticut, native is a force that can’t be stopped, forcing the Hoosiers to settle for simply delaying her inevitable offensive domination.

Beyond Kulpa, a long list of athletes on the roster contributes to the Nittany Lions’ offensive power, including Paige Kalal, Bella Ayscue and Hannah Jordan.

Kalal is right behind Kulpa in points with 16 this season via six goals and four assists. The senior forward has been a consistent contributor since her transferring in from Minnesota. Notching 30 shots, the Brooklyn Park, Minnesota, native is a strong playmaker to keep Indiana busy in its final third.

While Ayscue and Jordan aren’t in the top three stat-wise, the pair has given the blue and white meaningful and steady minutes over the regular season. The two are consistently involved in major offensive sequences, giving Penn State a wide range of attacking outlets.

Defensively, Mackenzie Gress has continued her stellar performance all season with a 0.817 save percentage and a mere 13 goals allowed. The Lyndhurst, New Jersey native, paired with defender Kayleigh Herr leading the back line, has been a lethal combination for the Nittany Lions all year long.

With Indiana already struggling to produce offensive figures, facing the blue and white backfield will be a hard task, especially with the extra motivation of looking to win their final regular-season match in front of their home crowd.

title: Best ‘Boo’k recommendations to activate the spooky spirit
author: Hailey Weber | For The Collegian
description:
With the fall season and Halloween festivities in full throttle, what better way to get into the spooky spirit than curling up with a good book, while watching the leaves blow around outside?

If you desire a Halloween story but aren’t sure where to look for a fall-themed novel, the English professors at Penn State have some suggestions on books they believe fit the essence of the season.

“Gone Girl” and “Dark Places” by Gillian Flynn

Recommended by Justin Rizzi, an English graduate assistant who teaches ENGL 30H, “Gone Girl” follows the story of Nick and Amy on their fifth wedding anniversary. Suddenly, Amy goes missing, and the police suspect that Nick did something to his wife, but did he? This book has heavy themes of suspense, mystery and crime, falling into step with the spooky vibes of October.

In a similar fashion, "Dark Places" dives into the life of Libby Day who experienced her entire family being massacred by her brother, Ben. Libby makes a guest appearance at The Kill Club, a group of true-crime enthusiasts who believe her brother Ben is not the killer of Libby’s family. She then must face her past trauma to figure out the truth behind her family’s demise.

Rizzi, 26, of Scotch Plains, New Jersey, praises these two books for their elements of thrill and suspense as opposed to the classic, gory slasher novel associated with Halloween.

“I think there’s a lot of good commentary there, as there is in all of her books, about class, power and gender," Rizzi said. "That makes her an elevated crime writer. I find myself drawn more to crime and thriller because it can be really easy to keep the tension up. I think tension is an important storytelling device to keep your reader interested.”

“The Haunting of Hill House” by Shirley Jackson

Shirley Jackson was an author primarily known for her books involving horror and mystery. While Jackson passed away in 1965, her stories live on as literary classics and books that are suited for the fall and Halloween spirit.

Assistant Teaching Professor Ellen Skirvin, 34, of Catonsville, Maryland, has always had an interest in scary stories. She has been teaching at Penn State for five and a half years, and she considers “The Haunting of Hill House” a must read for the spooky season.

“If somebody is not a super horror person, if they just want that fall or creepy vibe, a classic is ‘The Haunting of Hill House’ by Shirley Jackson,” Skirvin said. “I think "Haunting of Hill House" is one of the building blocks of horror you should read if you’re interested in that genre but don’t want to be too scared.”

As the story goes, when four people — Dr. Montague, his assistant Theodora, Luke and Eleanor — arrive at Hill House, they soon begin to deal with the bone-chilling situations brought on by the estate. Hill House is a force beyond their control, and it only seems to grow stronger.

“Our Share of Night” by Mariana Enriquez

“Our Share of Night” follows a father and son as they set off on a roadtrip after losing their wife and mother. During their trip, they encounter a family known as the Order that attempts to capture the son, Gasper, and influence him to join their operation. Both Gasper and his father try to escape the Order, but can they truly outrun their fate?

Skirvin enjoys this book because of all of the elements it combines together to amplify Halloween fear.

“That one has everything: horror, family trauma, a haunted house, cosmic horror and cults," Skirvin said. "There's a lot to love about it.”

As a child, Skirvin enjoyed writing her own scary stories. She said she remembers reading scary stories as a kid and the intense fright she got from them.

“Our Share of Night, it was so creepy and scary, it brought me back to that part of my life,” Skirvin said.

“The Birthmark” and “The Minister’s Black Veil” by Nathaniel Hawthorne

Nathaniel Hawthorne was a prolific American author who is known for his short stories. Born in Salem, Massachusetts, Hawthorne has experience with the Halloween essence which comes through in his writing.

“The Birthmark” is a short story that follows a scientist who becomes obsessed with a birthmark on his wife, trying to figure out if he can remove it or not. “The Minister’s Black Veil” follows a similar tale of obsession, as a minister shows up wearing a black veil, and his congregation becomes fascinated with why he's wearing it.

Assistant Teaching Professor Timothy Loperfido, 38, of Ocean Township, New Jersey, recommended these works by Hawthorne and finds short stories to be a great vessel for a good scare.

Loperfido also said short stories are perfect for the fall season. as the limited length creates a certain unsettling feeling; there’s an intensity in them that isn’t always present in drawn-out stories.

“This sort of New England gothic tail is kind of spooky," Loperfido said. "I think stories about intense human emotions or obsessions, there’s no monster really, but the lengths that people will go to is the scary thing.”

title: Penn State cross country readies for Big Ten Championships in Madison
author: Luci Palacios | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Big Ten Cross Country Championships will take place Friday in Madison, Wisconsin, with competition scheduled to begin at 11:35 a.m.

All Big Ten schools will field a women’s team, while Maryland, Northwestern and USC won’t compete in the men’s race. The men will compete in an 8k, while the women will run a 6k.

The Penn State men’s and women’s teams will look to build on last season’s performances, with the women coming off a second-place team finish and the men aiming to improve on an eighth-place result.

Oregon enters the championships as the defending champion in both divisions after sweeping the team titles last season.

Men’s Race: Penn State looks to improve

The Nittany Lions return several runners from last year’s meet, led by senior Nick Sloff and graduate student Ryan Watson.

Sloff finished 23rd overall last season with a time of 24:00.4, making him Penn State’s top finisher. He’s entering this year’s championship with momentum after being named the USTFCCCA National Athlete of the Week earlier in the season. Sloff earned the honor after winning the 8k Gold Race at the Paul Short Run.

Watson, who placed 40th last season in 24:18.7, provides Penn State with solid experience in the conference. The Nittany Lions also return sophomore Jaxon Schoedel, who finished 58th in 24:32.9, and senior Brian DiCola, who placed 72nd in 24:43.7.

Sophomore Adam Kingston, senior Logan Strawser, graduate student Caiden Leen and sophomore Isaac Oppermann are also among Penn State’s returning runners from last year’s championships.

Oregon will be among the teams to watch after winning last year’s title and entering the meet ranked No. 6 nationally. Michigan State, ranked No. 22 nationally, finished second last season, while Wisconsin took third.

The individual competition will feature a new champion after Oregon’s Abel Laadjel, who won last year’s race in 23:11.5, graduated. Michigan State’s Riley Hough and Thomas Westphal finished second and third, returning for another chance.

Women’s Race: Building on Success

The blue and white are seeing several runners return from last year’s meet, including graduate students Charlotte Costich and Lea Hatcher. They’re also nationally ranked No. 26, showcasing a hopeful meet ahead.

Costich was Penn State’s top finisher last season, placing eighth overall out of 165 runners with a time of 20:11.7. Her top-10 finish gives the Nittany Lions an experienced front-runner heading into this year’s championship. Her season-best time entering the meet is 21:03.6.

Hatcher also returns after finishing 29th overall last season in 20:43.2. She enters the championships with a season-best time of 21:28.5, adding another seasoned runner to Penn State’s lineup.

Senior Claire Zubey, who placed 49th last season in 21:04.6, and sophomore Eva Kynaston, who finished 58th in 21:15.9, are also returning. Graduate student Katie Dallas, who placed 71st, and sophomore Liliah Gordon, who finished 78th, provide additional depth.

Penn State has a strong history at the conference championships, winning two women’s team titles in 2009 and 2015. Last season’s runner-up finish gives the Nittany Lions a foundation to build on as they look to compete against high-level competition.

Oregon swept the top of last year’s women’s team standings and is returning individual champion Diana Cherotich, who won in 19:31.3. The Ducks also placed four runners in the individual top five, demonstrating the depth they bring into this year’s meet.

title: ‘A shining star,’ OC Taylor Mouser ventured from Little Caesars to Penn State
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Taylor Mouser was making pizzas and manning the cash register at his parents’ Little Caesars for nearly a year in Chandler, Arizona, after graduating from Adams State University in 2013. He worked shifts at the restaurant while searching for any coaching opportunity he could find, applying to dozens of college roles across the country just to come up empty.

But in 2015, Matt Campbell answered his call at Toledo and brought him on as an unpaid graduate assistant. Mouser packed up his life and moved to Ohio.

“I’d still be at Little Caesars if it wasn’t for coach Campbell,” Mouser said in February. “I don’t forget that. I’ve tried to do it all just to repay him back for being the only guy that returned my phone call when I was graduated, worked at Little Caesars, reaching out to every school. He’s the only person that hit me back.”

That opportunity launched Mouser’s coaching career, and he began a rapid climb through the ranks at Toledo and Iowa State before eventually becoming Penn State’s offensive coordinator this offseason, following Campbell from the Cyclones.

“Taylor has proven over his two-year period to be one of the up and coming bright minds in all of college football,” Campbell said in February. “I think he’s got fearlessness as a play caller. It’s been awesome to be part of his growth journey.”

Mouser’s rise required years of hard work, patience and a willingness to take on any responsibility. He said in February that he “just went to work and did everything they asked me to.”

The initial responsibilities Mouser had weren’t glamorous. Washington State wide receivers coach Derek Sage, who held the same position at Toledo when Mouser arrived, said he “was helping our recruiting guys lick stamps and send out recruiting mailers.”

“He just was always around,” Sage told The Daily Collegian. “‘Can I do it? What can I do? How can I help? What can I do next?’ No task was too small for Taylor, and he did it all with just a ‘yes sir’ mentality.”

Although Mouser’s time at Toledo was short-lived, he developed an important relationship with Sage that helped shape his early coaching career, as Sage soon let him join him at times and work with the receivers. That opportunity, which Sage and Mouser went at together, gave Mouser his first valuable experience coaching players, he said.

When Campbell moved to Iowa State in 2016, so did Mouser, as Campbell continued to give him opportunities. Sage remained at Toledo, meaning this time it was then-offensive coordinator Tom Manning taking Mouser under his wing.

Mouser remained a graduate assistant in his first year at Iowa State, but similar to his prior gig, he quickly began picking up more responsibilities and new titles, Manning said in an interview.

“For me, it was always pretty easy to see that he was going to be a pretty good football coach and a shining star,” Manning said. “(He) just needed to get as many opportunities as he can, and then eventually we were able to move him into the full-time position as the tight end coach.”

After years as an assistant, Mouser became Iowa State’s tight ends coach in 2021, giving him a larger role in developing players and building relationships with them. At just 30-years-old, Manning said Mouser’s relatively young age helped him relate to his players.

“Not being their buddy, but by coaching them. You just felt like there was something about this guy that you certainly could feel he had a future in what he was doing,” Manning said.

As Mouser was around the team more as a position coach, his knowledge of the game grew. He began developing a deeper understanding of Iowa State’s offensive system, learning the intricacies of different positions and how they worked together. Manning said his knowledge was evident right away.

“For a young guy, that’s always the sign of a guy that has a bright future and could be a really good football coach,” Manning said.

Manning’s influence extended beyond helping Mouser earn a full-time coaching position: Even after the two went their separate ways, Mouser continued to rely on him for guidance. Mouser credited Manning and Sage as two of his biggest mentors, as “they’ll tell you what you need to hear and not necessarily what you want to hear.”

Their guidance helped him navigate the challenges of climbing the coaching ranks.

“I wouldn’t be where I’m at without (Tom),” Mouser said in February. “What he’s done, the feedback that he’s given me the last two years. He’s been so influential.”

Just three years after becoming Iowa State’s tight ends coach, Mouser was promoted to offensive coordinator. Campbell had witnessed his development firsthand and entrusted him with leading the Cyclones’ offense.

Like the other opportunities he earned, Mouser quickly went to work and found success leading Iowa State’s offense. During his first season calling plays, the Cyclones recorded their first 11-win season in program history, while Mouser helped oversee an offense that featured several future NFL players, including wide receivers Jaylin Noel and Jayden Higgins.

Tight ends Charlie Kolar and Chase Allen also reached the big leagues after playing under Mouser earlier in his career.

“He did a hell of a job developing players in the National Football League at the tight end position,” Sage said. “(I’m) not surprised one bit. Taylor deserves every bit of this.”

Mouser spent two seasons as Iowa State’s offensive coordinator and appeared poised to take the next step in his coaching career when Campbell departed for Penn State in December.

Campbell believed his longtime assistant could succeed him as the Cyclones’ head coach, but Iowa State went in a different direction. So Mouser followed Campbell to Happy Valley, keeping his roles as offensive coordinator and tight ends coach and continuing a decadelong partnership. The decision was one of little hesitation.

“When coach Campbell told me what was going on, I sprinted to it, and I couldn’t wait to be able to come here,” Mouser said. “This is a dream job for anybody that likes to coach tight ends with what this place is and the people that they've been able to put out here. To be an offensive coordinator for a guy like coach Campbell was huge to me at a program like this.”

Mouser and Campbell brought several familiar faces from Iowa State, including Rocco Becht, wide receiver Chase Sowell and running back Carson Hansen. Their familiarity with his offensive system provided a foundation as he adjusted to his new home with the Nittany Lions.

Over a decade after Mouser struggled to find a program that would give him a chance, he found himself leading the offense at one of college football’s most prolific programs. It's a destination he was hard pressed to imagine while making pizzas in Arizona.

“This place is incredible, it’s a school that you dream about when you’re a small-school guy like me,” Mouser said in February. “Even the idea of coming and coaching in a place like this, it’s so far fetched. It doesn’t even enter your mind when you’re where I was at before.”

title: New environmental engineering degree offers students more hands-on experience
author: Charlie Wallin | For The Collegian
description:
Penn State launched a new undergraduate environmental engineering degree this fall, allowing for a new branch of learning and hands-on experience for many students.

After the university discontinued the degree in 1987, it was brought back after nearly 40 years. The degree, the fourth of the environmental engineering degrees, focuses on sustainability, municipal infrastructure, water quality and treatment systems.

Nathaniel Warner, an associate professor of environmental engineering and the faculty lead for the new degree, said student interest was the main driver to bring the degree — which would complement the minor — to Penn State.

“Students were like, ‘Hey, I want the minor,’ and we had maybe 10 (students) 10 years ago, and now it’s something like 60 to 70 each year. So that increase and the number of students interested kind of kicked off four years ago, but it took a long time to get from the idea of, ‘Let’s relaunch this degree,’ to have it launched and official this fall,” Warner said.

Warner also takes his students in Civil Engineering 475 out into the nearby streams, measuring bugs and looking at the quality of water.

“It’s an experience, and positive or negative, they remember it,” Warner said.

The smaller class sizes, especially the 400-level courses, Warner said, allows for more hands-on work rather than typical lectures. Since Pennsylvania has the most stream miles in the continental U.S. — beat by Alaska overall — the opportunities for involvement are practically in the school’s backyard.

Lauren McPhillips, an associate professor of civil and environmental engineering and agricultural and biological engineering, teaches the capstone design course in environmental water resources, and said she really enjoys being the “solution classes.”

“We often try to be working with local practitioners or partners that have an issue that needs to be dealt with, and that’s fun because the students work the whole way through,” McPhillips said.

McPhillips said that there has been an increase in students interested in the idea of sustainability, and making an impact in the world around them might be a highlight for prospective students.

“I think students are attracted to this kind of area because they are interested in sustainability, but also, maybe you like to be outside, but you also want to figure out the solutions to keep a healthy environment while also supporting development,” McPhillips said.

There are also a plethora of minors and certificates available at Penn State, and with the support from faculty and professors, can lead to opportunities that might not exist at other universities.

Jeremy Gernand, an associate professor of environmental health and safety engineering and the undergraduate program chair of environmental systems engineering, said that the diverse choices can be interesting for students.

“Students can get involved a little bit, they can get involved a lot, they can add environmental flavors onto other skillsets… all that is not common at other universities. There’s a lot of choice here,” Gernand said.

With Penn State College of Engineering consistently ranking highly year after year, offering heavy hands-on activities and engagement for students can solidify post-graduate opportunities.

“The students get to dive in and figure out how to fix sores in the environment, and those are the kind of real world impacts they get to do when they leave here,” Gernand said.

title: Penn State wrestling holds open race at 141, a title contender at 149
author: Gavin Leonard | The Daily Collegian
description:
As Penn State attempts to build on its dominance of collegiate wrestling, one of its first orders of business will be setting the starting lineup for the beginning of the season.

While some positions within the 141 and 149-pound weight class are nearly set in stone with returning players who have championship pedigree, others are up for grabs.

Here’s how the lineup lays out at those two weight classes in the 26-27 season.

141

The battle for the leading spot at 141 will be headlined by Nate Desmond, Masanosuke Ono and Braeden Davis.

There’s certainly an argument to be made for Davis, who’s currently No. 12 in FloWrestling’s preseason rankings. In the latest InterMat rankings, Desmond was the wrestler ranked at No. 18.

The Belleville, Michigan, native is the most accomplished option, as he’s won a Big Ten Championship during his freshman year at 125, followed by an All-American bid in his sophomore season at 133 pounds.

Yet the All-American dealt with triumph, as Davis notched a 2-2 record at the NCAA tournament without recording a win against a top 10 opponent during the season.

With the down year behind him, a move up to 141 could rejuvenate the All-American.

Redshirt freshman Nate Desmond will insert his name into the ballot. Desmond put together an impressive resume in his redshirt season at both 125 and 141, finishing 7-0, including a 5-3 win over teammate Luke Lilledahl in the Black Knight Open final.

After a midseason jump to 141, the Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, native defeated All-American Dylan Ragusin, showing he can compete against the best in the division if given the starting role.

Ono can be considered a wildcard, as it remains in question whether his talent as a freestyle wrestler can translate to NCAA folkstyle wrestling.

Ono has gained recognition for his wins against elite competition in non-NCAA sanctioned matches. He defeated Marcus Blaze and Spencer Lee during the 2024 U20 World Championships. Two years later, he routed 2026 runner-up Ben Davino 4-0 at RAF 12.

Ono did not wrestle any folkstyle matches last year, so there’s no telling how the transition will go. However, if there’s any program in the country that can make the switch seamless, it’s Penn State.

Two redshirt freshmen round out the roster: Hayden Cunningham and Cael Nasdeo. While Cunningham displayed a winning record at 10-5, Nasdeo held a disappointing 2-6 record last season.

Both will continue to develop under Penn State’s program and be ready when called upon.

149

While the starting spot is in play for multiple wrestlers at 141, Penn State has a clear leader at 149 pounds.

Shayne Van Ness will enter the season as one of the favorites to win the title after losing in the championship match in overtime to Stanford’s Aden Valencia. Throughout the season, Van Ness was consistently ranked the first in the country at 149 .

The two-time All-American earned a 25-1 record while notching six pins, 10 technical falls and four major decisions. The senior will have one final year of eligibility to reach the top of his weight class.

The talent behind Van Ness deserves to be mentioned as well. Connor Pierce is a major backup piece for Penn State and has shown potential in minimal opportunities last season. At the Southern Scuffle, Pierce went 6-0 to win the 149-pound title. He knocked off then-No. 24 Max Petersen and then-No. 26 Brock Herman to achieve the accolade.

Outside of those named, the rest of Penn State’s wrestlers who will look to develop this season. Brock Weiss and Dalton Perry, two redshirt freshmen, and true freshman Sam Herring will likely sit behind Pierce and Van Ness throughout the season and appear in minimal bouts.

title: Different paths lead Penn State women’s soccer teammates to same 2026 U-20 World Cup
author: Sara Castrovinci | The Daily Collegian
description:
Kealey Titmuss grew up watching what she called an “incredible dynasty” get built in the U.S. women’s national team. This fall, the Penn State goalkeeper earned a spot on the United States’ U-20 World Cup roster alongside a Nittany Lions teammate: Emma Johnson, a true freshman who carried the same childhood dream of representing her country on the world stage.

“I got to watch all these amazing players come through this system, hear their stories and watch them succeed. So it’s just so surreal that I’m kind of on the path that some of these players were a part of,” Titmuss said. “I was so excited to be doing it with her, to have EJ on the journey with me and be able to support her.”

Their paths to the same roster couldn’t have looked more different. After Titmuss, a Grand Blanc, Michigan, native, made her way through the youth national team setup in the U-16, U-17 and U-19 international camps, coach Erica Dambach recruited her when she was the nation's top-ranked goalkeeper in the class of 2024.

Though Johnson is new to the collegiate level, she has multiple caps for the U-20 squad under her belt, playing in five matches with three starts this year. She totaled nine appearances in her youth national career. She’s also been a constant in the system at the U-15, U-18 and U-19 levels.

Johnson, a Greenfield, Indiana native, started in her first two collegiate games against No. 2 Notre Dame and No. 22 West Virginia before leaving for the World Cup in Poland: She tallied 59 and 67 minutes in the matches, an impressive stat for a player new to the Penn State program.

“I'd consider her a junior. She had the freshman experience her junior year of high school,” Dambach said. “When I watched Emma play in her senior year of high school, she was ready.”

Johnson credited a lot of her confidence heading into the World Cup to Dambach’s wealth of advice. Dambach has deep coaching roots as an assistant and head coach with the United States youth and senior national teams for over 16 years. She said the coach helped her prepare for the world stage both on and off the field, especially with her mentality.

Despite her accolades, Titmuss has yet to see any minutes on the pitch for the blue and white.

“She has worked really hard to avoid the comparison game,” Dambach said. “She has played the role of backup goalkeeper, kind of as an apprentice, growing, learning and committing herself to her development.”

Working alongside Nittany Lions goalkeeper coach Tim Wassell has been a key factor in Titmuss’s success, she said. Wassell has drawn in seven top-five Top Drawer soccer classes since 2014 and has consistently produced professional-level NWSL and abroad recruits.

“He’s been in my corner every step of the way,” Titmuss, a redshirt sophomore, said. “I have a lot of faith in him in my development and I can feel myself getting better.”

Though they’re in different chapters of their personal athletic stories, that hasn't prevented Johnson and Titmuss from developing a close relationship. Johnson said their friendship formed in a “unique way,” having bonded through previous national team camps prior to joining the blue and white roster.

“It was a great moment to go into the World Cup on the same college team — not a lot of teammates get to do that,” Johnson said.

Despite doubts about her size, speed, injuries and mentality, Johnson maintained her confidence. Wearing the crest is “more than ourselves,” she said.

“You have a lot of pressure on social media from everything that the women of the U.S. team have done. But, owning that, I think pressure is a privilege,” Johnson said.

Despite a hard-fought 1-1 draw through regulation time, the States’ journey in the U-20 World Cup ended Sept. 16 in the Round of 16 when they lost to Brazil 5-4 in a penalty shootout. After the loss, Johnson and Titmuss made sure to channel their newfound international experience and game knowledge back to Penn State.

Johnson and Titmuss returned to Jeffrey Field to continue using their newfound confidence and knowledge to help push the Nittany Lions forward as the Big Ten and NCAA Tournament approach. Investing in her teammates and being the “best version” of herself is one of her top priorities. She plays alongside some of the best players in the country, Titmuss said, so it’s important to bring back her ability to adapt to her teammates' needs.

Dambach said the competitive experience of the World Cup helped them acclimate again to the Nittany Lion culture, and lent them a new perspective on approaching competition.

“They look at these opponents with respect, but not fear,” Dambach said.

title: Penn State men’s soccer defeats Duquesne on Senior Day, snaps winless streak
author: Ava Aguiar | The Daily Collegian
description:
Coming off a breakthrough match with Wisconsin last week, the Nittany Lions kept the momentum going with a 3-1 win to break their losing streak and post their first win since Sept. 4

Duquesne came into the match on a three-game win streak and a 9-3-2 record, but Penn State found its groove and performed like the top-tier team they’ve had the potential to be.

1st half

Penn State keeper Justin Ross saw his first start of the season in goal, rather than the traditional starter Daniel Peluffo-Wiese.

The Nittany Lions came in blazing after a first-minute shot attempt by Beckham Brown earned the team a corner. With an assist from Grant McIntosh and Noah Förster, Etienne Reck managed to get his foot on the ball to score the first point of the match just three minutes into play.

“This was important because after an early goal, they kept pushing us and we wanted to win the game for Grant. It was his old team and the pressure was good,” Reck said.

Reck has been a star player for the blue and white, totaling most of the shots and being the playmaker on offense. He holds himself to a high standard and hopes to continue to improve going forward.

“I want to score more goals, to be honest. I would say this season, where the full team is new and all the coaches, but we have a really good team,” Reck said. “The beginning was hard for us; we had some injuries, but we keep going now and we won. We want to win the last game in Maryland.”

Duquesne made its way down into Penn State territory, taking a shot in the far middle of the box, but was caught by Ross as he slid across the goal post.

The Dukes were persistent, but the blue and white kept possession of the ball and pressure in the Duquesne box. Noah Andreas took a shot that narrowly missed the side of the goal.

Fouls started to fly 15 minutes in, with both teams giving the other opportunities at a free kick, but were unsuccessful as the ball went back and forth.

Duquesne earned its first corner of the game in the 26th, as Cody Da took the ball down the field. A close save by Ross took the ball out of the box and back into the hands of Penn State.

What looked like it should have earned a handball on Duquesne led to an open-net opportunity for the Nittany Lions as Dukes goalkeeper Sam Coss scrambled to get back up from a dive. Peter Doran acted quickly, passing the ball to Joe Buckley as he launched the ball into the back of the net to put the score up 2-0.

Penn State’s offense continued to create opportunities as Andreas blasted a shot, hardly missing as it landed right outside the post.

The game was halted with three minutes left to go in the half for a VAR review for a red card on Duquesne’s Steel Bayer. The call was good and Bayer was ejected from the game.

The Nittany Lions capitalized on a shaken-up Duquesne, scoring their third goal of the game with two minutes left to go in the half. A powerful kick by Grant McIntosh went right into the goal and over the head of Coss, putting Penn State up 3-0 after its best-played half all season.

2nd Half

Both teams came into the second half ready to go, as a back-and-forth between the boxes made up the first five minutes of the half.

The Dukes found a way to put the pressure on Penn State’s Ross with a foul called on Arian St. Recinos, giving them a chance for a free kick. Ross had three tight saves, punching the ball over the net to keep the Dukes off the board.

However, Duquesne managed to get their first point on the board from a penalty kick shot by Dagur Hakon Matthiason after being fouled by Reck.

Ross had another great save, jumping onto the ball while being rushed at by two of the Dukes’ offense.

“We really see (Ross) as a six; he has earned the right to start and play 90 minutes. He had some great saves; he’s so athletic, quick reactions, are top-notch, distribution on the ball,” Dow said. “So proud of him for getting his first win at his first college game.”

Duquesne was able to keep possession of the ball long enough to take another shot before Amadou Kone took the ball back into Duke territory.

The blue and white had three substitutions before their corner on Coss, with Brown, Morgan Marshall and Moritz Weber coming back on to the pitch.

A slow back-and-forth between the teams filled the half, with both teams exchanging possession of the ball, but Penn State held strong with their defensive play. Blocking any chance of another Duke goal.

The Nittany Lions took the 3-1 victory on their Senior Day and final home game of the season.

“They deserve to be honored, they deserve our best game and they also showed up and played fantastic, and that’s what our team is about,” Dow said. “This is what we are building and it shows that we are heading in the right direction.”

Up Next

Penn State travels to No. 11 Maryland on Nov. 4 for the final game of its season, with start time set for 8 p.m.
