title: Penn State men’s basketball notebook | Mike Rhoades speaks at local media day
author: Myles Hannak | The Daily Collegian
description:
It’s a homecoming for Happy Valley hoops.

Penn State’s season resumes Monday, with the blue and white set to face Canisius at the Bryce Jordan Center. After a 2-0 exhibition stretch, the new-look Nittany Lions soon show home fans what they’re made of, yet before that, Penn State held local media day at the BJC.

Here’s a recap of what Mike Rhoades said at the podium ahead of the 2026-27 season.

Recruitin’

As the Nittany Lions retained only three players from last year through a transfer portal exodus, Rhoades and Co. were tasked with rebuilding Penn State in the warm summer months. It was a task they took in stride, building a team that touched many corners of not only the collegiate basketball scene, but also across the globe.

With Euro-freshmen and newbies from the JUCO and DII level, Rhoades revealed how the wide acquisitions came to be.

“Number one, relationships and then number two is the players that you like,” Rhoades said. “The first question you ask is, can you afford them? The second question is, do they fit us character-wise? … Would they be a good fit here at Penn State?”

The financial question was asked to Rhoades again, and he echoed the same statement he made over the summer, referring to his father’s advice: “It is what it is, figure it out and move forward.”

“We sit, and we discuss it a lot; we debate it a lot,” Rhoades said. “We try to do the best we can with what we have to get the players that we can.”

Bringing the energy

With new players comes a new identity, yet for a completely new roster it means a total culture switch. In any transitional period, it can take time for that vision to fully be widely accepted, but for the blue and white there wasn’t any doubt about where this team wants to be.

“We got to be tough and physical; we got to be a smart, high-IQ basketball team,” Rhoades said. “We may be different and look different than some other teams in our league, but when it comes down to it, we got to be tough and I don't mean dirty in a bad way, but dirty and grimy and fight every possession.”

In the pair of exhibition games, the Nittany Lions upheld that notion so far that season. Penn State has fought for buckets, going to the foul line in droves — shooting 59 free throws across those two games.

“Being aggressive, getting downhill, getting two or three on the ball, making the defense collapse. If you can do that and draw fouls, you get free points at the line, but also put your opponent at a disadvantage,” Rhoades said. “We are big and strong. We have some physical guys, so we got to use that. We have a couple of guards that can get downhill, but we got to be able to share the ball and spread it, get threes as well. That that's got to be our formula.”

Mentals

Getting a squad to that level is one thing, but doing it with a group that’s all playing together for the first time is another. With Rhoades having the tough task of doing both, he’s revealed his process for building those mentals for the Nittany Lions, who were already picked to be the bottom of the Big Ten by The Columbus Dispatch.

“We're putting this team together and trying to get better every day,” Rhoades said. “Just stacking days of the type of basketball we want to play and the way we want to approach it … We got a ways to go, but I'm I'm optimistic and excited about the way they've approached it all, so we're we're gonna I think we're gonna get better as we go through the year each week just because of the approach that they have.”

The Nittany Lions also got a lot older after being the youngest roster in the conference right now, which has been a key catalyst to this development.

“They're not miffed by something being different or being coached differently and stuff like that. So just really, we have a group of guys that I think are mature on and off the court,” Rhoades said. “They go to class, they're on time, they're early, they're doing a great job taking care of their bodies and then they get on the court, they're dealing with what's the most important thing, so that part has been fun and refreshing.”

The transition to State College can be harsh, especially with the number of players from overseas avenues. With those new faces, Rhoades gave praise to his returnees, 7-footer Ivan Jurić, fifth-year Josh Reed and guard Reggie Grodin, who had work on his knee this offseason, Rhoades confirmed after using his redshirt last year.

“All three of them are good students. They're on time. They're ready to go. They're ready to work. They're coachable,” Rhoades said. “We had a lot of new guys get here in June and throughout the summer who had a lot of questions — Those guys helped those guys, for sure.”

title: 'They’re ready to go’ | Penn State men’s basketball’s returners set to anchor new-look roster
author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian
description:
Josh Reed and Reggie Grodin are roommates. Ivan Juric lives next door.

In a locker room otherwise composed of newcomers, the trio will enter the 2026-27 campaign as the only continuity with last season’s iteration of the Nittany Lions, and are set to begin their second season under Mike Rhoades against Canisius on Monday.

At local media day, the fourth-year head coach pointed to them as having helped to anchor the largely new roster.

“They're just high-level kids,” Rhoades said. “They're about the right stuff, and I think the type of teammates they are helps with the leadership from everybody, and those guys have done a good job of that with all the new guys.”

Reed and Juric played significant roles in their debut campaigns in the blue and white, posting 11.5 and 10.2 points per game, respectively, and started together in 25 out of 32 games.

The duo should continue to consistently slot into Rhoades’ frontcourt throughout the upcoming season, likely alongside Miami (OH) transfer Brant Byers, and the rapport built last season will carry over into 2026-27.

“(We’ve) played a lot of games and a lot of minutes together, so the chemistry is pretty seamless,” Reed said. “We get along great both on and off the court. I love playing with (Ivan). He's been good in our exhibition so far. He's been good in practice, so I'm excited.”

Juric was a stalwart at center while Reed generally played power forward last season, but the Croatian identified the versatility that both he and Reed possess as something that could give Penn State an advantage while they play together.

“Both me and him can play both inside and out,” Juric said. “Depends on what the defense gives us. So yeah, I think it really will be (a) problem for other teams. Just (having) us both at the same time on the court.”

While his 7-foot stature might suggest otherwise, Juric has a relatively reserved personality.

After being tested as a true freshman, Rhoades has high expectations for Juric’s second campaign.

“Ivan's a quiet guy, and he's still one of the youngest guys on the team,” Rhoades said. “Getting thrown in the fire last year and the level of maturity he had, we were asking a lot of him last year. I think there was great growth there; his family and his people back home were really impressed how far he's come, and I think his sky's the limit for him.”

Reed was the only Penn State player celebrated on last season’s Senior Night against Ohio State. He graduated with an MBA in the spring, and completed an internship with Harris Blitzer Sports & Entertainment, the company that owns the Philadelphia 76ers, over the summer.

A variety of legal maneuvers in multiple states have ruled him eligible to return to Penn State this year, a move that Reed described as “pretty easy.” Still, the ever-shifting landscape of college sports means that there’s still a chance that his eligibility could be rescinded.

“Just taking it day by day, working, working it out on the court,” Reed said. “Just worried about basketball at this point. Not really focused on the outside noise and things like that.”

As the fifth-year from Atlanta wraps up his college basketball career, his roommate Grodin is just getting started after seeing no game action and redshirting last season.

Still one of the less-experienced members of Rhoades’ roster, he’s seen the group flip from mostly young players like himself to a more veteran-heavy team.

“I've never been in a situation with that, but I guess that's the norm in college basketball now,” Grodin said. “It's been great. I don't want to say you can't win, but it's definitely difficult to win with a bunch of young guys in the Big Ten versus (having) more experience.”

According to Rhoades, Grodin was injured over the summer and “had to get some work done on a knee.” All signs suggest that he’ll be good to go against the Golden Griffins, though.

With 11 players joining the roster since Penn State last took to the court against Northwestern on March 10, the Nittany Lions’ old guard has instilled the established ideals into the newcomers.

Byers, who averaged 14.2 points per game in the Redhawks’ magical run to the NCAA Tournament last season, said they’ve echoed Rhoades’ values in every facet so far.

“They know the way that Coach Rhoades wants to play, the practice style and game style and stuff like that,” Byers said. “They've done a pretty good job at leading in that way, whether it's vocal or by example.”

Five days before the 2026-27 season gets underway, Rhoades was full of praise for the character shown by his three returners.

“All three of those guys are great teammates,” Rhoades said. “Before you get to leadership, our number one rule is (to) take care of your own stuff. Those guys do that at a high level. All three of them are good students. They're on time. They're ready to go. They're ready to work.”

title: ‘He’s pounding away’ | Marcus Neal Jr. making most of long-term change to linebacker
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
When Marcus Neal Jr. transferred to Penn State in January, many thought he would be playing his usual position at safety.

Neal started for Iowa State at safety in all 12 games for Matt Campbell last year. He also started the first four games at that position for the Nittany Lions this season. But after Neal was without a defensive snap in the White Out game against USC, questions were raised about his role in Penn State’s elite secondary.

“I think today was such a unique football game, and I think as we went into it, coverage was at a premium in terms of you know what was going to go on,” Campbell said postgame. “I think collectively, as we're continuing to put this defense together, Marcus is a critical piece to our success.”

The following week, Campbell announced that linebacker Alex Tatsch would be out with a season-ending injury. He then said Neal was “a guy that can certainly find himself more in the linebacker rotation than just that safety rotation.”

Coming out of the bye week, Campbell said Wednesday that Neal has switched from safety to linebacker and spent the extra time practicing in his new position last week.

“I think Marcus is a guy that's got the ability to help us as well,” Campbell said. “I think (Marcus and Cam Smith) have bright futures there, and both guys really had great weeks last week.”

As a result of Tatsch’s absence, the Nittany Lions were down to just three linebackers in their last two games: Kooper Ebel, Tony Rojas and Cael Brezina. While Rojas was shining, Ebel was struggling and Brezina didn’t see much playing time. Smith, meanwhile, was out with injury.

But now, Penn State has a fourth option at linebacker, potentially even a fifth if Smith is healthy, which it seems like he is coming out of the bye. Neal will likely have some bumps along the way as he navigates a new position, but has a head start as he already understands the nature of D’Anton Lynn’s defense.

“It’s great to have another guy in the room, another guy that we trust,” Ebel said Wednesday. “He’s done a great job. He’s a really smart football player and he’s done a great job at practice.”

As much as the linebacker room has enjoyed the addition of Neal, he’s also reacted positively to the position change, according to Campbell. After going from starting in 16 straight games to being on the sidelines, the move will give Neal an opportunity to see the field again.

“Marcus just wants to play,” Campbell said. “There’s only one speed with Marcus. I think (he) was really excited about finding the right fit for him and the right home for him.”

Position changes have happened for the Nittany Lions before. During Campbell’s short time in Happy Valley, he has moved quarterback Peyton Falzone to tight end and linebackers LaVar Arrington II and Caleb Bacon to defensive end, with the latter appearing to pay off.

Now it’s Neal’s time to make that jump. The former safety, who’s been nicknamed “Shark” by both himself and his teammates, has shown physicality and toughness during his two years with the Cyclones and in his early start at Penn State.

Neal now has that opportunity to bring that attitude and skillset to a linebacker room which needs help.

“He's attacked it,” Ebel said. “No pointing fingers, no complaining, nothing. That's just Marcus' character, that's who he is. He's going to show up, he's going to find a way, and he's pounding away. He's doing a great job.”

title: Will WR Koby Howard play against Purdue? Penn State won’t take any risks with its budding star
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Wide receiver Koby Howard is close to a return, and Penn State is eager to get him back.

Matt Campbell said Howard’s been on the practice field Tuesday and Wednesday, but his status is still “questionable” heading into the Nittany Lions’ game against Purdue on Saturday.

Although the Nittany Lions want their top receiver from the nonconference slate back in action, Campbell said he doesn’t want to have Howard suit up too early and will likely keep him on a pitch count if he plays this weekend.

“We'll see what tomorrow really looks like, and feel confident that if he is capable of playing, what's that look like?” Campbell said. “How many reps does that look like? If he's not ready, I'm not putting him on that football field until he's 100% ready to go.”

The Nittany Lions haven’t had a fully healthy wide receiver room the entire season, as Chase Sowell and Brett Eskildsen were dealing with lingering injuries early in the season before Howard went down long-term.

Howard was Penn State’s offense through the first three weeks. He had over 100 receiving yards in two of the three games, his best being a 161-yard outing against Marshall in Week 1. Sowell has stepped up in Howard’s absence, now leading the team with 510 receiving yards.

But Campbell is excited to see how the pair plays together when Howard’s back.

“The unfortunate piece is you haven't had those guys on the field at the same time, probably playing in that same rhythm,” Campbell said Tuesday. “Getting Koby back will be a huge asset to our football team. That's why we got to make sure he's healthy and truly ready to play on the football field and make sure that we get the Koby that you saw the first three games of the season, not a shell of Koby.”

Sowell himself said he’s eagerly awaiting Howard’s return, not only because he brings the “swag” to the offense with accessories and infectious confidence, but because he can back up his talk with results. Sowell called Howard’s confidence an “F-U mentality to the defense.”

“It’s kind of like, ‘I want the ball, I want to make the play,’” Sowell said. “And that you need that from some guys. We can't wait for him back on the field for sure.”

Wide receiver Zay Robinson said having Howard back gives Penn State more options on the line of scrimmage, as the Nittany Lions then have multiple players who can run different routes and play at different spots.

Robinson said both Howard and Sowell can play from the slot and both can win individual one-on-one matchups from out wide, and Penn State fans will be “in for a treat” with the receiver room finally at full strength.

“(Howard and Sowell) can take it no matter where they're at on the field,” Robinson said. “They both complement each other greatly in that way, and they both are physical, want to play ball and just are really great football players.”

He also said Howard has looked “great” physically at practice this week and he’s approached the field with the same mentality as he always had.

“He's attacking every day, exactly how he needs to be,” Robinson said. “And we’re just happy to have him back whenever he's ready.”

title: Penn State notebook | Matt Campbell says Marcus Neal Jr. has made a long-term move to LB
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State is still in search of its first Big Ten win of the season after starting 0-4 in conference play.

Matt Campbell met with the media on Wednesday ahead of the Nittany Lions’ Halloween matchup with Purdue to discuss cornerback Audavion Collins, recruiting during the bye week and the depleted linebacker room.

Here’s what Campbell had to say.

Collins’ dominant first half

Penn State has a lock down corner on one side of the ball in Collins, who’s provided consistency to a team that’s struggled with it this season. Campbell recognized the talent he has with Collins and how he’s flying under the radar despite his strong first half.

“I think (Collins) has been exceptional, and we continue to talk about the type of team we want to have, tough and disciplined, having the ability to show player-driven leadership, one of the guys that I would say has embodied that to a T so far has been (Collins),” Campbell said.

Campbell believes that people “would certainly be” sleeping on Collins as a player who’s played like one of the best cornerbacks in the country.

Collins leads the country in highest forced incompletion rate at 42.9% and sits tied for second in fewest yards allowed per snap in coverage with .20 yards per snap. He’s also only allowed four completions on 15 targets, which leads the nation.

“If you go out to practice every day, the same guy you see on Saturdays, that is the guy that you see on Tuesday, on Wednesday, on Thursday, and to me, that's why he's playing at that rate,” Campbell said. “He embodies what it looks like to be great, to look like a pro at this point in his career and I'm really proud of (Collins).”

Bye week recruiting

Campbell went on the recruiting trail during the bye week, mainly visiting potential flip candidates in the 2027 recruiting class. He went all around the eastern part of the United States to check in on targets.

“I think for me that was probably the most enjoyable part that I've had in the last couple weeks is getting out on the road,” Campbell said.

The most notable player he visited was 3-star running back Jordan Hall, who committed to the Nittany Lions the next day after Campbell watched him play on Friday night.

Campbell had the ability to take a step back and realize the strength the Penn State brand has in this age of college football.

“The realization of number one, the power of what Penn State football is in terms of going in and having great conversations with high school football coaches and their family, but I also think the belief in us and our staff and what we've been able to accomplish, not just you know in our short time here, but over the long haul,” Campbell said.

Another target Campbell paid a visit to was Rutgers 3-star wide receiver commit Arnold Mugerwa. He made the short trip to Johnstown, Pennsylvania, and handed out an offer to the 6-foot-3 wide receiver.

During the week, he recognized the excitement still around the program despite a 3-4 start in his first season.

“I think there is really good energy and there is really a lot of excitement around where we're going and what we are trying to build here,” Campbell said. “The conversations are pretty simple. This is who we are, this is where we're trying to go and this is what we're looking for. We really haven't wavered from that. So I do appreciate it. It was a really great week for not only myself but our staff.”

Assessing the linebacker room

Penn State has had to work around a linebacker room that’s consistently dealt with injuries during the 2026 season.

Linebacker Alex Tatsch was ruled out for the season in the week after the USC loss, leaving just three linebackers who’ve played in every game, something that Campbell knows isn’t sustainable. However, they may get some reinforcements with the return of linebacker Cam Smith.

“We cannot (survive with three linebackers),” Campbell said. “I think number one, Cam is kind of in the same boat as Koby (Howard) was, like man, he's working himself back. I think last week we didn't feel confident that it was unfair to put him in that situation last week, but was a lot closer to being ready to play, so I certainly think that he has certainly got the ability to be a big help.”

The return of Smith will add needed depth at the position, as Campbell said he was one of the MVPs of the bye week.

Penn State will also gain more depth as Campbell confirmed that safety Marcus Neal Jr. has made the move to linebacker, something that’s more permanent this time. Neal has experience playing MIKE linebacker at Iowa State, and the full-time switch allows him to showcase what he does best.

“I think it allows his talent and his ability to be at a place where we can use it even more,” Campbell said. “Not only in first and second down, but multiplicity and situational football too. And again, trying to find ways to get our best players on the field and put those guys in position to be the best within the scheme.”

MORE FOOTBALL CONTENT

title: Penn State women's hockey notebook | Jeff Kampersal speaks on building upon mistakes, goalie battle
author: Mashiah Mitchell | The Daily Collegian
description:
Ten games into the season, No. 7 Penn State currently sits at 7-3 with a near-perfect 5-1 record in conference play, placing the team atop the Atlantic Hockey America standings. The blue and white are on a five-game winning streak since its overtime loss to Syracuse nearly three weeks ago.

The Nittany Lions carry this streak into Canton, New York, for a two-game series against the RIT Tigers. RIT is 2-8 on the year so far, but is undefeated in AHA matchups, sweeping Delaware before hitting a downturn, dropping four in a row shortly after.

Prior to this Halloween series hitting the ice, coach Jeff Kampersal took time to speak to the media on Wednesday morning.

Kampersal used his time to cover how he and his staff are handling the ever-evolving goalie battle between Maddy Campbell and Morgan Stickney, the balance of allowing mistakes in a winning environment and the biggest factors in closing out games so far.

Goalie competition continues

The title of starting goalkeeper has been a by-committee decision for the Nittany Lions coaching staff since the beginning of the season. So far, both Campbell and Stickney have started five games each, with Stickney getting the most recent series starts, earning AHA Goalie of the Week honors after her 95% save percentage in the St. Lawrence series.

Kampersal went on to say that both goalies are “neck and neck in terms of ownership of the net.” He noted that the decision is made based on practices and signs of improvement.

He also highlighted Stickney’s ability to “play the puck behind the net, which almost feels like having another D back there.”

“There are many things that go into the decision; both are really good talents, and we tell them consistently to take the decision out of our hands by the end of the week.”

Mistakes aren't the end of the world

The Nittany Lions added seven freshmen during the offseason following graduations and departures. All seven have played on a consistent basis and contributed a new layer to the blue and white, but that has not come without its mistakes.

“They’re gonna make mistakes, no question, but we’re looking for improvement upon such,” Kampersal said about reassuring the rookies. “We encourage mistakes to prevent fear because the margin of error is slimmer than last year. I get frustrated with certain things, especially repetitive mistakes.”

In addition, Kampersal talked about how the freshmen are still getting acclimated, and how “[they] don’t want to crush confidence, but those little things and habits are usually glaring issues, of course with the freshmen more so given they had more space in high school.”

Closing the door

The Nittany Lions have scored 16 of their 32 total goals on the year in the third period alone, showing that the blue and white show up for all 60 minutes of play every single game.

Kampersal doesn’t want his team to get complacent in the early stages of the game.

“We have been playing better when we’re down and not giving up when we’re down two goals,” the skipper said. “I want to carry the underdog mentality throughout all periods and not just when we’re down, though.”

title: Joe Petito, father of Gabby Petito, advocates for domestic violence support and laws at R-VOICE center
author: Marek Horgas | For the Collegian
description:
Content warning: This article contains mention of sexual assault. Resources and support are available through Penn State’s Counseling and Psychological Services.

Penn State’s Relationship Violence, Outreach, Intervention, and Community Education Center (R-VOICE) hosted domestic violence advocate Joe Petito for a discussion of relationship violence education and prevention on Tuesday in the HUB-Robeson Center's Freeman Auditorium. Petito’s daughter, Gabby Petito, was murdered by her fiancé in 2021, making nationwide news.

As law enforcement searched the area around Grand Teton National Park for Gabby Petito, her murder became the subject of several documentaries, including the 2025 docuseries “American Murder: Gabby Petito,” produced and released by Netflix. Joe Petito recalled the conflict between wanting his daughter’s story told and the true crime documentary culture, sharing a conversation with the audience where the documentary’s director told Joe Petito he was “going to hate it."

“If you have to exploit Gabby's story to get someone else's information out there to help find your missing loved one, f-----g do it," Joe Petito said. "I don't care. I want my daughter back, and I’d give everything in this world to get her back, just for a day. But that's not an option. I'm never gonna get her back. So if you need to use her name to get your story out there, do it.”

More than the sensationalism, the most frustrating part of the media’s handling of the case to Joe Petito was the way that Gabby’s stepparents had been “dismissed.”

“Tara's been Gabby's stepmom since she was one, right? Jim's been since she was two. They've done nothing but love that child. To not give them the same airtime or the same quotes that you give us, meaning me and Nikki, blows my mind,” Joe Petito said.

Within the talk, Joe Petito took a grounded approach, frequently engaging the audience in his responses to mediator and R-VOICE Associate Director Sophia Mills. He shared some of the specific narratives that he, with the Gabby Petito Foundation, for which he is the vice president, seek to change. He said “the shame of domestic abuse belongs on the abuser not the victim” and men specifically need to be taught about domestic violence because “everyone’s the problem.”

Joe Petito also shared his belief that domestic violence prevention is on all of us, beginning with education that he feels could progress through different maturity levels as children and adolescents grow. He outlined lessons that could shift from “proper friendships” to mature relationships, and said he believes that domestic violence could be ended within 15 to 20 years through “proper, thorough, comprehensive” education.

Education extends into professional spheres as law enforcement have the capability to step in during domestic violence and save lives. Joe Petito pointed out that “55% of all women that are murdered [...] are by a current or former partner” as part of a broader topic of lethality assessments. These assessments are mandated by some states and require officers responding to domestic violence calls to progress through an 11-question set to determine if danger is mortal.

Pennsylvania does not have a statewide lethality assessment law, and all counties except Cameron, Carbon, Clarion, Forest, Fulton, Juniata, Lehigh, Mifflin, Philadelphia, Schuylkill, Somerset, Sullivan, Susquehanna and Warren counties have lethality assessment police mandates.

“If that lethality assessment was done, I do believe that she would be alive,” Joe Petito said. “If they would have done what was the statue, which was arrest her, because they believed her to be the primary aggressor, then she would still be alive. If they would have done what was required, I believe that she would be alive.”

Mills echoed the sentiment that education is the key to ending domestic and dating violence while highlighting a picture of what relationship violence may look like outside the media.

“I think from what we see in media and various situations, oftentimes it's physical violence, and it's typically a man against a woman,” Mills said. “But we recognize that violence can happen to anyone, and it's not just physical, right? We can see things related to financial abuse, emotional manipulation, blackmailing, gaslighting, different things related to that, even digital abuse.”

Organizations like R-VOICE, who sponsored the event, seek to increase that education at the university level. In 2024, Penn State University Park ranked 4th in rapes and 7th for dating violence out of U.S. colleges and universities with 57 and 31 incidents, respectively. This semester from Aug. 24 and Oct. 3, 23 cases of sexual misconduct were reported to Penn State University Park, according to the University Police and Public Safety Daily Crime Log.

These numbers represent only reported cases while many victims choose to stay quiet as well. In 2025, Spotlight PA reported that the State College Police Department misclassified 254 counts of rape as lesser offenses between 2013-2021.

Mills suggested that while education is critical to destigmatizing and ending domestic violence, it starts with openness and potentially uncomfortable conversations.

“I think by, again, having these conversations normalizing some of these things, we're able to have those conversations, to check in on our friends, call our friends out if they say something problematic, right? We have the power to do these things, and I think recognizing that is a really important step, that we have the ability and responsibility to intervene when we witness any kind of problematic, harmful, or even abusive behaviors,” Mills said

Katie Brigham, 21, of Fredericksburg, Virginia, said she was surprised by the humor that Joe Petito was able to weave through an otherwise serious talk. She also said that the talk would stay with her beyond graduation.

“As a future teacher, I want to educate my coworkers, my students, if I teach high school, about domestic violence. And I also want to educate my friends and my family and even my future children as well to educate them about domestic violence and how we can work together to not be in a situation like that,” Brigham, a fourth-year studying rehabilitation and human services, said.

Following his daughter’s death, Joe Petito shifted much of his focus to work on the Gabby Petito Foundation, which currently has several apps in development to support survivors of domestic violence in safely finding justice.

“If you're asking me to choose between the foundation and my job, I'm going to pick the foundation every time,” Joe Petito said. “It's so much more meaningful. I really want to do nothing else but this. And it's really it's really a selfish reason I do it so when I leave this place, I get to see Gabby again, I'm going to ask her, ‘Did I make you proud?’ And hopefully she'll say yes.”

title: Sports editors weekly | Both hoops teams start on November 2; which should fans watch?
author: Myles Hannak | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State hoops returns to the Bryce Jordan Center on Monday for a men’s and women’s basketball doubleheader to kick off the season.

Mike Rhoades’ squad overhauled its entire roster and hit the portal, while the Lady Lions take the court for the first time in the regular season under first-year coach and program legend Tanisha Wright.

It can be a lot of basketball for fans in Happy Valley, so which one should you pick?

Gianna Dowling: Tune in to Tanisha

It’s the dawn of a new era for Penn State women’s basketball as all-time Lady Lion great Tanisha Wright is set to begin her tenure at the helm of her alma mater. Fans aren’t going to want to miss a second of Wright’s opener.

Penn State basketball fans have had three seasons of Mike Rhoades, but during this time it's been more of the same, following two losing seasons and one just above .500. Happy Valley hoops followers are in need of some change; let Wright be this change.

Wright brings in a fresh crop of Lady Lions that are ready to make a mark in their new home, and the team's fans should back them in this journey.

However, the biggest reason for attention to be drawn to the Lady Lions on opening night is, as mentioned above, that Wright is a Penn State legend. Fans who’ve followed the Lady Lions through their glory days and when Wright was a player should be more than excited to tune in.

Deciding which basketball game to attend at the Bryce Jordan Center is as easy as the saying goes: out with the old, and in with the new. Something new is brewing in Wright’s locker room, and I guarantee you'll want to be there to see it.

Myles Hannak: Miss no minute of Mike

Rhoades’ squad is soon to return to the hardwood, and it's finally the year that could turn the tide of recent program struggles.

Buy stock now, Nittany Lions fans: get in early, go to the season opener — enjoy Penn State men’s hoops before it’s cool.

The makeup of the blue and white’s squad is fun compared to last year’s group, which was wet behind the ears and the youngest in the Big Ten. With multi-positional versatility, an accomplished veteran core and depth of talent that wasn’t ever present in Rhoades’ tenure so far, this year’s squad won’t be a laughing stock in the conference.

No single player stands out; Josh Reed, Dasonte Bowen, Ivan Jurić and Brant Byers look to be penciled in as starters, but the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. The fun that comes with the Nittany Lions is that we don’t know what to expect, just that it’ll be better than before — you can’t say the same for a Lady Lions squad that's only amassed a measly 11 players, only one of whom averaged double-digit scoring last season.

You may be able to fast-forward this season for Wright, as her squad looks set to meet a similar fate to what Carolyn Kieger’s squad endured in the former boss’s final campaign. The nuts and bolts don’t come together for a Lady Lions team that can shake up an ever-competitive Big Ten.

You can skip the women’s hoops opener in the BJC; it’ll be a blip in the program identity Wright is building. Wait until the Lady Lions begin their season at Rec Hall, the same building where Wright charted that program history that’s inspiring the new era.

The atmosphere will be better, too.

title: Satire | Surviving Halloweekend at Penn State
author: Colleen Cratty | The Daily Collegian
description:
With Halloweekend fast approaching, you might find yourself a little stressed trying to find plans. Between struggling to find a group costume everyone can agree on and your Amazon package with last minute cat ears being banished to East Halls’ mailroom purgatory, actual plans have been the last thing on your mind.

You can’t just wear your vampire costume (which is just your everyday going-out outfit with fake blood on your neck) to any regular party. So, here are some recommendations on how to fill up your Halloweekend schedule this year.

Wednesday, Oct. 28

Stage West

For all the freshmen whose fake IDs are still in the mail, there’s an event just for you. Stage West hosts an 18-and-older dry event every year for those who are underage. Everyone will be dressed up, so you can pretend like you’re having a fun Halloween.

It’s the perfect night to take photos in your Amazon corset in front of the iconic “Tequila made me do it,” something super unique nobody has ever thought to put on a sign before, let alone include in your Insta dump. Make sure to get at least a hundred photos, so you can spend the next hour choosing which one to put on your story.

After the event, you can even do a sober walk of shame up to East Halls in your costume, while everyone else walks back from Wine Wednesday in their striped lounge sets. At least you’ll have photo evidence that you left your dorm this week.

Thursday, Oct. 29

Fraternity parties

If you managed to get that coveted invite for Halloweekend, you can enjoy a Thursday night at a fraternity party.

Get ready to hear “This is Halloween” in a cursed mash-up with “Doses and Mimosas,” accompanied by a bunch of guys frat-flicking in your face while wearing backward jerseys. Be careful not to ask them what they’re dressed up as, though, because this might get blacklisted from every party for the rest of the semester.

Police will probably be on the prowl this weekend, so make sure to walk in a straight line through frat row, even after you ultimately sacrifice your outfit by removing the knee-high heeled boots you originally thought were a great idea. Getting arrested with whiskers drawn on your face is probably a Penn State canon event you can be comfortable missing out on.

And remember: No costume is worth a whole night of explaining to your parents why you ordered a $30 Uber on their credit card.

Friday, Oct. 30

John Summit concert

A perfect pregame for your Halloweekend plans is the John Summit concert at the Bryce Jordan Center on Friday. Summit is an American DJ who has achieved over 430 million global streams on Spotify and has just started his CTRL ESCAPE Arena Tour.

This concert is a great way to get a head start on all of the house music you’ll hear throughout Halloweekend. By Saturday, you’ll be able to recognize the same beat playing at every party in a five-mile radius.

And, if you forgot to get that sacred third costume, then it’s an excellent way to still get Instagram photos without the stress of hitting Spirit Halloween last minute.

If you did get an extra costume, go ahead and wear it, but be prepared to accidentally photo bomb a group of girls wearing pashminas while you’re dressed in an animal onesie. At least you’ll stand out.

Saturday, Oct. 31

Football game

This year, Halloween falls on a Penn State football game day versus Purdue University with day-long tailgates since the game is at 4:15 p.m. If you want to get your Halloweekend festivities started early, head to the football game for an exciting start to your Saturday.

While many are just dressing up with a pair of Nittany Lion ears, you could go for a real costume to get some interesting looks from other students.

If you really want to cause a stir in the student section, dress up as the opponent’s mascot “Purdue Pete.” It’s a sure way to get some pom-poms or Fireball shooters thrown straight at your head. Just be prepared to explain your costume to everyone who mistakes you for a random guy wearing a giant head.

Bar crawl

For those who didn’t get season tickets, you could spend the day at the variety of State College bars instead of a tailgate.

Fortunately, LineLeap tickets for the bars are pretty inexpensive, starting at around $50. And that’s just for Doggie’s Pub, so prepare to spend over $200 on Saturday just to get in (talk about scary). You could always just wait in the line, but being stuck in 40-degree weather in a mini skirt and corset for over two hours may turn your princess costume to more of an undead bride vibe.

Of course, the real Halloween horror story is checking your bank account Sunday morning. Nothing says spooky season like realizing you spent your grocery budget on cover charges, rideshares and one overpriced drink.

Sunday, Nov. 1

The Recovery Period

After four days of carefully planned outfits, questionable decisions and approximately three hours of sleep, Sunday is your chance to recover. Order food, ignore the spam of blurry photos your friends tagged you in and begin preparing your formal apology to your Monday morning professor.

You might even start planning next year’s costume early. After all, Amazon delivery times are unpredictable, and you can't afford another Halloween crisis in the East Halls’ mailroom.

Whatever you decide to do this Halloweekend, remember to stay safe, keep an eye on your friends and have fun. If all else fails, throw on a pair of cat ears and call it a costume. At Penn State, nobody’s asking too many questions anyway.

title: Satire | Want to larp in the valley? Here’s how to Penn State-maxx
author: Ally Sons | The Daily Collegian
description:
As Penn State students know, the school pride here runs deep. With the “we are” chants at any given moment or seeing the exact same Penn State football sweatshirt on 10 people during your walk to class, the atmosphere can be distinct and electric. But as the year progresses, it can just become a part of everyday life.

In terms of clothing and behavior, all the way up to little sayings and nuances, the Penn State student pool is unique. Whether it’s the sound of someone's flip-flops against the sidewalk or passing a group of people discussing how they’re all from “right outside the city,” it’s impossible to forget where you are.

If you’re looking for tips on how to maximize your true Penn State student potential and truly larp in the fullest sense of the word, look no further.

The uniform

If you’re shooting for a more masculine outfit, try a Greek life THON hoodie, preferably from two or three years ago, paired with athletic shorts and, of course, flip-flops. Or, with the colder months fast approaching, feel free to switch out the shorts for a very oversized pair of gray sweatpants and the classic Birkenstock clogs.

For those seeking a more feminine take on the larp, try foldover yoga pants from your wine Wednesday outfit and a white tank or Comfrt hoodie with a claw clip located right on top of your head.

Another common theme for wardrobe, if you’re sticking to the uniform, is any kind of matching sweat set. The perfect outfit for the weather on the walk to your 9 a.m., but as soon as you start your walk to your noon class, it feels like you’re trapped in a sauna.

Book Bags

Achieving final form as a Penn State student is entirely dependent on the accessories. The Longchamp tote bag dupes and fake Adidas athlete bags have taken the streets of State College by storm.

It can feel impossible to walk up Shortlidge Road without seeing the same blue or white bag with the signature brown leather buckle, of course, all holding identical silver MacBooks.

With the switch from Nike to Adidas this school year, campus has been watching the experienced larpers change with the times. Switching from the original navy Nike backpack with some random words that almost look like they say football, to the new Adidas bag with the signature three stripes on the top. To really complete the look, attach some form of ID to the outside, so it almost looks like the official tag.

Claim to be from “30 minutes outside Philly”

This commonly heard saying could mean everything from being from Bucks County, Pennsylvania to Northern New Jersey.

Students on campus love to claim the city as their own, regardless of how far away they might live – riding for the Eagles and claiming they knew Saquon Barkley before he was a big name, back in his high school days. After all, regardless of where in Pennsylvania or New York you might be from, Barkley is “basically from your town.”

It raises the question, though, at what point do you draw the line about how many hours from Philly someone can claim is only “30 minutes away?” Is 30 minutes a true measure of distance or more of a lifestyle choice and state of mind?

Pay $1,500 a month for housing

Arguably the worst part of the Penn State experience: the prices of off-campus housing. Whether you’re looking at College or Beaver Ave., it can feel impossible to find any options under two million dollars a month, but that’s just part of the life here.

With the requirements of an apartment with a bed and running water, you can be looking at $1,500 a month to share a room. That doesn’t stop students from finding premium housing right downtown with windows facing the street that they can hang their Nittany Lion flags in.

Be anywhere but campus

As much fun as State College can be, a true student tends to find themselves anywhere but on campus. Being so close to the rest of the east coast, the second we don’t have a football game, students seem to disappear from the streets.

Whether it's everyone you know going to Montreal for Oktoberfest, entire frats up and leaving for formal in Toronto, big weekend trips to New York City or everyone going home on weekends to Pittsburgh and Philadelphia, students tend to always have a side quest they’re looking forward to. Arguably, to stay mobile is to fully embrace the Penn State way.

Eat at Irving's

If you want to max out your larp while here on campus, Irving's is a classic choice for students. Selling lattes, smoothies, bagels and so much more, it can be a great study spot and a lot of students' favorite hangover cure.

Even as one of the busiest and most bustling spots downtown, if you fight your way through a crowd of everyone you’ve ever met and get a table, there’s few spots that can beat it. So go and grab a bagel in your head-to-toe Penn State gear, and embrace the true larping potential of a Penn State student.

title: No. 13 Penn State women’s volleyball set for Ohio State, White Out contest against No. 11 Purdue
author: Madelyn Lawlor | For The Collegian
description:
Penn State looks to keep building momentum this week over a two-match home stand after taking two wins against ranked opponents over the weekend.

Led by right-side hitter Kennedy Martin’s offense, the Nittany Lions outlasted then-No. 10 Oregon at home. The blue and white then traveled to then-No. 18 Indiana and came out on top in a resilient performance. Its ability to win both matches despite travel and a quick turnaround helped propel Penn State up three spots in the rankings.

The Nittany Lions improved to 15-5 overall and 7-3 in Big Ten play, tying for fourth place in the conference with No. 25 Michigan State.

Penn State hosts Ohio State on Thursday at 7 p.m. for Military Appreciation Night. No. 11 Purdue then travels to take on the blue and white Saturday in a lively atmosphere at Rec Hall for White Out and Senior Night at 12:30 p.m.

Following these contests, the blue and white will have four straight road matches before closing out the regular season one final time at home.

Ohio State

These two matches serve as distinct tests for the Nittany Lions. Ohio State currently sits towards the bottom of the conference standings, with a record of 3-7 in the Big Ten and 10-10 overall.

The Buckeyes have lost to every ranked team they’ve played so far. They’re also on a three-game losing streak, including losses to the two teams Penn State just beat in Oregon and Indiana.

The primary standout player for the Buckeyes is outside hitter Naomy Govou. She leads the team with 3.90 kills per set and 4.31 points per set, ranking fourth and fifth in the Big Ten in those measures, respectively.

Ohio State is inconsistent on both ends of the floor. It posts the best digs-per-set figure in the conference at 15.24, but is weak in blocks per set, ranking only 250th in the country. The Buckeyes are also lackluster in most offensive measures, posting the second-worst hitting percentage in the Big Ten. The scarlet and gray are stronger in kills per set, ranking 81st in the country with 13.16, but still sit toward the bottom of the conference in that figure.

The Nittany Lions have won five straight matches against Ohio State, losing last to the Buckeyes in 2022. Overall, the blue and white sport a 56-21 record against Ohio State.

Despite the success, many recent matches have been close battles. In one of the two matchups in 2025, the Buckeyes led Penn State 2-1 going into the fourth set, but the blue and white rebounded to take the final two sets and the victory. In 2024, the Nittany Lions almost collapsed after taking two of the first three sets.

After taking on Ohio State, Penn State faces three straight ranked opponents in Purdue, No. 21 Minnesota and No. 8 Wisconsin.

Purdue

The Boilermakers are 13-6 overall and 6-4 in conference, sitting tied with four other teams for fifth. They have a two-game winning streak, including a victory over Minnesota. Before traveling to State College, Purdue hosts Rutgers.

Purdue has accumulated wins against ranked opponents, but mostly during the nonconference slate. It has failed to beat many of the top Big Ten teams it’s faced, dropping matches to No. 1 Nebraska, Wisconsin, Oregon and then-No. 22 Washington.

The Boilermakers’ best wins came in September in sweeps against then-No. 8 SMU and then-No. 12 Texas A&M. Since entering conference play, Purdue’s strongest win came against the Golden Gophers. The only other ranked Big Ten team Purdue defeated was then-No. 24 Illinois, who received votes in the most recent AVCA poll but didn’t make the list.

Purdue plays strong defense, ranking near the top of the conference in both blocks per set and digs per set, with numbers of 2.58 and 14.66, respectively. The Boilermakers’ offense is average, putting up 13.57 kills per set, which ranks 8th in the conference. They also rank 11th in hitting percentage at .256.

Purdue’s assists lead its offensive production, as it sits right above Penn State in fifth, averaging 12.90 per set.

Opposite hitter Addy Tindall is Purdue's primary offensive threat. The outside hitter leads the Boilermakers in kills per set and points per set and ranks fifth in the Big Ten for the first measure, averaging 3.79 per set. On defense, middle blocker Dior Charles has accumulated a team-high 77 blocks this season.

Recent history between the blue and white and Purdue is mixed. The Nittany Lions took both matches in 2022 but fell in both in 2023. Penn State then swept the Boilermakers twice during its 2024 championship-winning season. Purdue swept the blue and white during the teams’ only matchup in 2025. Penn State has dominated Purdue before, though, with a 62-12 record dating back to the first contest in 1981.

title: Penn State WR Chase Sowell says ‘focusing on the present’ is all the Nittany Lions need
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Wide receiver Chase Sowell is on his fourth team in five years. He started his journey at Colorado before stopping at East Carolina and Iowa State, eventually following Matt Campbell to Penn State.

For someone who’d been a regular in the transfer portal, Sowell’s glad he doesn't have to worry about that aspect of college football anymore. Despite his background, he’s not the kind of player who thinks too early about jumping ship and is more focused on doing his best at the present moment.

“It definitely feels good to be at the stage now where that type of stuff doesn't really affect me,” Sowell said Tuesday. “Focusing on the process and focusing on the present is all you can do, and it was the same thing when I was in the transfer portal.”

Sowell has become a vocal leader in the locker room amidst Penn State’s turbulent season. He spoke up at a player’s meeting after one of the team’s losses, stressing the importance of day-by-day consistency instead of thinking too far ahead.

He said everyone on the team should be focused on making meaningful plays and living in the moment to build a portfolio of game film. Sowell’s experience in the transfer portal gave him insight on how the “opportunities are the same” at every program, and having quality tape makes you stand out.

“We're not in a position for any of our guys to get picked up by anybody,” Sowell said. “So your mindset shouldn't even be on the transfer portal. You should be thinking about making some plays to even get looked at.”

For him, even coming to Happy Valley was a “last-second” decision. He wasn’t planning to transfer, but when the opportunity was brought to him, he followed his heart.

“I was focusing on, ‘What do I need to be doing now?’” Sowell said. “I was working out. I was trying to get my body right, those types of things, and then boom, it happened.”

The decision to follow Campbell to Penn State has worked out for Sowell individually, as he’s been a breakout star at wide receiver in the wake of Koby Howard’s injury. He’s on track for a career-best season, already racking up 510 receiving yards and three touchdowns through seven games.

Sowell said his goal was to “change the narrative of the receiver room” at Penn State. It didn’t matter what his role was on the team, he wanted to establish the Nittany Lions as a program featuring strong pass catchers, something they’ve lacked in recent years.

Since taking over the role of No. 1 receiver, Sowell’s done just that, as he’s been the top offensive performer since the start of Big Ten action. His most recent performance was a career-best, tallying 11 catches, 151 yards and a touchdown against Michigan.

“That was what Brett (Eskildsen), Amarion Jackson, Zay Robinson, Koby and I, all of us, talked about — no matter what, we're gonna do everything in our power to change the narrative,” Sowell said. “Because this is going to be one season that we're gonna remember for the rest of our lives, and whether it goes good or bad, I want to have the memories that I know our room changed history.”

title: Penn State wrestling’s brings national title contenders to 125, 133-pound weight classes
author: Ava Aguiar | The Daily Collegian
description:
Another wrestling season is almost under way, and Penn State will look to earn its 15th national championship title.

The Nittany Lions will have some of their key starters in the 125-133 weight classes, including 2025 national championship winner Luke Lilledahl and 2025 Big Ten runner up Marcus Blaze.

Here’s how the lower-weight classes stack up.

125

Lilledahl, now in his third year with the Nittany Lions, will lead the 125-pound weight class, entering the season as the top-ranked wrestler.

The junior earned the title of national champion after a 25-0 run on the mat last year and will be hungry to redeem himself after an unideal performance on the world stage. After losing to Spencer Lee in Final X, Lilledahl had his sights set on the U23 World Championships. However, he underperformed at the U23 championships in Las Vegas, finishing 1-2 at 57 kilograms.

Lilledahl is the No. 1 ranked wrestler at 125 pounds entering the season, and will be a crucial starter for the team. During the dual season, he’ll be key to the team's success as the likely opener to start matches.

The St. Charles, Missouri, native will look to add another championship to his name, and is sure to remain at the top of the rankings throughout the season.

Behind the reigning national champion is minimal depth. Branden Wentzel will be an important asset to the Penn State roster having come back as a midseason transfer from Lock Haven last year.

Wentzel provides more veteran presence at 125 pounds, something that’s not common across the country. He hasn’t competed much outside of Penn State’s room, so the experience isn’t that of a veteran in the room.

Wentzel will likely be Lilledahl’s lone backup during the season, and could see action at tournaments during the season.

133

Similar to Lilledahl, Blaze is a contender for the national title. Blaze is already ranked No. 4 in the nation after his first collegiate season. He had a 25-3 record last year, placing second in the Big Ten and fourth in the NCAA Championships.

Blaze will see action prior to the start of the collegiate folkstyle season. He’s slated to compete at the 2026 World Championships in Kazakhstan. He has a chance to add to his already impressive international trophy case as a U17 and U20 world champion.

Blaze will already be a promising starter in the lineup. He will come in as a contender to look out for this season, as he guns for a spot higher on the podium.

Kyison Garcia is another wrestler who returns from last season, and attempts to cap off his senior year stronger than last year. He struggled during the Black Knight invitational, beating Chattanooga’s Ethan Uhorchuk 4-2, before an 11-3 loss to Gardner-Webb’s Takeo Davis took him out of the competition.

The lone new face of the group is incoming freshman Braiden Weaver, who will be Penn State’s third competitor at 133. He has the potential to be a reliable backup behind Blaze. In his senior year, Weaver went 38-8, posting a first place finish at districts, second at regionals and fifth at states. He went 153-28 overall coming into his first season as a Nittany Lion with a 84.5% rate.

title: Penn State men’s hockey’s key struggles, takeaways from rocky start
author: Maggie Hardy | The Daily Collegian
description:
After losing much of its top talent and needing significant offseason retooling, Penn State wasn’t expected to be a frontrunner for the national title — but opening the season 0-4 wasn’t quite the anticipated start.

The Nittany Lions dropped their first two games on the road to then-No. 16 UConn and Sacred Heart, before coming back home and falling to then-No.8 Quinnipiac and Robert Morris.

After its struggling non-conference results, the blue and white finally righted the ship this weekend with a series sweep over Canisius.

“We all knew after the (Robert Morris) game that it’s really time now, like, we can’t lay back,” defenseman Jackson Smith said after the win over Canisius Friday night. “It’s pretty cool if we can come back from this tough start, but now we have a chance to have a pretty cool story.”

Here are some of the biggest contributors to the rocky start.

Mentality battles

Penn State’s shocking 5-2 loss to Robert Morris was a struggling performance all-around, but Guy Gadowsky pointed to mentality as the key takeaway.

“I’m just telling the honest truth about how I feel. I feel it's arrogance,” Gadowsky said postgame. “I feel that we feel we’re above what we had to do in the past to get where we got.”

The Colonials scored just 20 seconds into the contest, and added two more in the first period while Penn State remained scoreless. The Nittany Lions fought an uphill battle for most of the game.

Senior captain Dane Dowiak took responsibility for the mindset struggles and pointed to himself and the leadership team as needing to step up to get the team back on track.

“You got to do a lot of self-reflecting. I got to put that on me. I got to put that on the leadership group,” Dowiak said after the loss to Robert Morris. “I got to lead this team the right way. I haven’t done that yet.”

Penalty struggles

Penn State plays physical, and that isn’t a newly adopted style, but the team has struggled with too much time in the penalty box in recent years.

Last season, the Nittany Lions’ 18.4 penalty minutes per game was the highest in the nation.

That problem seems to be rearing its head again.

The blue and white gave up seven power plays in its loss to Quinnipiac, four of which were converted to a goal. The team also gave up five power plays in the loss to Robert Morris.

“It’s not just the penalties. It’s the penalties that you take,” Gadowsky said after the loss to Quinnipiac. “It’s not like we were going to the net hard and taking penalties, or hauling guys down because they’re in front of the net.”

In Penn State’s sweep this weekend, however, it played a more disciplined game. Penalties were less frequent, and when the team did find itself down a man, it held Canisius to zero goals on seven attempts.

New Nittany Lions shine

A bright spot recently for the Nittany Lions has been the performance of their new class.

Three of the team’s top five points leaders are newcomers, with transfer sophomore Justin Poirier leading the way with three goals and five assists. Freshmen Kale Dach and Justin Larose round out the trio, each with six points apiece.

On the back end, freshman Ethan Weber has established himself as a top defensive option, bringing a strong and versatile two-way style of play to the blueline.

“(Weber) does very subtle, smart, effective plays on both ends of the ice,” Gadowsky said after Friday’s win. “He’s a really well-rounded hockey player.”

Transfer sophomore Caeden Herrington’s toughness and physicality has also become a staple of the blue and white’s back end.

“(Herrington) gives us energy. He gives us toughness. He gives us size. He gives us grit,” Gadowsky said after Saturday’s contest. “He’s a tough competitor that helps at both ends of the ice.”

In net, freshman goaltender Ryder Fetterolf has also had a strong start to his collegiate career.

Fetterolf has started in three games for the blue and white and registered his first win over Canisius Saturday night after stopping 26 of 28 shots faced, including a diving save in overtime to keep the Nittany Lions in the game.

title: Column | Harassment about hell in State College treads thin line between free speech, hate speech
author: Michelle Diamond | The Daily Collegian
description:
Coming to Penn State, there are a few things you can count on seeing: Old Main, students relaxing and playing volleyball on the HUB Lawn and old men standing on the sidewalks, posters in hand, warning students that they’re going to hell.

Standing downtown the other week, I noticed a man planted firmly on the sidewalk, screaming through a megaphone at a line of college students outside of Doggie’s Pub. It was hard to make out what he was saying with his mouth so close to the device, but his poster was loud and clear.

In big, bold lettering written across a display of flames, he listed everyone going to hell. I can condense it for you: If you’re not a straight, white, Christian man, I have news for you.

While he was holding this sign with the weight of his privilege supporting it, he pointed at individual women, saying, “You should be ashamed for dressing like that. Cover up. You’re tripping these guys up.” Apparently those aren’t just outrageous phrases used to parody misogynists. Real people actually have these thoughts — who knew!

Not only was he singling out women, but he was calling people the “f” slur as well. When the cops came, they didn’t do anything. The man yelled at everyone, saying he had a right to free speech. And that he does. Even hate speech is something we all have a right to.

Not all types of speech are protected, though. There are five categories of unprotected speech: fighting words, true threats, false advertising, obscenity and incitement. But I want to focus on fighting words. (Though I encourage anyone living under the Constitution to understand the law and your rights.)

Merriam-Webster defines fighting words as “words which by their very utterance are likely to inflict harm on or provoke a breach of the peace by the average person to whom they are directed.”

When someone utters slurs, they have gone beyond hate speech. A person who is gay, who has likely faced discrimination before, is being blatantly targeted by this word. It’s verbal violence. Of course, I’m not a lawyer or a judge, and the law is all about interpretation, so I can’t assert that I’m right. However, using this word inflicts mental harm (I don’t see a distinction between mental and physical) to a gay individual being talked to as “less than” human.

Calling out individual girls for what they are wearing is likely to cause harm, undermining the bodily autonomy of that specific woman, perpetuating the notion that men have a say over our bodies.

I will say, there’s a fine line between fighting words and hate speech. This is what makes the topic so ambiguous and debatable. Is calling someone ugly hate speech or fighting words? Is calling someone stupid hate speech or fighting words?

When we put what this man outside of Doggie’s said into context (which the law takes into account) we’re in a college town that has a reputation of hiding sexual assault from the greater population. Undermining a woman’s bodily autonomy where sexual assault is prevalent further enables and encourages this behavior toward women. This kind of language stretches beyond the definition of hate speech. It’s language that objectifies women’s bodies. It’s language that undermines women’s humanity.

Degrading a person through language falls under the category of fighting words, in my opinion. How do you comfortably navigate a college town when people are warning you about your inevitable entrance to hell?

While I do believe the cops can take action on the grounds that this often violates the First Amendment, especially in the example I gave, it doesn’t seem action will be taken any time soon.

I don’t have exact steps I think you should take, but I wanted to leave you knowing it’s OK to question people’s arguments and their interpretation of the law.

Reporting will likely lead to nothing, but it can’t hurt to take action in situations where you feel threatened and unsafe. It can’t hurt to respectfully make a case for why this is unprotected speech. We all have a responsibility to help make the community more welcoming and less harmful to already susceptible individuals.

By no means am I suggesting I’m an expert, but holding a poster about hell and screaming slurs at people are two different things. I think Penn State needs to become clearer on what the First Amendment actually entails. While this specific incident didn’t occur on campus, it has several times in the past, and it’s likely to find its way back into University Park’s bounds eventually.

Above all, don’t let it get to you. These protestors don’t define your worth and they certainly don’t get to dictate the way you live your life. Be yourself and dress as you please. They’re just mad they can’t pull off a crop top.

title: Penn State men's hockey newcomers Ryder Fetterolf, Caeden Herrington reflect on home debut
author: Dominic Megats I The Daily Collegian
description:
It’s been two weeks since Guy Gadowsky and members of his team filled the media room for their weekly press conference.

In that time span, new players have experienced their first home game inside Pegula Ice Arena to mixed results.

After making 25 saves against Canisius in regulation through his first start at home, Ryder Fetterolf faced a crucial overtime period that would continue Penn State’s momentum if it was able to survive.

The Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, native didn’t wait long for any action after he made a clutch save off of the opening faceoff, sparking a two-on-one opportunity the other way. 6,249 fans worked in unison to blow the roof off the arena after Jackson Smith was able to bury home the game-winner, making it a memorable home debut for the freshman netminder.

“The biggest thing I can say is that I’d hate to be the goalie going against (that crowd),” Fetterolf said. “The chants are awesome, and they’re really loud. Super cool to be on the home team for that. Coming from junior hockey, it’s just a lot different. You have students here with so much pride in their school, and alumni; you’re really playing for something. In juniors, you get all these different fans, but at Penn State you get the same fans pretty much night in and night out.”

For Caeden Herrington, it’s a different backstory with being a transfer from Vermont. The sophomore spent his first year playing for the Catamounts, in which he recorded eight points in 56 games.

With most of his games played in front of a Hockey East crowd, his first taste of a Big Ten atmosphere was one he won’t forget.

“It’s unbelievable. There’s nothing like playing in (Pegula),” Herrington said. “Obviously, that Quinnipiac game was pretty nuts, and it’s too bad that we didn’t get the win. But on that first goal, the place erupted.”

The first few games at Happy Valley were much more physical for the sophomore defenseman. Herrington found himself on the other end of heavy body checks and in the middle of several scrums after whistles.

But one instance stood out to Gadowsky in particular from Game 1 against Canisius on Friday. After Herrington finished his check, the 6-foot-2 defenseman was tied up with Rhys Chiddenton, leading to physicality that warranted both players two minutes in the penalty box.

“If you watch Caeden Herrington at the end of the game, he was tied up – call it what you want. I really like how he handled himself,” Gadowsky said. “He didn’t acquiesce to anybody. I think he played it the way that Penn State toughness is. He stood up for himself. He’s tough.”

Both of the new Nittany Lions are set for their first road Big Ten test in Minnesota. However, they won’t let the spook of a ruckus Gopher crowd disrupt their approach.

“I think it’s fun going to an away barn sometimes. You get to be the villain,” Herrington said. “Our team’s going to approach it that way. We want to go in there and focus on us and focus on what we need to do. That’s been the mentality this week. We’re preparing to play Penn State hockey.”

title: Penn State women's soccer notebook | Coach Erica Dambach discusses final stretch, community support
author: Lola Brand | For the Collegian
description:
Penn State entered the week with two ranked opponents standing between it and a stronger position heading into postseason play. One upset and one hard-fought draw later, the Nittany Lions have made their case.

The newly ranked No. 23 Nittany Lions will host their season finale at Jeffrey Field this Friday against Indiana before heading into postseason play.

Coach Erica Dambach met with the media over Zoom to discuss the team’s confidence moving forward, home advantages and the “unsung hero” so far this year.

Team confidence and tenacity

Penn State brought it this weekend when they traveled to Michigan to battle two ranked teams. These outcomes were crucial for Penn State to gain confidence going into the postseason, and also helped the previously unranked Nittany Lions secure a No. 23 spot in the rankings.

“Going on the road and getting four massive points in Michigan this weekend, I think that was a huge confidence boost,” Dambach said. “It doesn’t matter where or when or who or any of those conditions. That we can go at teams and have success, even against the top teams in the country.”

Against No. 5 Michigan State, Nittany Lions junior forward Aubrey Kulpa notched a goal in the second half, a one-on-one attack against a Spartans defender, following her first-half assist. Kulpa’s goal helped shift momentum Penn State’s way early in the half.

“Going in at halftime, you try to make some changes and adjust and figure out what they're doing well and how we can get at them more, and the game always looks different in the second half… You just hope that what you did can counterbalance and actually give you the advantage, and then there’s a massive momentum swing.” Dambach said. “You're both kind of feeling each other out again, and then to impose yourself the way that we were able to impose ourselves with that goal just gets all the momentum going in our direction.”

Penn State maintained that momentum and tenacity a few days later when they played No. 24 Michigan in a back-and-forth game that ended in a 2-2 draw.

Kayleigh Herr and the team defense

A team’s defensive efforts often go unnoticed in the box score. Still, Dambach couldn’t say enough about the team’s defense, which proved to be particularly vital in the Michigan State showdown.

“We defended with numbers, and we defended as a team. I think obviously that's a group that plays very well together. Michigan State combines really well, so you have to group defend- you've got to defend as a team,” Dambach said. “You need the person next to you to be successful against the better teams, and that's exactly what they did.

Penn State’s defense has consistently held teams to low-scoring outputs, even against top-ranked opponents. When asked about what player has stood out as a leader in these circumstances, Dambach pointed to redshirt senior defender Kayleigh Herr.

“Kayleigh Herr has been our leader in that back line. She’s been exceptional with her voice and organizing, and she’s had a lot of people to organize. So I would give her a huge shout-out.”

Spooky soccer

The blue and white are set to close out the regular season this Friday at home against Indiana. The game, themed Kick or Treat since it will be played the night before Halloween, carries great significance. It gives the Nittany Lions their last chance to influence their national ranking, and they’re hoping to carry momentum from the matchup into the Big Ten tournament.

Dambach expressed her enthusiasm for the atmosphere surrounding the upcoming Friday night matchup.

“A Friday night matchup under the lights. It’s soccer weather right now: the leaves are turning, there’s a little chill in the air,” Dambach said. “Nothing screams Penn State soccer like a Friday night under the lights.”

Beyond the atmosphere, Dambach highlighted the crowd’s role in creating an electric home-field advantage.

“The community's turned up for us; the players are still talking about the last home game,” Dambach said. “They're talking about the energy that this community brings, and just how much we love playing in front of these home fans.”

The Nittany Lions return this Friday to take on Indiana at Jeffrey Field at 7 p.m. for their themed Kick or Treat match as they close out the season.

“There’s a Halloween event beforehand, a ‘Kick or Treat.’ Bring the kids, have fun, come in costume — Let's make it a great community night,” said Dambach.

title: Penn State women's volleyball notebook | Katie Schumacher-Cawley  discusses upcoming 2 home games
author: Riley Warner | For the Collegian
description:
Three weeks until tournament play.

The Nittany Lions return to Rec Hall this week in matches against Ohio State on Thursday and No. 11 Purdue on Saturday.

After a staggering loss to UCLA on Oct. 16, Penn State has gone on to win three in a row, two of which were against ranked opponents, then-No. 10 Oregon and No. 18 Indiana.

With the Big Ten Tournament approaching, Penn State wants to build on this three-win streak, and coach Katie Schumacher-Cawley reflected on the recent wins and the mindset moving forward.

Here’s what Katie Schumacher-Cawley had to say at her weekly press conference on Tuesday.

The big three

As Penn State looks toward two upcoming games and tournament play a few weeks from now, many look to players like setter Alexis Stucky, right side hitter Kennedy Martin, and outside hitter Whitney Lauenstein.

Recently, both Stucky and Martin received accolades within the Big Ten. Stucky won the Setter of the Week award, her first in the Big Ten and Martin won the Big Ten Player of the Week for the fourth time in the conference.

Schumacher-Cawley spoke on how all three of these Nittany Lions have become major assets to the team's success in the most recent contests.

“I think her (Stucky) decision-making has gotten so much better,” Schumacher-Cawley said. “...Kennedy scoring on the back row is just as important as a front row for us…”

While Lauenstein didn’t receive Big Ten honors this week, she did receive her flowers from her coach. Schumacher-Cawley said the Nebraska native is “really aggressive.”

Two Big Ten opponents

Against these next two teams, Ohio State and Purdue, Schumacher-Cawley said the team’s ultimate goal is to keep playing “good volleyball.”

Schumacher-Cawley remarked on the variety of results in college volleyball, echoing that sentiment in her own situation. While Ohio State and Purdue are two very different teams rank-wise, Schumacher-Cawley said that preparation remains the same.

Schumacher-Cawley recognized that Ohio State, though unranked, has historically been a tough opponent, particularly in Rec Hall.

“Their coaching staff is amazing, and…I think their players compete, and you know, they had a tough preseason, and I think they’ve handled the Big Ten very well.”

Still, Schumacher-Crawley said the Nittany Lions have been putting in the work in practice with no complacency, with the goal of “getting this team where it needs to be.”

Aggressive mindset

Throughout the press conference, coach Schumacher-Crawley stressed how important it is for the Nittany Lions to be aggressive in their play.

“Everyone is getting their chance to score, and when they do that, it’s pretty hard, I think, defensively to beat the net with us.”

The aggression the team has brought into their gameplay is something coach Schumacher-Crawley wants to see continue for the rest of the season. When asked what she thinks the team should clean up and improve, Schumacher-Crawley said she wants them to stay aggressive from the first whistle.

Players like Lauenstein have done a good job of this, but for continued team success, the other players should do the same.
