title: Penn State men's hockey notebook | Guy Gadowsky talks Jackson Smith improvement, more
author: Chase Fisher | The Daily Collegian
description:
Guy Gadowsky met with the media for his first midweek press conference in two weeks. The longtime Nittany Lions coach pioneered his team to its first two wins of the season last weekend against Canisius.

Still, Gadowsky isn’t satisfied. “We have a lot of work to do,” he said Tuesday evening.

Here’s what we learned from Gadowsky’s press conference as Penn State gears up to play its first Big Ten series this weekend against No. 18 Minnesota.

Gadowsky says team still has a lot of work to do

Gadowsky reiterated on Tuesday what he said after the team’s 3-2 win over Canisius Saturday night. While he’s happy Penn State secured two big wins against the Golden Griffins, he said his team isn’t close to where it needs to be.

The Nittany Lions sit at 2-4 before two dates in Minneapolis with the Golden Gophers and sit 58th out of 62 teams in the NPI rankings, an indicator that determines which clubs make the NCAA Tournament.

Gadowsky said because he is fielding half a new team, he never had expectations the program would be where it needed to be in October. He referenced two years ago, when Penn State was winless in conference play through December, but went on to make the Frozen Four.

“I think we took a step (this weekend),” Gadowsky said. “I don't think it was a big step. I think it was a step in a couple of areas. We're not close to where we have to be. So comfortable is not the word. I would say excited. I think that we're — I would say excited. I would say whatever the word is when you welcome a challenge, whatever that word is, but no, not comfortable by any means. I don't think you're ever comfortable in the Big Ten.”

Two sophomores out to good starts

Sophomores Lev Katzin and Shea Van Olm didn’t quite light up the stat sheet in their freshman seasons. Katzin had five points and two goals in 36 games, while Van Olm, the 2024-25 WHL goals leader, had just nine goals and 12 points in 33 games.

Gadowsky voiced his pleasure with both players' performances on Tuesday, starting with Katzin, who he said is more mature.

“Last year was interesting because he's a very successful player and a very successful offensive player,” Gadowsky said. “And last year he came into a situation unlike he's ever known before that he’s got to play completely different roles than he has in the past. And I think he was really motivated to do everything he could in whatever little way he could to help the team, and I think this year his maturity is just being a little more patient in that, a little more mature in the fact that he has confidence that he's a good player, that if he does the right things, that things are going to come.”

For Van Olm, Gadowsky said he played one of his most complete games Friday against Canisius, and that he’s “going to have a great year.”

“If you look at many of the analytics, he could have been our top forward on the weekend,” Gadowsky said. “He definitely was Friday night. … Like honestly, I think he played one of the more complete games that I've seen him play Friday night, and he didn't get a point. But he was excellent. He helped us win all over the ice. And yes, he is, for him to be really effective. He is a big, strong guy. He's physical. He's a power forward, and he scores that way, though. And it's not from lack of chances. So the chances were generated. The puck just didn't go in the net.”

Defenseman Jackson Smith is improving

Smith notched a four-point weekend, including a three-point showing on Friday. And on Saturday, he lasered the game-winning goal in overtime past Canisius netminder Jack Lisson. But it hasn't been all sunshine and rainbows this year.

Gadowsky hinted on Tuesday night that Smith hadn’t played well, especially against Robert Morris, pausing before saying, “Jackson Smith is a great player. And when he plays great, we're a much, much better team.”

However, Smith has improved since then and played much smarter over the weekend. Gadowsky thinks that’ll continue.

“Jackson Smith is an awesome hockey player, and we need him to be awesome for us to win,” Gadowsky said. “And I think when he has the opportunity to go, like he does, he's awesome. When he is playing with his feet, the thing about him is his hands are really good too, but I think his feet are what make him elite. And when he's playing with his feet and not just his hands, he's extremely difficult to stop. So I think that's maybe where I think you're going to see some more consistency.”

title: Penn State LB Tony Rojas has ‘a lot more to show’ in second half of 2026 season
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
After Tony Rojas was freed from a snap count in the first couple weeks of the season, his play took another jump on the field, proving to be Penn State’s top player on either side of the ball.

Rojas recently earned recognition as an AP Midseason All-America second teamer for his production in the first half of the season, and D’Anton Lynn recognized Tuesday just how special of a player he can be.

“He's one of the most athletic inside backers I've seen, not just talking about Penn State, but just in general,” Lynn said Tuesday.

Rojas has played like one of the best linebackers in the country, but Lynn feels he has “another level” to reach, and his hope is to get him there within the next couple of games. The linebacker has also recognized that he hasn’t reached his full potential yet.

“I think I've been playing at a good level,” Rojas said. “Obviously, kind of hard on myself, so I know I have a lot to improve on, a lot of things to work on. During the bye week and going forward, just watching films, I know I can be better at things… I'd say obviously I've been playing well, but I think I have a lot more to show.”

What that would look like on the field could push Rojas into even bigger conversations given what he’s done in the first half of the season. His 56 tackles, 10.5 tackles for loss and five sacks all lead the team by a significant margin.

The success that Rojas has had comes from his desire to be on the field and help the team emerge victorious in any way. Now fully recovered from his knee injury that ended his 2025 season, Rojas is a player that Matt Campbell understands wants to be on the field as much as possible, even taking upwards of 60 snaps in a game.

“I've never met a great player that doesn't want to play or be on the field,” Campbell said. “I think every great player I've been around, ‘I'm not rotating with anybody, I'm staying on the field and if you try to sub me in, I'm not letting you do that.’ And that's I think Tony to a T.”

Rojas himself said he doesn’t like when he’s on the sideline. He was itching to be on the field more in the first two weeks as he worked himself back to full strength.

“But at that point when I was at my snap count, I was like, ‘Nah, I need to play,’” Rojas said. “I don't like standing on the sideline, so I think at that point I think we got things rolling.”

In Lynn’s scheme, he’s constantly trying to get his playmakers in a position to make a difference, and he’s found that with Rojas. As part of his five sacks, the linebacker feels working against the interior of the offensive line is where his strong suit is when he’s rushing the passer.

However, when he’s off the field, he’s still making an impact on the team. Defensive end Yvan Kemajou has recognized the confidence that Rojas brings to the unit and his ability to give others confidence throughout the game. Kemajou also noticed the help he brings behind the scenes, almost adding another coaching voice in the linebacker room.

Rojas’ ability to lead by example is something both Campbell and Lynn noticed during the bye week. It’s not just his voice that has stood out, but he’s also been a leader on the practice field. His work ethic and persistence makes him a well-rounded leader on the defense.

“Tony's done some great things, and it's been really awesome,” Campbell said. “And as we know and statistically, there's a great catalyst when he's at his best. But I think there's some areas too where he can continue to improve, and he knows that. And what I love about Tony is he's probably one of the guys that has spearheaded last week of coming out with purpose and intent, really having a great week of practice.”

Rojas’ leadership and work at practice are part of his overall goal. He’s thrown personal goals out the window, focusing purely on the team and the rest of Penn State’s season.

“I just want to win out,” Rojas said. “I think just winning is my biggest thing, and all those accolades and whatever doesn't really do anything good for me. I just want to win.”

title: Former Penn State women's volleyball National Champion Nia Reed joins LA Orbit
author: Joey Bolger | For The Collegian
description:
Former Penn State National Champion Nia Reed has signed with the Los Angeles Orbit after eight seasons overseas.

The New Jersey native earned AVCA All-American honorable mention in her final season at Penn State in 2018, recording 336 kills and 54 assisted blocks.

She went on to play professionally in Brazil, Turkey, France, South Korea and Puerto Rico. In 2022, she made her U.S. national team debut, winning silver at the NORCECA Final Six and taking home bronze at the Pan American Cup.

Now, Reed joins the LOVB for their third season as a professional league, on the Los Angeles Orbit.

title: Penn State wrestling's Connor Mirasola added to NWCA All-Star Classic lineup
author: Ava Aguiar | The Daily Collegian
description:
Another Penn State wrestler will compete at the NWCA All-Star Classic.

Heavyweight Connor Mirasola has been added to the lineup for the Nov. 24 showcase in Rec Hall, after the heavyweight matchup was previously listed as to be announced.

Mirasola joins three other Penn Staters in the competition, with Shayne Van Ness, Rocco Welsh and Josh Barr already announced.

Mirasola will return for his third season with the Nittany Lions and will match up against Wisconsin heavyweight Braxton Amos, who's currently ranked No. 7 in the InterMat rankings.

Previously competing in the 197-pound weight class, Mirasola has made the jump to heavyweight. He's coming off a U23 Pan-American gold medal at 125 kilograms, the heavyweight of freestyle competition.

The Nittany Lions will battle one of the top returning heavyweights. A redshirt senior for the Badgers, Amos placed sixth in the Big Ten Championships last season and finished with a 20-7 record.

title: Penn State women’s soccer team moves into latest United Soccer Coaches poll rankings
author: Gabriel Kovadlo | For The Collegian
description:
After going on a two-game road trip against ranked teams, Penn State adds everything but losses to its record, advancing to 8-3-5 and jumping to No. 23 in the United Soccer Coaches poll. The team was last ranked in mid-August, when the first regular-season poll was released. The squad also got ranked at the No. 21 spot in the NCAA RPI metric.

Last Thursday, Penn State matched up against then-No. 5 Michigan State, and it came away with a 2-1 win. Both goals scored by Penn State came from forwards Aubrey Kulpa in the 80th minute and Paige Kalal in the 90th minute, right before regulation time came to an end. This was the program’s first win against a top-five team on the road dating back to 2021.

Just three days later, Penn State matched up with another competitive opponent in then-No. 24 Michigan when the Nittany Lions tied with the Wolverines 2-2. Penn State's two goals came from Kulpa and defender Lilly Burger.

Now, the Nittany Lions look to keep their momentum going when they face an unranked Indiana team back at Jeffrey Field this Friday at 7 p.m., before preparing for the Big Ten Women’s Soccer Tournament.

title: Penn State notebook | Matt Campbell shares update on WR Koby Howard, evaluates QB Rocco Becht
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Matt Campbell met with the media on Tuesday at Beaver Stadium after Penn State’s bye week.

He gave a status update on the wide receivers, spoke about his evaluation of Rocco Becht and shared his thoughts on the offensive line.

Here’s more on what Campbell said.

Wide receivers

Campbell was optimistic about wide receiver Koby Howard’s progress toward returning from injury. Last week, he said Howard was “questionable,” and his status hasn’t changed, but he was on the practice field Tuesday.

“We'll know a lot more by the time we get to the end of the week if he will be available to play this week,” Campbell said.

He said having Howard back will be “huge,” but the coaching staff also must ensure they’re getting their star pass catcher back at full health.

Chase Sowell has stepped up in a big way in Howard’s absence, and Campbell said he wished to have more time with the two of them playing alongside each other. He said when Howard got injured, the Nittany Lions had to reassess who they were and what they were able to accomplish.

“We were a way more complete football team than maybe we were probably those first two games back without Koby,” Campbell said. “I feel like the last two weeks we’ve found a rhythm. I do think getting Koby back will be a huge asset to our football team.”

Additionally, wide receiver Brett Eskildsen, who was shaken up at the end of the Michigan game, is fully healthy ahead of Week 9.

Evaluating Becht post-bye week

Campbell and his coaching staff used the bye week to evaluate where the team is currently in all areas of the game, going through seven weeks worth of film to pinpoint not just the negatives, but the positives too.

Campbell’s been adamant about continuing to believe in Rocco Becht through his ups and downs, and that stands true after the bye week. He said a lot of Becht’s mistakes are relatively simple fixes, and they may come down to decision making or general inaccuracy.

“It's fundamental, it's coachable,” Campbell said. “It's able to get corrected, and I think that piece of it is exciting because you're able to go to work and you're able to put the time, effort and energy not into scheme, but into the fundamentals and details.”

Becht has shown flashes of what he’s capable of, and Campbell’s banking on his quarterback harnessing his skills and being more consistent in his fundamentals.

“I feel very convicted about Rocco,” Campbell said. “There is a lot of good football in there. When he's at his best and when he's playing good football, he's giving us a chance to win the games. I think some of the areas where he has to be better to win the games is evident as well, and I think it gave us a lot of time and effort to go correct those things and have a great plan moving ourselves forward.”

Offensive line

Campbell said his offensive line is the healthiest it’s been this year going into Penn State’s game against Purdue, which could potentially allow the offense to get moving in the back half of the season.

Ryan Clanton’s group has had its fair share of ups and downs, with various linemen getting injured through seven weeks. Campbell said progress started with center Brock Riker returning to form two weeks ago, and the room can grow from there.

“It always starts with the offensive line,” Campbell said. “I feel like there's probably been at times where we maybe tried to fix it by scheme rather than by fundamental.”

Campbell also said because the offensive line is a group that’s starting together for the first time, the coaching staff has been getting a feel for who can do what things best.

“We were able to catch ourselves and zoom focus a couple weeks ago of really trying to dial into what we can do best and what that group does best,” Campbell said.

title: Penn State notebook | DC D'Anton Lynn discusses defensive inconsistencies, pass rush
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Coming out of the bye week, D’Anton Lynn met with the media inside Beaver Stadium on Tuesday.

Lynn discussed the defense's inconsistencies, the Nittany Lions' lack of pressure and more ahead of Penn State’s Saturday afternoon matchup against Purdue.

Here’s a look at what Lynn had to say.

Inconsistency on defense

After starting the season 3-0, Penn State has lost its last four games. The defense has been a major factor in those struggles, as it’s failed to stop the run and read-option plays from opposing offenses.

Last week against Michigan, the Nittany Lions gave up 211 yards on the ground, with a majority coming later in the game as the Wolverines pulled away. Lynn emphasized the need to be consistent in the running game and play strong all 60 minutes.

“It’s been inconsistent, and our biggest thing is can the fourth quarter and third quarter look like the second and first?” Lynn said. “We still haven’t figured out a way to finish games. There’s periods where you watch us stop the run in the first half of a couple of those games, and man, it's as good as it gets. And then there's times where man, we're in the exact same position, and it's later in the game, and we're not making those plays.”

Some of the run-game struggles have come from missed tackles. The Nittany Lions whiffed a bunch three weeks ago against Northwestern and have prioritized toughness and tackling ever since.

But even with that emphasis, missed tackles allowed Michigan to defeat Penn State two weeks ago.

“There’s times where you can’t get bored doing the same thing over and over again,” Lynn said. “Not getting bored, doing your job, and really just missed tackles in space, not letting the ball get outside of us on the edge.”

Generating pressure

Penn State’s defense has struggled to generate significant pass pressure this season. The Nittany Lions only have nine sacks through seven games, with five coming from linebacker Tony Rojas.

As a result of the struggles, many have asked about a potential lineup change to attempt to generate more pressure.

“We need to do a better job putting guys in a position to do that and then continuing to take that advantage,” Lynn said. “We do have some inside backers and some DBs I think can blitz, some of them are better from internal or off the edge. Some can do it from on the ball. But just finding different ways to get more of those guys involved because it's just something that we have not been doing to our standards up to this point.”

Two of the more talked about players that could be utilized to generate pressure are Rojas and safety Marcus Neal Jr.

Rojas has had success pressuring the quarterback, but he’s arguably the best player on Penn State’s defense and is utilized across the field as a result.

“He definitely has the talent,” Lynn said. “He's one of the most athletic inside backers I've seen not just talking about Penn State, but just in general.”

On the other hand, Neal is a player who the coaches have gone away from when they’re looking for a safety to play in coverage. So there’s been more talk of him playing a linebacker-like role where he can make more of an impact up front.

Zion Tracy’s versatility

With Penn State’s struggles defensively, cornerback Zion Tracy has been a major bright spot.

Tracy started the season coming off the bench due to injury, he quickly entered the starting lineup and has made plays lining up all over the secondary. The past two games, he’s been playing more safety, letting cornerback Josiah Zayas take over the nickel spot.

“Zion's a guy that can play boundary safety, can play field, he can play in the slot, he can play outside,” Lynn said. “He can kind of do it all.”

Neal’s inability to play in coverage has given Tracy an opportunity to showcase his versatility and has given the Nittany Lions a “more athletic” player at safety.

“You put a guy like him at safety, and it just opens up some things you could call that you probably couldn't call if he was not in the game,” Lynn said. “He's a guy that we trust in that position.”

title: Penn State awarded $39.9 million from U.S. Dept. of Commerce for DuBois manufacturing hub
author: Marek Horgas | For the Collegian
description:
Penn State is set to establish a regional manufacturing hub in DuBois, following a $39.9 million grant from the U.S. Department of Commerce. The funding will lead a $200 million public-private partnership to create the DuBois Center for Innovation Regional Manufacturing Hub.

Penn State Dubois is among the Commonwealth Campuses set for closure at the end of the spring 2027 semester. The investment is intended to strengthen manufacturing and the economy in DuBois and its surrounding counties, a region described as facing “long-term economic challenges” according to a press release from the university.

“The DuBois Center for Innovation will provide the United States the domestic pressed materials production needed for a strategic manufacturing capability essential to economic and national security and technological leadership, while creating opportunities for businesses and workers across north central Pennsylvania,” Penn State senior vice president for research Andrew Read said in the release.

This manufacturing hub will focus on the production of pressed materials, including bonded neodymium magnets, which have been produced in DuBois by Applied Magnets since 1992. Neodymium magnets are the most widely used rare earth magnets, and their production has been dominated by China, who produces 95% of the world’s supply, according to Applied Magnets parent company Bunting.

The federal grant, supported by U.S. senator David McCormick (R-PA), will support the redevelopment of DuBois facilities for advanced manufacturing labs, the establishment of training centers, which aim to train 150 workers by year five, and the creation of 200 jobs at regional companies.

The announcement comes after the Penn State Board of Trustees voted in September to sell two closing Commonwealth Campuses – Penn State Shenango and Wilkes-Barre. The DuBois site of the center will remain within the campus for now, before expected transfer to the Dubois Educational Foundation.

The center will be north central Pennsylvania’s first shared applied research and development center, specifically for pressed materials.

The site is expected to be operational within 16 months.

title: 3 takeaways from Penn State men’s basketball’s exhibition win over Drexel
author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian
description:
PHILADELPHIA – Exactly a week before their 2026-27 regular season gets underway against Canisius on Nov. 2, the Nittany Lions hit the road Monday for an in-state exhibition against Drexel.

“We love Philly basketball,” Mike Rhoades said. “There's a lot of Penn Staters down here in the greater Philadelphia area. We love cheesesteaks. So why wouldn’t we?”

Penn State staggered out of the gate, but pulled away in the second half to secure a 68-57 victory over the Dragons. Here’s what stood out from the Nittany Lions’ preseason finale.

Another slow start

In its last exhibition, the blue and white trailed St. Bonaventure 36-25 at the half. Penn State would’ve been trailing at the break against Drexel if it wasn’t for a driving, buzzer-beating layup by Dasonte Bowen to end the first half.

The Nittany Lions turned the ball over nine times in the first 20 minutes, and shot 1-for-8 from three-point range. Drexel took advantage of the sloppy play and led by as many as six points in the first half.

“We can’t afford to be passive starting the game, or, as guys like to say, get in the flow of the game,” Mike Rhoades said. “You (do that) with our schedule, you’re down 20. It’s a huge emphasis.”

Ultimately, Rhoades and the Nittany Lions pulled away. An 11-point run in the middle of the second half shifted all of the momentum to Penn State and helped it to avoid a preseason upset.

“We’ve got to set the tone,” Rhoades said. “That second half, the way we played defense, if we can carry that on the road and throughout the year, that’s going to help us a lot. But we’ve got to get off to better starts, without a doubt.”

Long-range woes

In September, Rhoades described this season’s group as the “best shooting team I’ve had since I’ve been here.”

Penn State shot a combined 2-for-12 from three-point range against Drexel on Monday.

“We had a couple open ones early; we didn’t knock (them) down,” Rhoades said. That could loosen some things up, but sometimes it's gotta be dirty and grimy. Today was dirty and grimy, and I'm glad it was early in the year because we're gonna have to play that way at times.”

The slump forced the Nittany Lions to play in the paint rather than fire the long ball, but Rhoades noted that the Dragons' defensive scheme forced them to play that way regardless.

“The way they were guarding us and trying to be real physical, we knew we were going to drive more,” Rhoades said. “We want to get 30 threes a game. We only got 12 today. That was the way the game was played.”

Penn State made only one 3-pointer in the first half: a step-back jumper by Brant Byers that sailed smoothly into the nylon after the 6-foot-8 wing faked out a Drexel defender. It didn’t get another until François Wibaut buried one near the second half’s midpoint.

“Some nights you're not going to make all your shots,” Rhoades said. “You’ve got to find a different way to win. Today was an example of that.”

Personnel questions

After the game, Rhoades was blunt when asked if this year’s group was deep enough to play the press on defense.

“We're totally playing different than I have in the last 10 years,” Rhoades said. “But I play different ways at different places. I'd be an idiot to try to press with this team for 40 minutes… In certain games we might be able to find ways to get turnovers and turn people over in half court; we might not do it in full court, but we don't have the roster to press.”

Still, the fourth-year coach is embracing the challenges that the newly minted group has presented him with.

“That's been the fun of it with this group,” Rhoades said. “These guys are very coachable. They're high character guys… We'll be different the way we play, but I think the way we can play and be successful in this group, we just [have] to continue to improve.”

Roko Prkačin didn’t play or participate in warmups on Monday, but was seen on the sideline in an all-gray sweatsuit. The Croatian also didn’t participate in Penn State’s first exhibition against St. Bonaventure.

“Still going through the eligibility process and all that stuff,” Rhoades said of Prkačin’s status. “We're honoring the process.”

Prkačin played last season for Nanterre 92 in France, the same club that produced NBA standout Victor Wembanyama. When deemed eligible, the 6-foot-8 forward could provide a spark that’s been missing in both exhibitions’ first halves.

“I thought both games, we had not very good starts, turnovers and passive plays,” Rhoades said. “We gotta really address that.”

title: Penn State men's soccer seeks win for Senior Night game against Duquesne
author: Sienna Pearce | For The Collegian
description:
This Wednesday, the Penn State Nittany Lions will go head-to-head against the Duquesne Dukes at 7 p.m. The game will take place on the Nittany Lions’ home turf at Jeffery Field.

Penn State, now approaching the end of its season, is scrambling for a win. To add even more fuel to the fire, Wednesday’s game is its Senior Night. The Nittany Lions are going to have to summon all of their effort to bring home a win for their seniors.

Duquesne’s season so far

Unfortunately for Penn State, Duquesne has been riding a high all season. In fact, 2026 marks its sixth winning season in a row.

The Duquesne Dukes have been holding their own this season, managing a 9-3-2 overall record. They hold the coveted first-place slot in the Atlantic 10 Conference.

The Dukes are led by head coach Chase Brooks, in his 14th season at the helm. Under his influence, Duquesne tied its record for the longest stretch of consecutive winning seasons. Duquesne has dominated with a 6-0-1 home record, and its only tie this season was against Lafayette, which ended in a scoreless draw.

However, its games on the road are a different story. During their away games, the Dukes have lost to notable teams such as West Virginia (1-0), Saint Louis (1-0) and Pittsburgh (2-1).

Duquesne has still ended its regular season on a high note, earning a 3-0 win over VCU during its Senior Day this past Saturday.

Sophomore Jameson Micheal scored the first goal of the game from a pass by senior Cody Da. The Dukes continued their streak when Micheal passed to senior Ashwin Menon, whose header allowed sophomore Hákon Dagur Matthíasson to score the next goal.

Junior Ofek Sasson blocked multiple shots to ensure his team's victory. Soon after, junior Roni Balder sealed the deal by scoring the last goal of the night.

Penn State’s season so far

The Nittany Lions have had a rocky season, to say the least. They are currently sitting at a 2-8-3 record. The blue and white is ranked 87th in the NCAA Division I RPI rankings.

Even so, coach Rob Dow’s unit upped its game against No. 13 Wisconsin this past Saturday. The matchup ended in a 2-2 draw, a major improvement from the previous game against Rutgers when they lost 5-0.

Freshman goalkeeper Daniel Peluffo-Wiese was a standout, posting a career-high in saves.

“What a bounce back from last game,” coach Dow said about the netminder after the Wisconsin game. “One of the best games of his career.”

Senior Noah Andreas also made a triumphant comeback after being in rough condition, as he was sick.

“He had composure, and he was playing for the team first. It’s excellent,” said Dow.

If the blue and white continue these habits, they could have a real chance against Duquesne on Wednesday, as the rest of the season rests on the players’ shoulders.

“We have great people in the locker room,” Dow said. “Guys that are looking at themselves in the mirror and that hold themselves accountable.”

title: Preview | Penn State women’s basketball's upperclassmen
author: Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State returns just one player for 2026-27, but that doesn’t mean Tanisha Wright’s squad lacks veteran experience. The Lady Lions have six upperclassmen on the roster, and three of them are graduate students.

One of those fifth-years is the lone returner, Vitória Santana. The São Paulo, Brazil, native appeared in 28 of 29 games last season and made one start.

Before her time in the blue and white, Santana spent two years at Eastern Arizona in the NJCAA, where she averaged 15.9 points and 8.1 rebounds in her second season. Penn State announced the Carolyn Kieger recruit’s return to Happy Valley on Sept. 29.

“I love Penn State. I love State College,” Santana said at local media day. “I love the community, the fans. So when I heard that I have (the) opportunity to (spend) another year playing basketball in the States and being in school, I took the chance.”

The guard has emerged as a leader on and off the court, even under a new regime.

“I think she has a great voice,” Savannah White said at local media day. “Even just when she came in learning, whether it's the offense or learning the drills, she hasn't let that cripple her from being a leader and having a voice and making sure that we're all on our P's and Q's, so I think she's done a really good job since she's been here for sure.”

White, a graduate student from St. Paul, Minnesota, is one of the most traveled players on the team. The 6-foot-2 forward played at Wisconsin, Indiana State and Xavier and is now making her final stop in State College.

Last season at Xavier, White started all 29 games and averaged 7.0 points and 7.3 rebounds. White operates primarily in the post, but Wright and the coaching staff have encouraged the forwards to expand their skill sets this offseason.

“I think a big part of our work as a team is skill work,” White said. “I think that we put the work in, and (Wright) believes in us because we put the work in. She encourages the guards to believe in the post, and the post to believe in the guards because of the work that we put in consistently every week.”

White and Enjulina Gonzalez were the players selected to speak at local media day. Gonzalez hails from Miami and is also on her fourth school.

Her most successful season came in 2024-25 at Miami University, where she earned All-MAC honors. The guard started 27 of the team’s 30 games and averaged over 16 points.

Gonzalez’s 5-foot-9 frame packs plenty of personality. She was the first one onto the court at Ball at East Hall to celebrate her teammates in the skills competition, often just ahead of Cristen Carter.

Carter, an Indianapolis native, has three years of Big East experience. She began her career at Butler, appearing in 64 games and starting in 30 in two seasons. As a sophomore, Carter led the Bulldogs in blocks and was second on the team in rebounds.

The 6-foot-4 forward spent her junior campaign at Georgetown, where now-Penn State assistant coach Kelly Mazzante was on the staff. The Lady Lions’ all-time leading scorer returned to Happy Valley this offseason to reunite with Wright, a former teammate and fellow Penn State great.

“When we were building this roster, we all kind of sat in the war room and brought different players to the table,” Mazzante said at local media day. “Cristen was someone that stood out to me when we played at Georgetown. I knew we needed a post player, and we're recruiting a certain type of student-athlete, so she kind of encompasses everything that we want.”

Two more players who stood out to the staff in the recruiting process are Devyn Quigley and Petra Božan. Each has two years of Power Four experience: Quigley at NC State and Božan at Nebraska. The pair also represented Penn State at Big Ten media day in Chicago.

Quigley, a Manchester, New Jersey, native, is a quick 5-foot-10 guard who should make an impact early and often on both ends of the court. She helped the Wolfpack make NCAA Tournament appearances in each of the past two years, appearing in 62 total contests.

At 6-foot-4, Božan is tied with Carter for the team's tallest player. She racked up 387 points, 202 rebounds and 31 blocks in two seasons with the Cornhuskers while starting 19 games. The Split, Croatia, native also started two games in the 2026 NCAA Tournament.

While nothing is guaranteed with an overhauled program, Božan and Quigley are two names likely to be heard often inside the Bryce Jordan Center early this season.

The Lady Lions open the 2026-27 slate on Nov. 2, at 5 p.m. when Cleveland State comes to town.

title: Nittany Lions in the NFL | TE Mike Gesicki’s touchdown catch, strong defense headline Week 7
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
While Penn State was on its bye, several former Nittany Lions took the field for Week 7 of the NFL season.

It was a quieter weekend offensively, as tight end Mike Gesicki was the only letterman to find the end zone. However, several players had big performances defensively, including Kevin Winston Jr., who led his team in tackles.

Here’s a look at how former players performed across the NFL.

Mike Gesicki, tight end, Cincinnati Bengals

Gesicki opened National Tight Ends Day with a touchdown on his only reception of the day.

The former Nittany Lion ran a short out-route to the back corner of the end zone, reeling in the six-yard reception from Joe Burrow to put the Bengals on the scoreboard.

Gesicki has been an elite touchdown weapon for Cincinnati this year. He’s scored in five of the team’s six games, including in each of the last four, while hauling in just 13 catches.

He was Penn State’s only tight end to score on National Tight Ends Day.

Chop Robinson, linebacker, Miami Dolphins

The Miami Dolphins earned their first win of the season behind quarterback Malik Willis’ best game of the year. However, the defense also played its part, including former Nittany Lion Chop Robinson.

With the New York Jets driving to the end zone with a chance to tie the game, Robinson burst past tight end Mason Taylor and ran unguarded at quarterback Geno Smith. Robinson took him down 15 yards behind the line of scrimmage, forcing the Jets to settle for a field goal.

The former Nittany Lion also recorded a pair of tackles Sunday.

Robinson has recorded two sacks on the year, tied with defensive tackle Zach Sieler for the most on the team.

Saquon Barkley, running back, Philadelphia Eagles

After missing the last two weeks with a hamstring injury, Saquon Barkley returned to the field for the Philadelphia Eagles on Monday night.

Barkley recorded 62 yards on seven carries against the Cowboys, producing one of his better performances of the year, although he left the game early with a back injury.

The former NFL Offensive Player of the Year has had an underwhelming start of the 2026 season, but trended in the right direction on Monday with his first touchdown of the year.

Kalen King, cornerback, Arizona Cardinals

With the Arizona Cardinals’ starting nickel Max Melton out due to injury, former Nittany Lion Kalen King earned the first start of his NFL career.

King had multiple tackles for the first time this year, ending the day with six tackles.

While the Cardinals ultimately came away with a loss, King made several big plays, including a tackle on third down to hold the Denver Broncos to a field goal. However, he also had several miscues in his first start, including an illegal block in the back penalty on a kickoff and a collision with his teammate that resulted in a dropped interception.

Kevin Winston Jr., safety, Tennessee Titans

After missing Week 6 due to a quad injury, safety Kevin Winston Jr. returned against the Cleveland Browns on Sunday, recording his best performance of his two-year NFL career.

Winston played every defensive snap for the Titans as he tallied a team-high 14 tackles.

The former Nittany Lion was everywhere on the field and has continued to be one of the best defenders for Tennessee, not missing a tackle so far this season.

Nick Scott, safety, Carolina Panthers

While the Carolina Panthers were blown out 43-13 by the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Sunday, former Nittany Lion Nick Scott had arguably his best game of the season.

Scott tied his season-best seven tackles and recorded a stuff against the Buccaneers.

He’s split time in the backfield with fellow Penn Stater Zakee Wheatley. However, Sunday’s contest saw Scott lead the way, as Wheatley only tallied one tackle.

title: Recruiting roundup | Matt Campbell gets first recruiting win during 2026 season
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Matt Campbell and the coaching staff went on the recruiting trail during the bye week and picked up Penn State’s first commit of the 2026 season.

However, the Nittany Lions also lost a recruit during the bye week weekend, but they continue to push for other flips in the 2027 class while adding more focus on future classes.

Here’s a roundup of what Penn State did over the bye week on the recruiting trail.

Filling in gaps, more open

Penn State earned a commitment from 3-star running back Jordan Hall on Saturday and lost a commit in 3-star linebacker Blake Betton on Sunday.

Hall filled a hole that opened with the flip of 4-star Aiden Gibson to Rutgers, who reclassified and joined the Scarlet Knights for this season. Gibson’s switch left Chukwuma Odoh as the lone running back in the class, and while the Nittany Lions didn’t necessarily need two running backs in this cycle, Hall’s addition could definitely add to a struggling running back room.

The Ohio native ranks as the No. 852 player, No. 60 player at his position and No. 32 player in his home state, and he’s quickly risen to the eyes of Power Four coaches. The biggest part of adding Hall was that Campbell beat out Ohio State and Missouri, two high-power recruiting programs.

On the other side of the ball, Penn State lost one of its two linebacker commits a day later, when Betton flipped from the Nittany Lions to Wisconsin. There’s now an additional hole in the recruiting class, with only 4-star linebacker Case Alexander remaining at the position in the 2027 class.

Penn State is likely to look to replace the hole Betton leaves in the class, but it only has less than two months before early signing day, which is when a majority of the recruits sign.

Push for flips

After Penn State lost 3-star quarterback Will Wood to Boston College, it inserted its name into some of the Eagles’ current and former commits while also trying to turn its attention to a different quarterback in the class.

Current Boston College linebacker commit Michael Harden Jr. could be a name to look at to fill the spot left open by Betton. The 3-star recruit goes to the same high school as Wood at Xaverian Brothers, but he’s yet to receive an offer from Penn State despite visiting State College on June 10 for a camp.

3-star defensive lineman Markius Woods recently decommitted from Boston College and has set up a visit with the Nittany Lions. Woods will visit Happy Valley for Penn State’s game against Rutgers on Nov. 21. The No. 576 player in the class holds offers from Missouri, Kansas State and Illinois.

Campbell took a visit to 4-star quarterback Braylen Warren and extended an offer from the Nittany Lions on Wednesday. He’s currently committed to Missouri, but Campbell’s visit to Omaha, Nebraska is likely the start to push for a flip.

Warren was teammates with current Penn State safety Bryson Williams at Omaha Westside High School, and Campbell has experience recruiting the area. Warren was an Elite 11 Finalist and is currently the No. 18 quarterback in the class, according to 247Sports composite.

On the trail

Campbell began his bye week with a midwest visit to Warren in Nebraska. He continued on the trail the rest of the week, staying closer to Happy Valley. He ended his week in Ohio, visiting Hall a day before the running back committed to Penn State on Saturday.

Other coaches also went onto the trail to pay visits to targets. Taylor Mouser and assistant tight ends coach Sam Seonbuchner visited one of the top targets in the 2028 class, 3-star tight end Quinn Weber.

Weber ranks as the No. 15 player in New Jersey and No. 24 tight end in the 2028 class.

Quarterbacks coach Jake Waters made his way to the Pittsburgh area to watch his future quarterback, James Armstrong. The Hopewell product had a dominant showing in front of his future position coach, going 9-of-14 for 314 yards and five touchdowns. He also ran in a touchdown en route to a 50-0 lead at halftime.

Penn State’s future quarterback situation appears to be in the hands of Armstrong, and with performances like he had on Friday, his ranking could skyrocket. He’s currently the No. 145 player in the class, No. 10 quarterback and No. 3 player in Pennsylvania.

title: 3 Penn State wrestlers to compete in 2026 NWCA All-Star Classic

Henson, who wrestles at Virginia Tech, won a national title in 2024, and redshirted in 2025. He’s also coming off back-to-back ACC Wrestler of the Year awards in 2023 and 2024.

Welsh defeated Mantanona three times last season, eliminating the Wolverine in both the Big Ten and National Championships.

Barr, the No. 1-ranked 197-pounder, will face No. 3 Stephen Little, who wrestles at Little Rock.

Little placed third at last season’s NCAA Championships and was also named the Pac-12 Wrestler of the Year.

title: College Democrats host Gov. Shapiro for ‘Rally in the Valley’ event on campus
author: Jacob Godshall I The Daily Collegian
description:
On Sunday night, Gov. Josh Shapiro stopped on the steps of Old Main as part of a 10-day tour through 29 state counties. Shapiro was joined by local Democratic Party members, including representatives Paul Takac and Scott Conklin and local Congressional candidate Ray Bilger.

Despite the cold, dozens of students and community members crowded around the steps to listen to Shapiro and his supporters speak about the upcoming midterm election on Nov. 3. The event, “Rally in the Valley,” began with speeches from Penn State College Democrats, Students for Shapiro and the Centre County Democratic Committee.

The speeches centered around discussions of corruption in our current government, the importance of Centre County in the upcoming midterms and how Shapiro has worked to help rural Pennsylvania.

State College Mayor Ezra Nanes spoke to the audience, highlighting Shapiro’s leadership qualities. He said Shapiro “knows how to work within the government.”

“Josh Shapiro says what he means and means what he says,” Nanes said.

Representatives Conklin and Takac also shared words of support for Shapiro, with Conklin calling Shapiro “smart” and “articulate,” and Takac stressing the possibility of flipping the Pennsylvania Senate and House, which would result in a Democrat trifecta for the first time in over 30 years.

Ethan Galley, 23, of Houston, Texas, attended the rally because he wanted to see Shapiro interact with Penn State students and community members.

“When there is a candidate running for office providing the chance to actually interact with students, I see it being fairly imperative for me to show up and make myself available to make, either that feedback known, or to show my support for said candidate if I do support them,” Galley, president of Civic Engagement Alliance and a second-year studying public policy, said.

Galley said that the biggest issue for him is affordability for students, local residents and all Pennsylvanians.

“Obviously cost of living is continuously increasing and I think if any candidate up here actually stands a chance in receiving both a vote from students, and a vote from further generations, the biggest thing they should be focusing on is finding ways to help students navigate housing challenges,” Galley said.

State College resident Katherine Allen said she attended the rally to support Shapiro and to hear more from Bilger. Bilger is running against incumbent Republican Glenn (GT) Thompson in the 15th Congressional District, which includes Centre County. Thompson has held the seat for nine terms.

“I'm tired of GT Thompson representing this area, particularly when he claims to work on behalf of agriculture,” Allen, 67, of Memphis, Tennessee, said. “I think the farmers are in really dire straits right now, and as far as I know, he hasn't taken any real steps to assist them.”

Since State College is both a university-town and an agricultural area, these candidates “work on behalf of both of those groups,” Allen said. In his speech, Shapiro voiced plans to support Pennsylvanian farmers and agriculture and invest in higher education.

“I think higher-ed has been unfairly targeted by the White House, and by, frankly, the movers and shakers within the Republican Party for far too long,” Allen said, “But I also think the farmers in the agricultural community, they're sort of taken for granted by one party, and I think they really need actual help.”

The rally concluded with a speech from Shapiro himself, which spanned a variety of topics. He said President Donald Trump has made upward of $2 billion since he entered office. He also spoke about affordability, gas prices and tariffs, and said the federal government is operating with “cruelty” and “corruption.”

According to Bilger, the rally showed the “unity” of the democratic party, and that this needs to be replicated by the national party.

“This was an example that we have all these people up here supporting every single other person,” Bilger, 66, of Pleasant Gap, Pennsylvania, said. “Not only that, but we're also supporting our state, we're supporting our government, our constitution, and I think that is the biggest thing.”

title: Spooky films, community events | Here’s what’s happening in the valley
author: Brennan Kramp I The Daily Collegian
description:
Monday, Oct. 26

THON Dream Forward Picnic

Continue to show out for THON, the nation's largest student run charity, at the Dream Forward Picnic. From 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. get your grub on at the HUB-Robeson Center lawn to celebrate the beginning of the fundraising campaign.

With lawn games, merch stands and a wide variety of food, the picnic is a key event in this annual tradition and never ceases to deliver as a great afternoon of Penn State spirit.

Tuesday, Oct. 27

The Blair Witch Project

If found-footage horror is your jam, head down to the State Theatre at 7:30 p.m. for a viewing of the horror film “The Blair Witch Project.”

Released in 1999, “The Blair Witch Project” created a frenzy out of audiences, with some moviegoers even calling the police in fear that student film-makers actually went missing.

Tickets can be purchased online or at the theater.

How To Build Flavor

Hosted by the Student Farm and Food Systems at Penn State, this workshop will help you add a little more panache to your cooking.

This free event is a great opportunity to learn how to make your food more enjoyable and take a step up from salty ramen packet seasoning.

Head over to Headhouse 1 on 160 Curtain Road from 5 to 6 p.m. for this lesson in flavor.

Wednesday, Oct. 28

Sinners

Maybe you’ve heard about it, maybe you’ve seen clips or maybe you’ve already seen it. Either way, take a seat at the State Theatre for a viewing of the modern horror film “Sinners” that took home four Oscar wins out of 16 nominations at the 2026 Academy Awards.

At 7:30 p.m., watch Michael B. Jordan and Hailee Steinfeld perform in one of the most raved about horror movies in the last few years.

It’s probably still giving Josh Allen nightmares.

West Ghost Swing Halloween Dance

Every Wednesday at The Press, the Swing Dance Club hosts intermediate and beginner-friendly dance lessons from 7 to 8 p.m. followed by a dance party from 8 to 9 p.m.

This week’s party is spooky themed and free to attend. A partner or prior experience isn’t required.

“Monster Mash” the night away, and spook your skeleton with some West Ghost Swing.

Thursday, Oct. 29

Dark Storm Step Team’s Scream Fest

On Thursday from 6:30 to 8:30 p.m. in Heritage Hall, the Dark Storm Step Team will be hosting their annual Scream Fest.

This night of scares and sequences will feature horror-themed dance numbers from various dance teams on campus. These dances will showcase fear and grace all wrapped into one thrilling night.

There will be free food and no admission charge.

Friday, Oct. 30

Corpse Bride

Round out the week with the childhood horror classic, “Corpse Bride.”

Showing at the Friedman Auditorium at 6:30 p.m., the legendary Tim Burton film featuring Johnny Depp and Emily Watson will take you back to memories of classroom Halloween parties and mobs of trick-or-treaters passing down the block while rushing towards the bowl that says, “take one.”

Rocktober Climbing Games

Stop by the IM Building and try your hand at some games and competitions in the Climbing Suite.

From 4 to 6 p.m., you can test your skills on the wall and hopefully claim victory at the top. There’s no need to register or RSVP, simply stop by and enjoy the air up there.

John Summit

This Friday, Penn State will host EDM superstar, John Summit, as part of his CTRL ESCAPE Arena Tour in the Bryce Jordan Center at 7 p.m.

Happy Valley will be the fifth show in Summit’s tour and the first college stop on the tour. Penn State students are getting amped for his amps after the release of his second album, “CTRL ESCAPE.”

Doors open at 5:30 p.m. and the BJC will showcase the talents of Alok and Mesto as the opening acts. Summit’s music was made for the partygoer, and Penn State definitely has no shortage of those kinds of fans.

Saturday, Oct. 31

Back To Back Screams

Close out your Halloween with a shriek at the State Theatre for a 10 p.m. viewing of “Halloween,” followed by the timeless, “Evil Dead II,” at midnight.

These two movies have become the horror version of “A Charlie Brown Christmas,” as an October staple that would make the spooky season incomplete without watching them.

Penn State Women's Volleyball

Penn State’s Women’s Volleyball will take on Purdue in Rec Hall at 12:30 p.m., with doors opening at 11:30 a.m.

The Lady Lions are 13-5 on the season heading into their matchup with the closely contending 11-6 Purdue Boilermakers. This win could be big for Penn State as they continue to grind out a competitive season.

title: Big Ten roundup | Indiana survives, midwest schools pull off upsets in Week 8
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Six teams may have had bye weeks, but the Big Ten still featured some exciting results in another crazy week of college football.

No. 6 Indiana survived an upset scare from Michigan in Ann Arbor, and both Minnesota and Wisconsin pulled off ranked upsets to keep the middle of the Big Ten chaotic.

Here’s what happened in Week 8 in the conference.

Indiana survives in overtime

Indiana went into The Big House looking to rebound after losing for the first time in 22 games. Michigan sent out true freshman quarterback Tommy Carr, who made his first career start.

Neither offense had any success in the game, as the Hoosiers led 6-3 with under 10 minutes left in the fourth quarter. Carr led Michigan on a game-tying field goal drive as time expired to send the game to overtime with a 6-6 score.

In the overtime period, Indiana’s offense scored with ease, something it couldn’t do all game. Josh Hoover completed a 21-yard pass to tight end Brock Schott, a pass that marked 25% of Hoover’s yards on the game, as he totaled 81 passing yards on 8-of-18 passing.

Michigan had a chance to respond following Indiana’s touchdown, but after a rush on fourth down to move the sticks for the first time, the offense stalled out. Carr’s fourth-down pass was incomplete and Indiana survived a scare against the Wolverines.

The Hoosiers moved to 7-1 on the season and remain in a strong position to have a first-round bye in the College Football Playoff, moving up to No. 4 in the AP Poll.

Minnesota, Wisconsin pull off upsets

Minnesota and Wisconsin both hosted teams inside the top 16, as the Golden Gophers battled No. 15 Iowa and the Badgers took on No. 16 USC.

Minnesota and Iowa had an old fashioned Big Ten battle. The Golden Gophers had a 10-3 lead heading into the fourth quarter after a 1-yard rushing touchdown from Darius Taylor.

Iowa marched 98 yards down the field with a little over five minutes left in the game to knot it up on a 37-yard touchdown pass from quarterback Hank Brown to tight end Reece Vander Zee.

Both teams went three-and-out on their ensuing drives, and Minnesota had possession of the ball with 1:46 left. A 39-yard completion from quarterback Drake Lindsay to wide receiver Jalen Smith set the Golden Gophers up in field goal range, and kicker Luke Drzewiecki sealed the game with a 46-yard field goal to pull off the upset and beat Iowa, 13-10.

For Wisconsin, it was a much different story. The Badgers’ defense slowed down USC’s high-powered offense, limiting the Trojans to just one touchdown and recording five sacks, including 2.5 from Sebastian Cheeks.

It was Wisconsin football at its finest, as the Badgers rushed for 142 yards and two touchdowns, leading the way to a dominant win. Running back Abu Sama III had 17 rushes for 71 yards as the leading rusher, while quarterback Colton Joseph played efficient football.

Joseph only threw 14 passes, completing 12 of them for just 58 yards and a touchdown, but it was enough for the Badgers to pull out the 24-7 victory, leading to a field storm in Madison, Wisconsin.

The win pushed Wisconsin into the top 25, slotting in at No. 25 in the updated AP Poll.

UCLA, Northwestern continue to roll behind rushing attacks

UCLA and Northwestern are both overperforming from preseason expectations. The Bruins are into the top 10 for the first time since 2022, and the Wildcats are ranked for the first time since 2020.

Both teams dominated their opponent in Week 8. UCLA relied on the run game against Michigan State, as quarterback Ty Dieffenbach continued to get settled into the starting role.

Running back Anthony Woods led the way with 112 yards and a touchdown, but Wayne Knight and Jaivian Thomas both reached the end zone as well, allowing the Bruins to win with ease, 28-10, against Michigan.

For Northwestern, it faced one of the worst teams in the conference in Rutgers. At its new Ryan Field, the Wildcats dominated the Scarlet Knights, beating them 42-14. Quarterback Aidan Chiles was sensational on Saturday, accounting for five of Northwestern’s six touchdowns.

Running back Caleb Komolafe recorded 150 rushing yards and a touchdown as the leader of the Wildcats’ 283 rushing yards. Chiles totaled 83 rushing yards as well as the ground attack continued to be the most successful part of offensive coordinator Chip Kelly’s offense.

Northwestern is currently fourth in the Big Ten standings with a 3-1 record, and it has a chance to make statements in November with games against Ohio State and Iowa.

title: Penn State recently terminated its Flock Safety contract. UPUA members work to address ongoing concerns
author: Jonathon Chiu | The Daily Collegian
description:
On Oct. 14, university police and Penn State Chief Financial Officer Sara Thorndike confirmed on-campus Flock cameras will be taken down after reviewing the operational value and cost of continuing their usage.

But concerns still linger on campus, and two members of the University Park Undergraduate Association’s (UPUA) are working together to plan out how the organization intends to address the issue.

James Dugery, 22, of Skippack, Pennsylvania, said he first learned about the presence of over 20 Flock Safety automated license plate reader (ALPR) cameras in April. John Wozniak, UPUA’s division of undergraduate studies representative, had become interested in Flock cameras in April.

Dugery, a fourth-year studying political science, presented the issue during the UPUA’s July 22 meeting to seek assistance from other members in investigating the universities Flock cameras, including those installed at commonwealth campuses Behrend, Altoona and Harrisburg.

The cameras were installed on campus in August 2025 as part of a one-year pilot, and have raised concerns from community members on privacy and transparency from University Police & Public Safety (UPPS) on how the cameras are being used and what measures prevent their misuse.

Dugery said it was during a September meeting with Wozniak and other UPPS representatives that they both learned of the pilot’s lapse earlier in the month. Despite the development, Wozniak, a second-year studying finance and political science, said the issue of Flock cameras at Penn State is far from over.

He said he’d like to see UPUA continue to pursue a resolution on automated license plate readers (ALPR) and collect more survey responses.

“Even though that survey was created before the decision was made, I still think it's extremely important for students to make their say on it because it still gives us in UPUA a good metric as to how the student body feels about this subject,” Wozniak said.

He also said it was important for the UPUA to remain involved on the UPPS advisory board to ensure that student opinions at University Park are made clear, including having the UPUA president sit in on the advisory board meetings.

Dugery said he would also like to see the UPUA continue to receive new survey responses and that he would like to see the organization continue to pursue a resolution on ALPRs to provide a reference for future assemblies.

“We want to be thorough with the work that we've done, if this issue were to ever come back, because an administration can change its mind,” Dugery said.

Dugery and Wozniak’s combined findings, which included testimonies from Penn State students on their views on the presence of Flock cameras at University Park, and a meeting between Dugery, Wozniak and three other UPPS representatives knowledgeable about the pilot program, were compiled into an informational report presented during their Sept. 30 meeting.

The report included a roadmap of UPUA’s next steps in addressing student concerns about Flock cameras on campus, including a survey published on its Instagram on Oct. 5. The survey responses were used in the creation of a resolution establishing the organization’s official stance on the use of automated licence plate readers.

Parker Wallis, 19, of Villanova, Pa., has made several social media posts regarding his and other’s views of Penn State’s use of Flock cameras as part of his podcast, “Parcast with Parker.” On Oct. 11, Wallis made an Instagram post about the survey posted by the UPUA about the cameras and encouraged people to fill it out.

Wallis, a second-year studying broadcast journalism, said the report didn’t give him a clear answer on if and how the UPUA was going to take more concrete steps against Penn State’s use of Flock cameras prior to the announcement of their removal.

However, he said he found it important for students to make their voices heard through the survey so that the UPUA knows what direction it should take in the future should the issue of ALPRs come back to campus.

“We are the representation of the student government and they represent us so whatever voice we put out there … if we can thoroughly communicate to them that this is a problem, they will be by our side and they will help us and they will advocate for a position regarding those concerns,” Wallis said. “They're not a policymaker for Penn State — that's what the Board of Trustees are for — but they play a role in advocating for us, and that's what we need to do.”

title: Penn State graduate creates digital tool to help organize, mobilize Democrats ahead of midterms
author: Jonathon Chiu | The Daily Collegian
description:
When he started working for Ray Bilger’s campaign to represent Pennsylvania’s 15th Congressional District in March, Nish Barot said he began to hear about how the campaign was struggling to effectively coordinate its supporters throughout the district, even with the use of event and volunteer management tools like Mobilize.

Nish, 24, of State College, Pennsylvania, interviewed Democratic campaigns and organizations across Pennsylvania, Maine and Kansas over the next several months to see if they were experiencing similar issues to the Bilger campaign going into the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Through his research, Barot found these problems, which hinder the success of new campaigns in rural areas, were not isolated to the 15th District.

“The problem in rural communities is everybody starts at zero, they get to one, some people lose elections and some people win elections but all of the resources then get scattered and then we lose access to a lot of those volunteers and support networks so when the next candidate comes in, they have to start from scratch,” Barot said.

Bilger, who’s running against incumbent Republican Glenn “G.T.” Thompson, said his campaign has been working with other committees in the District to improve its local outreach, but difficulties with reaching out to and meeting supporters still remain due to disparities in the region’s infrastructure.

“A lot of what we have to deal with here are two lane roads and backcountry ways, so what would normally take a person maybe an hour, hour-and-a-half to get to one of the farthest locations takes about three hours. And then when you get there, it's a challenge to try to organize something on the ground,” Bilger, 66, of Bellefonte, Pennsylvania, said. “It goes into the broadband and the cellular infrastructure as well, because a lot of these places, because of the economic problems they face and have faced for decades, a lot of the print media that they used to have is gone. It's a piecemeal and you have to really go out there and find how people get their news.”

Having graduated from Penn State in 2024 with a degree in human-centered design and development, Barot realized he could use his knowledge and background to help improve the coordination of campaigns — especially grassroots ones like Bilger’s. He began working on a volunteer and campaign coordination tool InvolveOS.

InvolveOS, which first came online in June and is currently being used by several Democratic campaigns and organizations across Pennsylvania, is intended to improve the coordination of grassroots political campaigns by allowing them to upload and map out the presence and locations of donors and volunteers within a county or congressional district.

Barot left the Bilger campaign in September to work full time on InvolveOS. He said the tool provides campaigns with the ability to communicate with supporters.

Users can be added to it once they’re vetted by the organization using it, Barot said, but new users are only able to see the map of their own county or district. They can’t interact with other areas unless given permission by users in those areas.

He also said InvolveOS offers a “path to victory” projection based on voting records from previous elections and areas’ potential to be flipped in the midterms, which helps advise campaigns on how to best direct their resources.

Rose Petrunyak, who works for the Bilger campaign as its volunteer coordinator, said she used to have to keep track of how many people filled out sign-in sheets at events and manually compile the information of individual supporters into Excel spreadsheets.

With the help of the tool, Petrunyak said she’s able to import existing volunteers from her spreadsheets to InvolveOS’s map of the 15th District and upload new ones from event sign-in sheets. She’s also able to make and broadcast requests for volunteers, called “asks,” to help find volunteers best able to assist with certain tasks.

“If I'm looking for somebody that wants to do a postcard writing campaign in Warren County, I can go in and find people who are interested in doing that exact thing in that exact county,” Petrunyak, 55, of State College, Pennsylvania, said. “Then it shoots all of that to your email interface, so then you communicate after that via email. It's been amazing.”

She added that since she’s able to record her asks on InvolveOS to help track the participation time of the volunteers, she plans to thank those who have contributed the most time to helping the campaign.

Sarah Ocampo, Bilger’s campaign public relations manager, said she often uses InvolveOS’s data to help in researching how to contact media throughout PA-15 and to assist in tailoring media scripts to certain regions of the district based on what issues have been expressed in the past.

Ocampo, 18, of State College, Pennsylvania, said InvolveOS offers new ways for campaigns to support themselves, especially rural areas that don’t usually receive backing from the wider Democratic Party outside of presidential elections. Rural areas, Ocampo added, have a presence of Republicans, so drumming up support is more difficult for Democratic candidates.

“When you don't have a lot of support from either the party or your district, it's really important to get as much help as possible,” Ocampo, a first-year studying public relations, said. “It's a lot of work to keep in track of everything to coordinate and log everything, but InvolveOS does do that for the staff members of the campaign.”

Barot said his hope is for InvolveOS to spread throughout Pennsylvania, and he predicts the increased usage of the tool will make it easier to launch grassroots political campaigns in the future by allowing past campaigns to transfer their supporter networks onto new candidates through InvolveOS. But the expansion of InvolveOS would require additional support to pay for the infrastructure needed to run the tool and to fund the development of new features, such as text banking campaigns, he said.

Barot also said he intends for its users to remain solely comprised of Democrats, especially progressive Democrats, and he has no plans to offer InvolveOS to Republican candidates and organizations.

“If we look at Pennsylvania or just rural region states, Republicans have been in power for years, but we still have areas with no broadband connectivity, no cell service, hospitals that are decaying — just infrastructure that is poor,” Barot said. “It's time for change.”

Bilger said he sees having access to more tools like InvolveOS will help to “level the playing field” by allowing smaller campaigns to better compete with larger ones despite having more limited resources and funds.

Because of this, he said such tools, if used “smartly,” stand to have a greater impact for the future of the United States than just helping Democrats like Bilger win their elections.

“The whole purpose of this campaign is to win, but winning for a purpose: to finally get in and try to change politics in our country so that we have public servants who actually understand what public service means,” Bilger said. “Our jobs are supposed to be to serve every single person, to try to make their lives better, to try to make this country better … and I think this is one of the tools that we can use to do that.”

title: No. 16 Penn State women's volleyball defeats No. 18 Indiana, earns consecutive ranked wins
author: Riley Warner | For the Collegian
description:
After a 3-1 win at Rec Hall against No. 10 Oregon, Penn State took to the road to face No. 18 Indiana for another ranked matchup.

The blue and white ultimately defeated the Hoosiers 3-1, improving to 15-5 on the season.

Indiana and setter Teodora Kilkovic had the first serve of the set, resulting in an opening kill by Penn State middle blocker Kendall Northern, assisted by Penn State’s starting setter, Alexis Stucky.

Following this first Nittany Lion kill, the Hoosiers quickly bounced back. The two teams alternated kills for the next few points of set one. This didn’t last long, as following an early tied score of 6-6, Penn State would proceed to dominate the remainder of the set.

Libero Ava Falduto would serve two aces for the Nittany Lions, and Stucky would have one of her own as well. Opposite hitter Kennedy Martin had six kills, leading the offensive barrage.

Indiana struggled to catch up as the blue and white excelled on both ends: the Nittany Lions committed only six errors on 15 kills, compared to the Hoosiers’ six errors on 10 kills. Penn State earned set point on an attack error by Indiana outside hitter Jaidyn Jager and won the opening frame 25-16 on a kill by outside hitter Whitney Lauestein.

Indiana started the second set strong with a kill by outside hitter Izzy Clark and earned a second point off a Northern attack error. The second set proceeded to be the opposite of the first. The blue and white were composed and more attack-driven in the first set; however, after those two scores, the team had to play catch-up for most of the set.

The Nittany Lions’ serves were subpar in the second set, as five of their nine errors came from serves. Despite having three aces in the previous set, Penn State’s setters couldn’t produce one this set, whilst the Hoosiers created two of their own.

Penn State displayed a stronger desire to come out from behind compared to Indiana in the set prior. While the blue and white did go on to lose this set as a result of both service and attack errors by Martin, the score difference of 25-22 was narrow.

The Nittany Lions made a third-set comeback, starting the set they would go on to win with four sequential points: two kills, an ace by Falduto and a Hosier attack error. The red and white made a legitimate attempt to take control of the score, profiting from an ace by Hannah Leftridge and kills by opposite hitter Avry Tatum.

These helped tie the score early in the set to 7-7 and 8-8. However, Indiana's effort proved to be for little, as Penn State went on to add 12 more kills and three aces, two of which came back-to-back from Martin.

Entering the fourth set, Penn State was leading Indiana 2-1. The Nittany Lions started the set strongly with a kill by Lauenstein and an ace by Falduto, but the remainder of the set would be a battle. Errors continued for both teams, and the Nittany Lions still struggled to deliver solid serves and avoid attacking errors.

Still, the blue and white continued their fight, producing two more aces both delivered by middle back Gabrielle Nichols, one of which yielded in a match set and granted Penn State the win.

Up next

The blue and white return to action Thursday for its Military Appreciation Night against Ohio State, which starts at 7 p.m.

title: ‘It’s really special’ | Annual THON 5K crosses the finish line
author: Sophie Fried | For the Collegian
description:
Penn State THON’s annual 5K took place at the Bryce Jordan Center on Sunday, marking the first event for the THON 2027 Dream Forward Campaign and beginning the race towards THON weekend on Feb. 19-21, 2027.

THON is the world's largest student-run philanthropy that aims to provide emotional and financial support to Four Diamonds families who have been impacted by childhood cancer.

Prior to the start of the race, runners and supporters joined together at the BJC to enjoy merchandise, food trucks, a children’s race and musical entertainment. The event was crowded with families, volunteers, staff and alumni.

At 11:30 a.m., racers started their journey across campus, passing notable places such as the Berkey Creamery and Pattee and Paterno Library. Throughout the race, volunteers handed out water to the runners and encouraged them to keep going.

Emma Sabulsky, 19, of Elkins Park, Pennsylvania, is a member of THON’s Rules and Regulations Committee, which works to ensure the safety of all those present in the BJC during THON weekend. Sabulsky said that supporting THON and its mission is what’s driving her to cross the finish line.

“As college students, we’re coming together and we're fighting for this,” Sabulsky, a second-year studying advertising/public relations, said. “I think that’s really what's pulling me through.”

According to Sabulsky, THON weekend is a one-of-a-kind experience for anyone who volunteers or attends. Although this is her second year supporting THON, it's her first time participating in the 5K, and she loved how the race brought people together for such an important cause.

“I don’t think there's anything like it,” Sabulsky said. “I haven't experienced anything like it, so I think it’s really special.”

Caleb Mowery, 21, of Cannonsburg, Pennsylvania, is a Technology Committee captain, and has participated in THON every year since he arrived at Penn State.

Throughout his time as a THON volunteer, Mowery, a fourth-year studying computer science, said that his favorite memory was from his sophomore year when he stayed for Final Four, the last hours of THON where families affected by pediatric cancer share their stories and the final fundraising total is announced.

“It’s such an emotional moment, and it really brings together what we do this for,” Mowery said.

According to Mowery, navigating THON your first year can be overwhelming because of the wide variety of committees and organizations students can participate in, but if you take the leap, it will all be worth it.

“The more involved you become, the more in love you're gonna fall with it,” he said. “That’s something that I can promise.”

Layne Anderson, 21, of Malvern, Pennsylvania, is also a member of the Rules and Regulations Committee and said when it comes to THON, it’s important to be open-minded and say yes to everything.

“It’s positively affected my life just by knowing that this is going to such a great cause,” Anderson, a third-year studying biobehavioral health, said. “Having all of Penn State focused on something that is so amazing.”
