title: Penn State women’s soccer travels to Michigan to face the Spartans and Wolverine
author: Zach Schroder | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State is heading into its last three matches of the regular season. After a 1-0 win over the Rutgers Scarlet Knights, the Nittany Lions now face a tough two-game road trip. They will head to Michigan to face off against the No. 5 Spartans and the No. 24 Wolverines on Thursday and Sunday, respectively.

Here's what you need to know.

Michigan State

The Spartans are coming off a 2-0 win against the Indiana Hoosiers. They are currently ranked fifth in the IWSOC poll and 3rd in the Big Ten standings and 6-1-1 at home this season.

Penn State coach Erica Dambach spoke with the media on Tuesday about the upcoming games and had this to say about the Spartans.

“What they do is what they do and they do it really well,” Dambach said. “It’s not a team that’s necessarily full of surprises; it’s a team that’s full of really experienced, talented players.”

The leaders of that experienced, talented team rank high in some Big Ten categories. Leading the team in points, senior forward Kennedy Bell has eight goals and eight assists this year. The Charlotte, North Carolina, native ranks fifth in shots on goal, second in assists, fourth in goals and third in points.

Not far behind Bell and right up there in the Big Ten rankings is senior midfielder Kayla Briggs. Briggs leads the team in assists with nine and is tied second in goals with six. The Toronto, Ontario native also ranked first in the conference in assists, third in game-winning goals, and fourth in points.

Michigan State has split goalkeeping duties almost 50/50, with Noelle Henning having eight starts and Bella Schopp seven, with each having only one loss this year. The better of the two is sophomore Henning with 24 saves and only four goals allowed.

The Milton, Ontario native ranks second in the Big Ten in goals-against average, third in saves, and seventh in shutouts per game.

Dambach said there's evidence to show her team can beat any team in the country.

“I want us to play that way. I want us to carry ourselves that way,” Dambach. “I want us to have the mentality from minute one to minute 90 that this is a team that can beat anyone in the country, regardless of what the number is before their name.”

Michigan

The Wolverines are coming off a 2-0 win against Oregon and will face off against the Maryland Terrapins on Thursday before playing the Nittany Lions. Michigan is currently ranked 24th in the country and seventh in the Big Ten, one spot behind Penn State.

Speaking to the media, Dambach said she and her team were focused only on the opponent in front of them.

“I don’t know anything about Michigan, in full transparency,” Dambach said. “Thursday’s a big one.”

What we do know about the Wolverines is that their leader in points is junior forward Ella Jablinskey, who has 18 points with eight goals and two assists on the year. The St. Clair native ranks tied third in goals in the conference, sixth in points and seventh in shots on goal.

The Wolverines’ second-best offensive weapon is senior midfielder Lilley Bosley, who ranks second on the team in points and goals and leads the team in assists. The Rochester, Michigan native also has two game-winning goals on the season.

Inside the box for Michigan is freshman keeper Mailia Zillman. The Waunakee, Wisconsin native has 50 saves to 16 goals allowed. Zillman also ranks eighth in the Big Ten in saves per game.

“I think that they’ve been very focused,” Dambach said. “They’ve been very intentional … just staying right here in the moment, staying off social media, staying off all of it, just win the games. You win the games, we’ll be fine.”

MORE SOCCER COVERAGE

title: Preview | No. 19 Penn State field hockey hits the road for 2 ranked Big Ten matchups
author: Annie Gleba | The Daily Collegian
description:
Nittany Lions’ field hockey is officially ranked and primed to defend its post.

Penn State will play its last away games of the season against two ranked Big Ten teams. The Nittany Lions will face tough competition against No. 13 Indiana and No. 6 Iowa.

The blue and white enter this game ranked higher overall in Big Ten Play at No. 3 but lower in NFHCA rankings at No. 19. Coming out of this weekend with wins could help secure a top spot in the Big Ten tournament for the Nittany Lions.

Before this weekend’s games, Penn State has an overall record of 10-4 and 4-1 in conference play, with its only Big Ten loss coming to No. 1 Maryland. They have managed to keep up a seven-game win streak and have a record of 4-1 away.

Indiana

Indiana comes into this game with a 9-4 overall record and is tied with Penn State in conference play at 4-1. At home, they have been able to keep up a 4-1 record and have been able to beat two ranked opponents, Iowa and Michigan.

In Big Ten play, the Hoosiers have lost to No. 2 Northwestern and No. 6 Iowa when they played the Hawkeyes in a split weekend at Iowa City. That weekend showed that Indiana has dominated top teams in the past, being able to take the first win over Iowa 3-1, and just falling short 1-2 when the second game went to triple overtime.

The Indiana team has been able to showcase their tough offense by taking wins over ranked teams, but not falling short in a tough matchup. The team has scored a collective 34 goals this season and has an average of 2.62 goals per game.

The Hoosiers have two top offensive players, Molly Stutte and Celia Arroyo Cabezudo. Stutte has a total of 23 points and a breakout 42 shots on the season so far. The sophomore ranks No. 6 in shots and No. 9 in goals overall in the Big Ten.

Arroyo Cabezudo is another sophomore who has collected 20 points and 30 shots. She has a shots-on-goal percentage of 0.667 and has started and played through each game this season. Arroyo Cabezudo ranks No. 13 in shots and No. 10 in goals for the Big Ten.

Their main goalkeeper is Sadie Canelli; she has played in 12 games and started 11 of them, playing a total of just under 715 minutes. She has 38 saves and has a save percentage of 0.792, only allowing 10 goals this season.

In net for the Nittany Lions, the reliable Aby Deverka will continue to start and play the full game. She has amassed 54 saves, posting a 0.750 save percentage and allowing 18 goals this season. The Junior has climbed to No. 2 in saves per game among Big Ten goalies.

The two Big Ten teams will meet at 3 p.m. Friday.

Iowa

No. 6 Iowa sits at an overall record of 11-2 with a conference record of 3-2. The Hawkeyes have taken Big Ten losses to No. 13 Indiana and former No. 1 Northwestern. They have been able to defend their goal when at home and are 5-1 in Iowa City.

Iowa has developed a powerhouse offense, with players in the top of the Big Ten polls and a spread of players who have collected a significant number of points. Dionne van Aalsum, Frederique van Cleef, Felicia Zonnenberg, and Lieve van Kessel have topped the charts for the Hawkeyes.

Combined, they have a total of 120 points and 48 goals, but the player leading them is Van Aalsum, who has contributed 59 points and 28 goals. The Senior is the No. 1 player in the Big Ten for shots, game-winning goals, and shots on goal. The Nittany Lions will have to be on the lookout to cover the midfielder, not giving her opportunities to reach the circle if they want to keep goals and shots low.

Another Iowa player who is heavily ranked is Van Cleef; she is No. 1 in average goals per game and average points per game in the Big Ten. She is a 5th-year leader on the Hawkeyes and another key piece of their offense.

Flipping to Penn State’s offense, the Nittany Lion standouts continue to be Ella Gaitan, Oliva Martins, Sienna Dunn and Natalie Freeman. Gaitan leads the line with 24 points and 11 goals; she tops the Big Ten rankings at No.2 in shots and game-winning goals. Following her, Dunn leads the Big Ten in assists per game in the Big Ten. The duo will have to work together consistently this weekend to get past two top teams.

Penn State's last road game of the regular season will take place at noon and will feature Iowa’s Senior Day.

MORE FIELD HOCKEY COVERAGE

title: Penn State men's soccer has its work cut out for them against No. 18 Wisconsin this Saturday
author: Sienna Pearce | For The Collegian
description:
The Penn State Nittany Lions and Wisconsin Badgers will face off this Saturday at 7 pm in Jeffery Field in Happy Valley.

This game will be far from happy, though, as the Nittany Lions will be fighting to win over the Badgers, which they haven’t been able to do in past years. During the 2025 matchup, Penn State failed to get anything going and suffered a 2-0 loss. It will have to pull out all the stops to have a fighting chance this week.

This will be the 42nd time the two teams have played each other. Out of all of its meetings, Penn State has a 23-14-4 record.

Penn State’s season so far

This season, the Nittany Lions are 2-8-2. They haven’t had much luck against Big Ten opponents such as Washington, Michigan State, Indiana, UCLA and Ohio State.

Penn State has also been on an odd streak lately, tying its game against Michigan, finishing in a scoreless draw and a 1-1 game against Northwestern.

In their most recent game on Tuesday night, the Nittany Lions were crushed by the Rutgers Scarlet Knights, losing 5-0.

Penn State started the game off on the wrong foot after it failed to stop forward Dan Karsten from scoring Rutgers’ first goal in less than a minute.

“You give up a goal that early in the game, from a momentum standpoint, like in any sport, it sets the tone for the match,” Penn State coach Rob Dow said postgame after Rutgers. “We need to start games better; we need to respond to adversity better.”

The game continued to progress less than smoothly as forward striker Amadou Kone, defender Sheridan McNish and midfielder Dylan Carlson all earned yellow cards for unsportsmanlike behavior.

All hope was lost when the Scarlet Knights earned a 5-0 lead at the hour mark.

“I'm to blame for getting the team prepared for the game,” Dow said. “Collecting around the room to make sure that we're ready for matches and we're spotting diversity better.”

In goal for Penn State has been freshman Daniel Peluffo-Wiese, who’s played all but five minutes for the blue and white this season in net. Wiese posted a 2.17 goals against average with 37 saves and a disappointing 0.587 save percentage.

The 6-foot-7 netminder has notched two shutouts this season, but only one resulted in a win.

Wisconsin’s season so far

The Badgers enter Happy Valley at 9-2-3 this season. They have beaten notable Big Ten teams recently, such as defeating UCLA and Rutgers by one goal each.

Additionally, Wisconsin has tied against teams such as Washington (0-0), Indiana (1-1) and Ohio State (1-1).

In their most recent game Tuesday night, the Wisconsin Badgers earned a 2-1 victory over the Evansville Aces, scoring the game-winning goal in the last minute.

Midfielder Matthew Zachemski took the penalty kick awarded to Wisconsin and slammed it into the net, sealing its victory.

Netminder Judewellin Michel has seen most of the action in front of net for Wisconsin so far this season, starting in 13 of 14 potential games. The 6-foot-5 goalkeeper posted a 0.93 goals against average so far this season, with 36 shots for a 0.750 save percentage. The sophomore has also posted five shutouts this year.

title: ‘Everything should be max effort’ | Andrew Destin reflects on journey to The Athletic
author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian
description:
In 2018, Andrew Destin toured Penn State in the midst of a late-spring State College blizzard. A week earlier, he toured his father’s alma mater, Cal Poly, on a contrastingly gorgeous day in southern California.

Battling the elements, he tucked into The Daily Collegian’s office and, at the suggestion of his parents, chatted with some of the staffers inside.

“I remember walking outside the building, and I went back into that sh—ty weather, where it was snowy and cold and windy,” Destin said. “I turned to my parents, and I was like, ‘Damn it!’ And they're like, ‘What? What is it?’ I was like, ‘I have to go here.’”

Now a full-time reporter, Destin has worked for several highly regarded sports journalism publications since graduating from Penn State in 2022. His journey started at the college paper.

“That visit to the Collegian office, it told me that I wanted to be a sports reporter,” Destin said. “That's what I wanted to do one day, and here I am, still doing it.”

Destin grew up in Saratoga, California, a suburb of San Jose not far from Levi’s Stadium, the home of the San Francisco 49ers.

A die-hard college football fan, he’d wake up at 6 a.m. on autumn Saturdays to catch the beginning of College GameDay. And as the child of two parents who met in a Penn State MBA program, he made the five-hour drive to Pasadena for the Nittany Lions’ Rose Bowl losses to USC in 2009 and 2017.

He was never one for video games or YouTube. Instead, when a young Destin was stressed, avoiding homework or simply sitting at the dining table before school, he’d peruse a copy of the San Francisco Chronicle or San Jose Mercury News.

Thanksgiving football was a big deal for the Destin family, and after one year’s iteration, he recapped the action by writing a game story in a spiral notebook.

“That was the first inkling of like, ‘Wow, he's doing this,’” Maureen Destin, his mother, said. “Some kids don't like to write. He was doing that for fun.”

Destin initially envisioned other careers, but his focus shifted toward journalism in high school. As a varsity baseball and basketball player, it seemed like the best way to keep pursuing his passion for athletics.

“It kind of dawned on me, after I got a B in freshman biology, that being a marine biologist maybe wasn't in store,” Destin said. “I realized I am a good athlete; I am not a great athlete. If I am going to stick with sports, the best way to do it is to go to games.”

So Destin headed to Happy Valley and forfeited the Golden State’s picture-perfect sunshine for the unpredictable meteorological patterns of Centre County. At the Collegian, Destin held roles as a sports editor and men’s hockey reporter. He also served as a CommRadio sports director and play-by-play broadcaster for Big Ten Plus.

Destin interned with the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette the summer before his senior year, then covered the Nittany Lions’ football team for the same outlet upon returning in the fall. Toward the end of his time in college, he earned the opportunity to cover Super Bowl LVI in Los Angeles.

“When you become a really professional journalist at a very young age, it can lose the luster of it a little bit,” Destin said. “Yes, it's good to be professional. It's good to be mature. It's also really good to still be like, ‘Hey, this is really freaking cool. I'm covering the Super Bowl.’ That's something I've had to learn as I've pursued my career.”

Noah Hiles was working for the Beaver County Times in 2022 when he heard rumors that a position on the Post-Gazette’s Penn State beat would soon be opening up. He expected to have a shot at the job, but was surprised to learn the paper already had a candidate in mind.

That candidate, of course, was Destin.

“I was kind of annoyed,” Hiles said. “I was like, ‘Who the heck is this kid? He's in college.’ And it turned out (that) he ended up being probably the best young reporter that I've ever worked with, and also one of my best friends.”

Hiles still ended up at the Post-Gazette, covering Pitt instead, and would co-host a podcast with Destin as the duo wrote about the in-state rivals.

Eventually the paper decided it was no longer interested in having a full-time Penn State reporter, and Destin shifted into a role where he’d split time on its Pirates and Penguins beats. About a year later, Hiles got a similar promotion and began partnering with Destin at PNC Park.

Together, they formed a dynamic reporting duo. In the year that Destin and Hiles shared on the Pirates beat, they combined their skill sets to break news and get scoops that other outlets weren’t able to.

“We were both young and hungry,” Hiles said. “We were so sourced, we had our fingerprints all over that organization and we could find out anything.”

In the process, the Mount Union alum also saw Destin further develop as a journalist. Ahead of writing a story on star Pirates pitcher Paul Skenes, Destin was careful to make a connection with the ace before proceeding, which Hiles pointed to as a moment that embodied his skill on the beat.

“He was just so smart,” Hiles said. “Before reaching out to the family, he had the wherewithal to ask Paul for permission, and Paul appreciated that so much. I think Andrew was the first guy's name on the beat that Paul took the time to learn.”

After spending years in Pennsylvania, Destin looked onward to opportunities back on the West Coast and broke the news to Hiles during a spring-training round of golf in Bradenton, Florida.

“He was telling me about his interviews that he had lined up,” Hiles said. “I just said, ‘This is really it, huh?’ And he was like, ‘Yeah.’”

In April 2025, Destin moved to Seattle after accepting a role at the Associated Press, a new gig where he’d cover sports throughout Washington.

In the process, though, he started to struggle. Earlier in the year, he was diagnosed with mental health conditions including anxiety, depression and insomnia.

“It was all very rapid onset,” Destin said. “I went from highly productive, highly functioning, mentally doing great and within like three, four or five months, got insanely burnt out.”

Coupled with the many responsibilities that came with the new role, it made for a tough start to his time in the Emerald City. But he persevered. From late 2025 through the summer of 2026, Destin worked at some of the world’s highest-profile sporting events.

After covering the Seattle Mariners’ ALCS appearance, he made his way to Levi’s Stadium and covered the Seahawks’ victory in Super Bowl LX, not far from his childhood home. Then, he worked the several World Cup games played in Seattle, including the United States’ 4-1 loss to Belgium in the Round of 16.

It was a challenge, but one he’d grown to handle.

“When 2026 hit, it was in some ways the hardest thing I've ever done professionally,” Destin said. “Super Bowl, World Cup, covering the Mariners, covering the Kraken, covering (University of Washington) football. But I got myself into a place (where) I can not only handle all this, but I can thrive and show up and be the best version of me, and that's super rewarding.”

Destin joined The Athletic, the New York Times’s sports department, in August 2026. He remains in Seattle as a Seahawks reporter and has been pleased with his time there so far.

“It’s forward-thinking, it’s progressive,” Destin said of The Athletic. “It’s, ‘Let's try different things, let's be creative, let's try and do the best work we possibly can.’ And I love that. I absolutely love that.”

Covering the Super Bowl would be a career-defining assignment for any journalist. So would a byline from the World Cup. At just 27 years old, Destin has both under his belt. And as far as he’s concerned, he’s not slowing down anytime soon.

“I'm very adamant, and I probably overdo it to some extent, but you should do things that make you happy as frequently as you possibly can, because at the end of the day, we're not going to be here forever,” Destin said. “That means hug your parents when you see them. Give it your all every time you go to the gym. Everything should be max effort. When you stop doing things (with) max effort in life, that's when you know you need to reevaluate.”

title: Students participate in 'Walk a Mile in Her Shoes,' raise awareness for sexual assault, domestic violence
author: Curtis Johnson | For the Collegian
description:
Content warning: This article contains mention of sexual assault. Resources and support are available through Penn State’s Counseling and Psychological Services.

More than 100 Penn State students gathered for the “Walk a Mile in Her Shoes” march hosted by Voices Against Violence at the Allen Street Gates on Tuesday night. Participants, particularly men, were encouraged to walk a mile in high heels to raise awareness of sexual violence perpetuated against women.

Vice president and co-founder of Voices Against Violence, Carrisa Fan, 21, of Gilbert, Arizona, was initially drawn to the march because of its unconventional nature.

“I felt this was a very good way to get people turning their heads. You don’t see it in State College, Pennsylvania… multiple guys walking down the street in high heels,” Fan, a fourth-year studying nursing, said.

Fan and other organizers sought to balance the lighthearted nature of the march while maintaining the seriousness of sexual and domestic violence.

“People are not always going to come to an event if it’s not something that they think is fun,” Fan said.

However, she emphasized to all participants that “we were uncomfortable for 40 minutes, but people who were sexually assaulted in the past or have been in a domestically violent relationship will be uncomfortable for the rest of their life.”

Before the march began at 5:30 p.m., students created signs with messages such as “Abuse Has NO Excuse” and “Break the Silence, End the Violence!” Participants also wore purple ribbons in recognition of Domestic Violence Awareness Month.

Nick Shriner, 18, of Arlington, Virginia, created a sign saying “No Means No!” and hoped the event could raise awareness about the experiences of sexual violence survivors to outsiders.

“Especially in light of recent events, we need to reinforce, like my sign says, that no means no and consent is always mandatory,” Shriner, a first-year studying agribusiness management, said.

The march began with cheers as participants waved their signs and started their mile-long walk in heels. Some participants who were unfamiliar with heels stumbled or even fell. As the march continued, onlookers cheered while passing cars honked their horns in support.

Connor Hoey, 20, of Carroll County, Maryland, described his first experience in heels as “definitely a calf workout” but said he hoped demonstrations such as these could spark conversations about sexual and domestic violence.

“Don’t be a bystander. If someone seeks out for help, help them,” Hoey, a second-year studying supply chain management and information systems, said.

Aiden Shepro, 20, of York, Pennsylvania, said he felt fraternities have to play an important role in organizing against domestic and sexual violence, particularly in light of recent sexual assault allegations at Cornell University. When Shepro, president of the Theta Chi fraternity at Penn State, received an email from Voices Against Violence about collaborating, he said he and his fraternity brothers were eager to participate.

“When can we go and do I need my own heels? There were just questions of how to get immediately involved,” Shepro, a third-year studying microbiology, said.

Shepro said participating in the march motivated him to take a more “proactive” role in preventing and ending sexual violence.

Other collaborating student organizations included the University Park Undergraduate Association (UPUA), which assisted with event planning, Serve State, which provided volunteers and Penn State Reproductive Justice Project, which provided first-aid assistance.

Beyond the march, Fan said she hoped Penn State would take additional steps to educate students about sexual and domestic violence.

“I’ve seen the emails… I just simply don’t think that’s enough. For most people, it goes to their spam,” Fan said. “I would love for people to have a course on campus that’s required by the school where they talk about statistics and resources that they do have.”

Fan encouraged survivors of sexual and domestic violence to seek assistance from the Relationship Violence Outreach, Intervention and Community Education (R-VOICE) Center at Penn State or the National Domestic Violence Hotline to reach help.

Looking ahead, Fan said she hopes that the success of the Walk a Mile in Her Shoes march will help establish the demonstration as an annual Penn State tradition every October.

“Don’t let the conversation die out now that the event is over,” Fan said.

Resources

Medical services include Mount Nittany Medical Center; Penn Highlands State College; and University Health Services.

On-campus resources include Counseling and Psychological Services (CAPS); the Office of Sexual Misconduct Reporting & Response; the Relationship Violence Outreach, Intervention, and Community Education (R-VOICE) Center; and The Center for Sexual and Gender Diversity (CSGD).

Off-campus resources include Centre Safe.

title: Penn State men's soccer struggles without captain Joe Sheridan in blowout loss to Rutgers
author: Sawyer Klasnick | For The Collegian
description:
Last Friday night against Northwestern, sophomore Joe Sheridan delivered what might be the highlight of Penn State’s season by scoring the game-tying goal in the 81st minute.

However, just under ten minutes later, Sheridan received a red card after an apparent verbal altercation, which disqualified him for the rest of the game and Tuesday night's game against Rutgers.

Sheridan’s absence proved costly, as the Scarlet Knights blew out Penn State 5-0.

First-year coach Rob Dow mentioned the loss of his center back captain as part of the reason Penn State’s defense suffered Tuesday.

“We missed his leadership, his intensity, his reliability,” Dow said. “That’s 80 to 90% every single game, and he doesn't waver from that. You hear him up in the crowd trying to keep the guys motivated. He’s a top class player and a top class leader.”

The final score was indicative of the play on the field, as Rutgers outshot the Nittany Lions 19-6 and had 11 shots on goal to Penn State’s three.

With Sheridan sidelined, Dow had to rely on Noah Förster and freshman Sheridan McNish at center back. The Penn State coach was not impressed with what he saw.

“I saw a lot of first balls lost,” Dow said. “I saw a lot of times on the ball responding to the pressure they were getting on us, so it was like a snowball effect where we lost composure based on the pressure from direct play of Rutgers. We needed to see much more composure out of Noah, especially Noah here. He's a little bit older and has more experience. Sheridan's getting his first season in college, and has got a tremendous trajectory.”

The 6-foot-6 Sheridan was second on the team in points and minutes played entering Tuesday’s contest. He is also a team captain and Dow said he showed his leadership following his untimely red card.

“Yeah, he owned that,” Dowe said. “It was the first thing he did before the team trained in return from Northwestern. That's something he regrets.”

The lone Penn State player ahead of Sheridan in scoring, Amadou Kone, also didn’t start Tuesday’s match. However, it was not because of an injury or suspension.

“I think some other guys have performed better in the last two games, and so we got them off the bench a little more hungry, and you know that was the decision,” Dow said.

Kone, a senior from Ottawa, Canada, received a yellow card for unsporting behavior in the 42nd minute after entering the match. The inability to keep emotions in check was a theme for the Nittany Lions all night. After Rutgers forward Dan Karsten scored just 58 seconds into the match, Penn State was on its heels for the remainder of the night.

“Same thing, composure,” Dow said. “Next play mentality. But I'll be the first person, and so is the rest of the coaching staff, to be in the boat here, about getting beat. And I'm to blame for getting the team prepared for the game.”

Despite still being winless in Big Ten play, Dow knows what it takes to coach a winning team. During his time as the head coach at Vermont, Dow won the 2024 NCAA national championship. This season, as difficult as it has been, hasn’t discouraged him from believing that Penn State can reach those same heights.

“This team has worked too hard to not get a win,” Dow said. “You know, to get wins in the league. And personally, we're developing this team long term. And these are the days we'll look back in one year, two years, and have that channel in our mind that these are difficult but important lessons. We will learn from them.”

title: Penn State men’s hockey battles mentality struggles amid loss to Robert Morris, winless start
author: Maggie Hardy | The Daily Collegian
description:
In the past two seasons, the Penn State program has seen new heights — its first-ever trip to the Frozen Four, acquiring the top prospect in college hockey and propelling itself into the spotlight as a national championship contender.

This season, however, the Nittany Lions have fallen to a 0-4 start, looking far off from the team that made history just last March.

The blue and white’s struggles continued Tuesday night with a 5-2 loss to Robert Morris, and head coach Guy Gadowsky pointed to the team’s mentality as a key factor.

“Very disappointed in the result, and very disappointed on how it happened,” Gadowsky said. “I’m just telling the honest truth about how I feel. I feel its arrogance. I feel that we feel we’re above what we had to do in the past to get where we got.”

The blue and white were fighting an uphill battle when, just 20 seconds in, defenseman Jackson Smith’s slapshot was blocked by Colonials captain Patrick Johnson, leading to a breakaway which Johnson finished with a shot that beat freshman goaltender Ryder Fetterolf on his blocker side.

Smith made another costly turnover which led to a 3-on-1 opportunity for Robert Morris, and junior forward Michael Felsing tapped it in on the doorstep with about four minutes to play in the first period.

“Jackson Smith is a great player,” Gadowsky said. “When he plays great, we’re a much better team.”

The Colonials added one more to their lead with just under 30 seconds to play in the first period. After Penn State was called for its fourth penalty of the period, senior forward George Krotiris buried a loose rebound and sent the home team into the locker room down three scores.

After 20 minutes, the Nittany Lions were heavily outplayed by a non-conference opponent that had also yet to win a game. They were outshot 15-6, and chasing a three-goal deficit that was fueled by self-inflicted wounds.

“I think it's just being more consistent, not letting a bad play affect how you react on the bench, and not letting a bad play affect your next shift,” captain Dane Dowiak said. “I think it's just coming out with the mentality that everybody's got to be pulling the rope the same way, and we haven't been doing that.”

Sophomore forward Justin Poirier cut into Robert Morris’ lead late in the second period with a backhand shot that got the blue and white on the board and breathed some life back into Pegula Ice Arena.

Poirier’s goal proved to be the only score of the middle frame, however, and Penn State continued to struggle with turnovers, failed zone entries, and difficulty gaining any sustained momentum.

“We're going to have to find a different way to prepare the team because it's not preparing them the same way,” Gadowsky said. “It was not getting the mentality results, and to me, that's what happened, and it's extremely disappointing.”

The final 20 minutes were much of the same struggles for the Nittany Lions.

Poirier pulled the blue and white within a goal after firing a shot from the left faceoff dot off the crossbar and in about five minutes in for his second of the game.

Penn State continued to get caught on its heels, however, and Krotiris also tallied his second of the night — this time giving Robert Morris back its two-goal lead — after going coast-to-coast and breezing past multiple defenders before tucking the puck behind Fetterolf.

An empty-net goal from Robert Morris’ Jackson Reineke sealed the Nittany Lions’ fourth straight loss, 5-2.

“It's unacceptable, being 0-4. That's not what we do here. I take full responsibility,” Dowiak said. “That's on me. I got to prepare the group better. But I'm confident we'll turn this thing around.”

title: Where to find fall, winter clothes worth your money
author: Ally Sons | The Daily Collegian
description:
The temperature in State College has largely sat below 70ºF, so it seems safe to say warm weather has officially exited the borough. The cold days are taking over, and Penn State students are switching out their flip-flops and shorts for a closed-toe shoe or a boot and a puffy winter coat.

As everyone gears up to take on the frigid months that lay ahead, it can feel hard to find high-quality, long-lasting winter clothes. But there are options everywhere, especially in State College.

Here’s some local options as you look to update your wardrobe.

Appalachian Outdoors

Appalachian Outdoors, located at 131 S. Allen Street, is an outdoor merchandise store that sells brands from Patagonia to The North Face and Smartwool. Open Monday through Sunday, its currently marketing winter collections and offering a 10% discount for first-time buyers who order online.

This store offers everything you might need for winter, whether it’s a new pair of Uggs or a sherpa zip-up. In addition to its high-quality winter wear, it also has a large variety of snowsport clothing and merchandise, like snowboards, snow goggles and skiing gloves.

Fabletics

Fabletics might not be a place you can walk to downtown, but it has a wide range of jackets and a new line of knitwear on its online store. As a self-proclaimed "eco-conscious" store, it prioritizes using sustainable and higher-quality fabrics in its products.

Offering both men's and women's attire, its selection is hard to beat. As an added bonus, it's currently running an 80% off sale on many of its winter items if you don’t want to break the bank. Sweaters and sweatshirts that usually sell upward of $100 are now $20.

Check out its cardigans, turtleneck sweaters, Don Cord Cruiser jackets and Teddy Shawl Long Coat for pieces that are both stylish and functional.

Uptown Cheapskate

Shopping second-hand is a great way to add to your wardrobe while staying on a budget. It also provides you with the opportunity to discover new brands and expand your reach in the fashion world, and Uptown Cheapskate is a great local option for this kind of shopping.

It's currently rolling out most of its winter options as well as accepting new items if you’re looking to rotate out old clothes from your closet and upgrade.

In terms of winter clothing, it has recently been selling winter boots and a large number of different jackets and sweaters in almost all sizes. It also has a lot of Penn State-themed merchandise if you want to show your school pride in your winter wardrobe.

Harpers

If you’re willing to spend more money for higher quality and longevity in your clothing, Harpers is a great choice. With most of its clothing being 100% cashmere and wool, these outfits are sure to keep you warm even when the snow is completely covering the sidewalk.

With options from Peter Millar and Central Park West, these clothing items can be an investment that is worth it and very on trend with recent winter fashion.

These pieces are more of an upscale addition to your wardrobe, yet still incorporate the best elements of simple basics while keeping it classy.

title: A trending fixation among students comes in the form of a tiny, plastic box
author: Lily Dorf | The Daily Collegian
description:
There are certain things in society that weave their way into the daily lives of people. For some, it’s pilates, and for others, it's trying a new coffee shop. However, there is one trend that has made a significant mark as of late: blind boxes.

Blind boxes originated in Japan as early as the 1980s, and they began making their way over to the United States around the same time. In 2024, the trend took off, after Lisa, a singer in the K-pop group Blackpink, posted a photo with a Labubu keychain.

These collectibles have created a strong fan base nationwide. Influencers spend hundreds of dollars and countless hours searching at stores like Pop Mart to find the one they want. But what do Penn State students and alumni think about blind boxes?

Hope Hannings, 21, of Lansdale, Pennsylvania, said blind boxes are something she’s grown to love — but it hasn’t always been like that. Hannings recalled the first time she saw a blind box in New York City with her cousins, and she wasn’t too fond of them.

“I was like, ‘Who's going to pay $13 for a little toy that you don't even know if you're going to like?’” Hannings, a fourth-year studying elementary and early childhood education, said. “But it's kind of the surprise that I think made everyone else, and myself, start to like them.”

Hannings has since curated a collection of figurines from blind boxes. She likes Sonny Angels, human-like babies with wings in varied themed hats and accessories.

While Hannings’ collection has grown in the last few months, she’s now weighing whether or not she’ll cut herself off once she graduates.

“I feel like as a teacher, too, they're kind of fun to put them in my classroom. But I do think finances would be taken into account. Thirteen dollars for a little, naked angel toy — I might have to reconsider,” she said.

The way some people feel about blind boxes tends to be absolute — they either love them or hate them. Recent graduate Laura Komar, 23, of Springfield, Pennsylvania, doesn’t feel so strongly about the plastic toys.

“I will be excited if it's one that I want,” Komar said. “If it's not one that I want, I'm like, ‘Okay, now I have this new trinket that I'm gonna put on a shelf and never touch again.’”

Komar has known about blind boxes long before they became popular in the States. She bought her first one in Akihabara, Japan when she was 12. Ever since then, blind boxes haven’t been worth it, she said.

“If they were cheaper, I probably would have more,” Komar said. “I don't know if it's a lack of whimsy now, but I would be more inclined to do a blind box of stickers. I was in an Italian market with one of my friends, and there was a little machine that you pay $1, and you get a random sticker.”

Blind boxes are meant to be for fun, but Beyla Holbrook said they can be a form of gambling depending on the intent behind buying them.

“I feel like it gets into that category where it can be a hobby in the same way that Pokemon cards or K-pop photo album cards are, but you are taking a little bit of a risk that you might get the one in the box that you're not in love with,” Holbrook said.

She has a small but mighty collection of blind box figurines herself. Even though some figurines liven up the space in someone’s home, Holbrook feels that her love of blind boxes has developed into something beyond a quick thrill.

Their biggest appeal, she said, is the opportunity to customize them. People can add their own style to them, but the toys themselves become a part of their style too.

“Especially with the key chains and stuff like that you can add. I love when people bedazzle them, because I think it just adds more personality,” Holbrook said.

title: Transfer portal roundup | TE Luke Reynolds, DT Xavier Gilliam shine at new homes
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State lost 47 players to the transfer portal after the 2025 season and the firing of James Franklin. Many have gotten off to strong starts with their new colleges.

Franklin brought 12 of his former Penn Staters with him to Virginia Tech, with multiple earning starting positions, and three players followed defensive coordinator Jim Knowles to Tennessee.

Here’s how former Nittany Lions are doing at their new homes.

Following Franklin

Among the 12 players who are now Hokies, Ethan Grunkemeyer and tight end Luke Reynolds have made the most of their new roles.

As the starting quarterback, Grunkemeyer has shown out in his first year as a full-time starter. In seven games this season, he’s thrown for an ACC leading 1,984 yards and has accounted for 20 total touchdowns. Grunkemeyer has helped Virginia Tech to a 5-2 record so far this season, unleashed under former Penn State tight end coach Ty Howle’s offensive system.

Reynolds has been one of the best tight ends in the country, living up to his former 4-star status. He has 449 yards and four touchdowns on 43 receptions, leading the country in receiving yards by a tight end this season.

On the defensive side of the ball, linebacker Keon Wylie leads the Hokies in tackles with 36, stepping up in a larger role with Virginia Tech than he had in his three seasons with the Nittany Lions.

Edge rusher Cortez Harris, who was a freshman at Penn State last year, is second on the team in sacks with five as one of the Hokies’ starting edge rushers.

The rest of the Penn State transfers to follow Franklin are in more of a depth role on the team, similar to what they had with the Nittany Lions.

Tennessee players

Three of Penn State’s biggest impact players to hit the portal followed Knowles to Tennessee in his first year with the Volunteers.

Linebacker Amare Campbell leads Tennessee with 46 tackles and is half of one of the best linebacker duos in the country, playing alongside Arion Carter. Campbell has flourished in Knowles’ system in his second year under the complex defensive scheme.

Safety Dejuan Lane stepped into a starting role after Edrees Farooq was ruled out for the year prior to the start of the season. Lane is the team’s leader in interceptions with three while also totaling 28 tackles. He’s taken the next step in his game after starting with the Nittany Lions last year.

On the interior, defensive tackle Xavier Gilliam has been an unstoppable force. Gilliam has notched five sacks, including three in the Volunteers’ first game against Furman.

The trio of former Nittany Lions has helped one of the top defenses in the nation, with the Volunteers ranked No. 11 in the AP Poll. Tennessee limited Alabama’s high-powered offense to 10 points in its upset win over the Crimson Tide in Week 7.

Transfers to the ACC

Multiple former Penn Staters made their way to the ACC.

Quarterback Beau Pribula is on his third team in three years, slotting in as Virginia’s starter after spending one year at Missouri. Pribula has thrown for 1,211 yards and 13 touchdowns with just one interception. He has the Cavaliers in the middle of the ACC with a 4-3 record.

Safety King Mack has carved out a rotational role with NC State, tallying 18 tackles. He’s listed as the third safety on the depth chart, with his best game coming in Week 0 against Virginia, where he totaled seven tackles.

Cornerback Elliot Washington II has had some big moments at Clemson under defensive coordinator Tom Allen, another former Nittany Lion playcaller. In six games, Washington leads the Tigers with three interceptions and four passes broken up, including a game-winning interception against North Carolina. He’s been able to make plays alongside one of the best corners in the country in Ashton Hampton.

In one of the top rivalries in the ACC, edge rusher Jaylen Harvey at North Carolina and defensive lineman Owen Wafle at Duke played against each other in Week 7. Harvey notched four tackles against the Blue Devils in North Carolina’s win, while ranking second on the Tar Heels with five sacks on the year.

Wafle has played a depth role for Duke. He didn’t record a stat against North Carolina, and he has five total tackles this season.

title: Penn State graduate Igor Jablokov doesn’t want to be ‘a conformist’ in the AI industry
author: Jonathon Chiu | The Daily Collegian
description:
Igor Jablokov’s name might not be easily recognizable to those unfamiliar with the artificial intelligence (AI) industry, but the impact and reach of his accomplishments can be traced back years before the 2022 release of ChatGPT.

Hailing from Poros, Greece, Jablokov is best known for his decadeslong work with IBM and Yap, which is now a part of Amazon, where he played a pivotal role in the creation of AI programs which would go on to become IBM’s Watson, Apple’s Siri and Amazon’s Alexa.

Jablokov, 52, now serves as the chairman and CEO of his own AI company named, Pryon — a tribute to Amazon’s codename for Alexa during its development. Pyron seeks to create “high-performing, resilient, and responsive organizations” through the aid of Pryon’s AI tools, such as its ingestion, retrieval and generative engines, according to its site.

He founded the company in 2017 with the prediction of an AI-knowledge management “collision” in the near future. Jablokov said he wants to use Pryon to explore how natural language experience interfaces can be applied to the workplace — like people creating and modifying computer programs using the sound of their voice.

Jablokov said Pryon also deviates from his previous work with Siri and Alexa in considering AI’s applications in places like hospitals and power plants.

“When I started the company, nobody was really using AI at work. Siri existed in our iPhone and Alexa existed in our kitchens, but I didn't see natural language experiences existing at work and so I started looking at why that was,” Jablokov said. “Nobody really knew what we were working on until ChatGPT came out, so we were early in the field.”

Jablokov’s past and present achievements in artificial intelligence, however, almost didn’t come to pass. He said he originally planned on pursuing nuclear engineering when he began at Penn State Abington in 1991 but later switched to computer engineering, a degree he graduated with in 1997.

Jablokov said the decision came down to a lack of available jobs for nuclear engineers at the time and computers being integrated into everyday life, which signalled a new development in the information age.

“I realized that even if I had a latent interest in nuclear engineering, everything is going to have computers,” Jablokov said. “It doesn't matter if I'm interested in energy. It doesn't matter if I'm interested in biology. It doesn't matter if I'm interested in transportation, or anything else. Computers were the underlying fabric of everything.”

Alongside his interest in computers, Jablokov said he became fascinated with the potential of natural language processing and speech recognition as AI assistants. These developments can democratize access to computing resources by providing a “better” interaction method between AI and users, he added.

Jablokov said allowing people to interact with AI through speech makes it a tool to solve problems, which is what attracted the “OGs of AI” in the first place. Some problems he mentioned included increasing accessibility resources for the youth, seniors and people who are disabled, and breaking down language barriers via machine translation.

During the summer of 2023, Jason O’Neill, 50, of Hilo, Hawaii, met Jablokov to interview for the position of Pryon’s chief people officer.

Having done research into Jablokov’s background prior to the interview, O’Neill said he felt nervous the conversation would become too technical and exceed his experience in the tech industry. Instead, O’Neill said he found the conversation with Jablokov to be “a very human one.”

“We talked more about the humanities and philosophies versus the technology itself, and I thought that was pretty cool,” O’Neill said. “Every single word he said, I understood, despite not having a deep technical background. He'll take these very complex ideas, whether it's AI or other things, and he'll distill it into a very simple metaphor. And it leaves you with a good understanding of what he's trying to say.”

Having now spent several years as Pryon’s chief people officer, O’Neill said the position allowed him to better know Jablokov and what kind of leader he is. He’s found Jablokov to be a man with “zero ego,” despite his achievements.

“He hates the words, ‘You did this, Igor.’ He’ll say, ‘No, no, no, we did this,’ and, I think that that is something that's very unique about him,” O’Neill said. “He just wants to make sure that the glory is shared by the team or by others, and he wants none of the credit.”

Sheridan Clemins, 41, of San Diego, California, works as Pryon’s chief information security officer and has known Jablokov since 2024.

Several tech industry leaders have become “narcissistic and self-absorbed,” especially if they believe they’re creating unique technologies, Clemens said, but Jablokov is not one of those leaders.

“Part of what makes (Pryon) successful is that he finds people that he really connects with, that he trusts, and he gives them the latitude and the freedom to do what they need to do and listens to them when it's time to make some changes or to pivot,” Clemens said.

Jablokov said his leadership style comes from a desire for people to “embrace” their individuality.

When he was still a student, Jablokov recalled, he did an interview in “rundown clothes” instead of a suit and challenged interviewers who rejected him for his appearance by asking them: “Are you hiring me for my mind or for my threads?” Jablokov said this initiative ultimately got him offered many of the jobs he was being interviewed for.

“In some ways, if all they're seeing is the same product over and over again, your mind and heart aches for something completely different,” Jablokov said. “Don't be just a conformist. Find that thing that is a unique plot twist and stuff like that so that you show people that, ‘hey, I'm one of a kind and this is what I can do for you.’”

title: Blue and White Society connects students through alumni networking, campus involvement
author: Fabiola González-Cruz | The Daily Collegian
description:
Being at a large campus can make finding a community challenging, but a student organization is bridging that gap through campus events, professional development opportunities and connections with alumni.

The Blue and White Society, the student membership organization of the Penn State Alumni Association, has more than 8,000 members, making it one of the university’s largest and most active student organizations, according to its website.

Blue and White Society President Gorja Yadav, 21, of Raleigh, North Carolina, said the university’s size initially made adjusting to campus life intimidating. She became interested in the organization after seeing the events it hosted and the opportunities it provided for students to meet one another.

“The biggest mission is making sure we’re connecting students to alumni constantly,” Yadav said.

Yadav, a fourth-year studying supply chain and telecommunications and media industries, said she was particularly drawn to the organization’s emphasis on “creating connections and making the school feel a lot smaller.”

The organization offers several levels of involvement, including general membership, programming board and executive board positions.

Members can participate in general body meetings, professional development workshops and social events, according to Yadav. Students seeking additional leadership opportunities can apply to the programming board, which oversees initiatives related to areas such as marketing, philanthropy and alumni relations.

One of the organization’s professional development opportunities is Quick Connect, a program that pairs programming board members with alumni based on their career aspirations. Yadav said previous participants have secured internships and employment opportunities through connections established with alumni.

The organization also promotes campus involvement through seasonal activities, homecoming celebrations and participation in THON. Yadav said these activities are among the opportunities students may overlook when considering membership.

“It’s a very student-run organization, it’s very involved, and everyone wants the best for each other,” Yadav said.

One of Yadav’s priorities is increasing awareness of the organization through campus tabling, meeting prospective members and expanding its presence on social media platforms, including TikTok.

Director of Membership Recruitment Payton Brainerd, 19, of Medina, Ohio, said the organization attracts prospective members through community service opportunities, social events and professional development programs.

Brainerd, a second-year student studying mechanical engineering, said the organization promotes helping the community, social activities and membership benefits when introducing prospective members to the organization.

“I think it’s super easy to find people that have similar interests to you at our (general member meetings), our service credits, stuff like that, because you do what interests you, as do the people who show up,” Brainerd said.

The organization allows members to choose their level of involvement according to their interests and availability, rather than requiring participation in every event.

“You get out whatever you put in, so nothing’s required,” Brainerd said.

However, maintaining consistent participation remains a challenge. Although the organization has approximately 8,000 registered members, Brainerd estimated only around 100 regularly participate in the organization’s activities.

The society promotes its service opportunities, campus events and connections to Penn State alumni when recruiting students to try offsetting this challenge, she said.

Brainerd said the society’s alumni connections and potential career opportunities distinguish it from other campus organizations. In addition to professional networking and membership opportunities offered by the Blue and White Society, its events also aim to create spaces in which students can interact and build friendships.

Recruitment efforts are also centered on different areas of involvement, including service opportunities and membership incentives such as football-related giveaways. Director of Events, Madison Asprelli, 20, of Boston, Massachusetts, said she prioritizes activities that appeal to the broader student body while also reflecting Penn State’s traditions and campus culture.

“The goal of all the events we plan is to enhance tradition and community at Penn State, and to make everybody feel like they belong here,” Asprelli said.

Asprelli, a second-year studying marketing, said she considers students’ interests and experiences when planning activities. During the Blue and White Society Bash in August, students could customize different items, such as license plates for their dorm rooms and hats for football games.

“My main goal is not to have, like, a student walk through, you know, grab some popcorn and leave, but I want them to kind of stay, walk around, talk to the person next to them in line,” Asprelli said.

She said her favorite event is “PS I (Heart) You Week,” which concludes with a carnival-style gathering on the HUB Lawn. The event includes activities such as inflatable attractions, food and music.

“Everybody’s so stressed out, but when they see Blue and White Society on the lawn, they have a place where they can go, kind of de-stress, get some food, jump in the bouncy house and just kind of have fun at the end of the year,” Asprelli said.

Aside from this event, the organization has activities ranging from Homecoming celebrations and THON fundraising to alumni networking trips, LinkedIn workshops and even clothing swaps.

Although certain membership benefits are exclusive to registered members, Asprelli said the organization's broader campus events are open to students regardless of membership status.

“There’s almost like a place for everybody,” Asprelli said.

title: Off the Record | The truth about being a virgin
author: Miss Behave I The Daily Collegian
description:
To have sex or not to have sex? That is the question.

One of the most beautiful things about life is that no two people are the same, and we can all choose to do our own thing on our own time. It’s no secret that hook-up culture runs rampant among Generation Z.

As a college woman, there’s some pressure to participate in it. It can feel as if everybody’s having sex, as if you should just get your first time over with to catch up.

Just as no shame comes from being sexually active, no shame comes from not wanting to have sex for any rhyme or reason. There’s nothing wrong with being a virgin. But how do women win in society’s eyes? Society will call a woman a whore for having sex. They’ll call a woman a prude for not having sex.

I don’t know about you, but winning society’s ignorant, distorted race would feel more like losing to me. Why would we want to adhere to a systemically broken social construct?

We win instead by honoring our own values and hearts — not the old men who think they know what it means to be a woman when they don’t even know what it means to be a decent human being.

Society really isn’t just old men, though. It’s our classmates and neighbors who are experiencing college just as we are. They’re the people we compare ourselves to, whether that be appearance-wise, academically or sexually.

It can feel awkward when your friend group talks about sex and their experiences when you can’t relate. Answer this question, though: Losing your virginity to “catch up” with your friends may give you something to relate to, but at what cost?

In a survey conducted by The Daily Collegian earlier this year, 65% of 160 students reported they were sexually active. While that seems like the overwhelming majority, it doesn’t mean that’s where you’re supposed to be. Even if 99% of students were having sex, it would be completely alright to be a part of the 1% who aren't. I mean, if everyone jumped off of a bridge, would you?

OK, that was a cliché. But my point is that we’re not meant to live our lives through a checklist developed by a society that disregards nuanced, individual complexities. There’s only one reason to have sex: if it’s without a doubt an absolute “hell yes.”

Pressure, catching up or embarrassment are never reasons to have sex with someone, but it can be hard to avoid these feelings — especially in a college town. “Comparison is the thief of joy,” as they say.

However, life is so much more peaceful when you accept that no two lives are the same, and no two lives should be the same. Living a life on someone else’s timeline is not living your own.

It’s never embarrassing or shameful to stay true to your values, decisions, or feelings — whether that means having sex or not.

Yours truly,

Miss Behave

title: Sports Editors Weekly | Should Penn State fire Athletic Director Pat Kraft?
author: Gianna Dowling & Myles Hannak | Sports Editor
description:
Penn State Athletics is in the gutter, and everyone online and on campus is gunning for the man at the helm — Athletic Director Patrick Kraft.

The Nittany Lions tanked last school year to their worst record in all varsity sports since 2018-19. The leaves are changing this fall, but their fate isn't.

Football brought a sequel to last season’s disappointment so far this year: men’s hockey dropped out the national polls; men’s soccer failed to rally under first-year coach Rob Dow; and both women’s hockey and women’s volleyball hit brief snags in years they looked to be competitive.

The lone bright spots have been field hockey cracking into the national rankings under new coach Hannah Prince and women’s soccer’s resurgent year. But these blips of success haven’t been enough to appease fans, as overall athletic expectations still sit out of reach.

Should the University pull the plug on Kraft and look for someone else?

Gianna Dowling: Don’t jump the gun yet

Penn State sports fans aren’t happy right now with certain decisions that have been made by Kraft, and for good reason. Fans were optimistic about Kraft’s choice to appoint Matt Campbell as the new leader of Penn State football, but things aren’t turning out exactly as hoped.

Now, it goes without saying that football is the biggest money-maker in Athletics and has the most attention. That said, it’s not the only sport, so no decisions should be made just yet.

Since Kraft’s hiring in 2022, he’s made good moves in appointing program leaders. One of his first hires was baseball coach Mike Gambino, who led the Nittany Lions to appearances in the Big Ten Tournament championship and semifinals in his first two seasons at the helm. Gambino was strong on the trail, bringing in the No. 43 class in 2026.

In 2025, Kayla Treanor became the new leader of women’s lacrosse, and her first season was a strong one. Treanor’s start in 2026 was the program's best since 1989, and the team's 12 wins were the most in a season since 2017. The team also made the NCAA Tournament for the first time since 2024.

One of Kraft's most recent hires was field hockey coach Hannah Prince, who’s off to a stellar start in her first campaign. Prince’s squad is currently on a seven-game win streak and found themselves in the top-20 rankings this week for the first time under Prince — one move by Kraft that paid off.

Kraft certainly deserves some criticism, but I don’t think Penn State football should be the sole barometer of his time here. His other program hires have shown promise, and coaches like Gambino, Treanor and Prince are building momentum in their sports.

Kraft should be given the chance to see his decision through, and fans should consider the bigger picture before demanding change. Penn State Athletics is much more than just one program, and its success should be measured as such, even if football is king.

Myles Hannak: The experiment has failed

Penn State hired Kraft because he did more with less, turning around Temple and Boston College with quick, low-budget fixes. That made Penn State’s outlook look rosy. What would the new AD do with these big budgets?

Well, he took big swings with the blue and white war chest at his disposal: He brought in Gavin McKenna to the largest NIL deal in collegiate hockey history; kept the wrestling juggernaut churning; and funneled money into the gridiron via a stadium deal, roster overhaul and coaching switch.

Yet with all this investment, Kraft has nothing to show for in his tenure.

The wrestling dynasty continued, but that happened before he got here. Besides that, there’s not one bit of national hardware. The only thing that has changed is the over $500m in debt that’s attached to Athletics’ hip now, which is a figure that tripled between financial reports released for 2024 and 2025.

The finances aren’t all Kraft’s fault, but he deserves blame for not mitigating the situation, especially when the on-field product has all but disappeared and could corner the department if continuously ignored.

There’s not a figure for the AD job at Penn State who understands the culture, identity and values that need to be upheld for this job more than Kraft, but that doesn’t mean he’s not in over his head.

For the future and present of Penn State, on and off the field, it needs someone who has the expertise, not just the moxie, needed to lead the Nittany Lions to glory. He clearly isn’t ready to lead an institution of this caliber.

title: Penn State men’s soccer falls to Rutgers 5-0 in rough defensive outing
author: Luci Palacios | The Daily Collegian
description:
When it rains, it pours.

In the midst of a difficult season, Penn State traveled back home after a 1-1 tie to Northwestern to face Rutgers, who were fresh off an upset over No. 2 Indiana, in another conference matchup.

In a one-sided battle, the Nittany Lions fell 5-0 to the Scarlet Knights.

The Nittany Lions, as a result of Tuesday’s matchup, fell to 2-8-2, while Rutgers improved to 7-6-1. The blue and white have an opportunity after this matchup to finish strong, with three remaining games on its schedule.

First half

Penn State struggled to find their footing early on in the game as they conceded a goal within the first minute of the game. Junior forward Dan Karsten shot the ball in the top left of the net with his right foot, assisted by Amer Lukovic and Francesco Di Ponzio.

With a key defender out in Joe Sheridan, the Nittany Lions defense continued to fall apart with Rutgers continuously getting through. The Scarlet Knights were pressuring offensively and didn’t plan to stop.

A Rutgers player was tripped outside the box for a penalty kick, and Lukovic took it, but Daniel Peluffo-Wiese made a diving save to keep the Nittany Lions in the game.

The flaws of the blue and white defense showed as they conceded another goal in the seventh minute to make it 2-0. Di Ponzio scored his own goal of the game after assisting the first; this time, Lukovic and Devon Stopek assisted.

“We need to start games better. We need to respond to adversity better,” head coach Rob Dow said.

Rutgers continued to play at its own pace after two goals, while Penn State produced some offense that the Scarlet Knights shut down quickly.

On the counterattack, Rutgers scored its third goal in the 19th minute, this time with William Pierce, assisted by Nick Collins. An unlucky bounce led to the goal as the Nittany Lions looked disoriented.

Peluffo-Wiese continued to be tested as he faced another shot a minute after the goal but blocked it with his forearm.

Penn State presented an attack in the 33rd minute but were unable to finish the ball. Rutgers counterattacked once again and tested the Nittany Lions’ defense.

Amadou Kone tried to get things going for the blue and white as he dribbled up the field, but he drew a yellow card for unsporting behavior.

Rutgers ended the half in the Nittany Lions’ attacking third, leading 3-0 against a struggling defense.

Second half

The Scarlet Knights came out with the same intensity as the first, instantly applying pressure to the Nittany Lions' defense. This time the blue and white were able to withstand it and lead a counterattack of their own, but it was stopped early.

As Rutgers headed up the field, Di Ponzio took another rip at the goal, but Peluffo-Wiese was able to block it in the 49th minute.

That didn't last long, as junior forward Thomas Angelone beat four defenders and knocked a goal into the top right for a 4-0 lead. Angelone’s first collegiate goal came in the 54th minute.

Angelone continued to apply pressure and tried to earn his second goal shortly after his first, but Peluffo-Wiese blocked his shot. Zach Mastrodimos followed, but his shot was also blocked.

Rutgers’s continued pressure proved difficult for the blue and white to contain, as the Scarlet Knights extended their lead in the second half.

“We didn’t respond to that level of pressure very well," Dow said. "But I told the guys to remember it.”

The Nittany Lions are riled up as Sheridan McNish gets a yellow card for unsporting behavior in the 59th minute after a controversial penalty called inside the box against Penn State.

Coach Dow called for a VAR review on the previous penalty, but the appeal was unsuccessful, and the Scarlet Knights earned a penalty kick inside the box.

Rutgers’ Collins stepped up to take the kick and nailed it in the top right of the net, making it his third goal of the season. Rutgers took a 5-0 lead in the 60th minute, putting a stop to the scoring frenzy.

As the Nittany Lions stormed up the field, Dylan Carlson fouled Etienne Reck outside the box in the 63rd minute. While setting up for the penalty kick, Dylan Carlson was handed a yellow card for unsporting behavior.

Penn State remained in the Rutgers attacking third and earned back-to-back corner kicks but was unsuccessful in putting it in the back of the net.

Rutgers played a game of keep-away from the Nittany Lions, but the blue and white were able to possess the ball to earn a corner. Same Fielding was able to crank a shot at the goal in the 71st minute, but it was off target.

The blue and white continued to push on the offense despite the score to get anything going but just couldn’t; in the process, Reck received a yellow card for unsporting behavior in the 79th minute.

The Nittany Lions couldn’t hold on in the beatdown as they still haven’t won a conference game.

“This team has worked too hard to get a win, to get wins in the league,” Dow said. “Personally, we’re developing this team long term.”

Up next

Dow’s blue and white return to action against No. 18 Wisconsin on Saturday at 7 p.m.

title: Penn State women’s soccer notebook | Erica Dambach discusses mindset for ranked matchups
author: Lola Brand | For the Collegian
description:
Postseason soccer is almost here.

Penn State picked up its fifth clean sheet in Big Ten play in a hard-fought 1-0 win against Rutgers on Saturday, yet the blue and white will have a chance to build on that momentum as it hits the road this week.

The Nittany Lions endure a pair of tough Big Ten matchups, taking on No. 5 Michigan State on Thursday before facing No. 24 Michigan on Saturday.

Coach Erica Dambach met with the media over Zoom to discuss the team’s recent defensive performance, along with the squad’s goals and mindset heading into a jam-packed week with playoff implications for the 7-3-4 Nittany Lions.

Playing with swagger

Penn State’s recent games against the Scarlet Knights, No. 12 Washington and Oregon were all decided by a single goal, signaling the importance of capitalizing on scoring opportunities for a blue and white squad that hasn’t had any shortage of opportunity, as it ranks in the top half of the Big Ten in all shot-related categories.

When asked what her team needs to do to become more effective in front of the net, Dambach noted the simplicity of finishing chances as just “Rolling the ball into the net.” The Nittany Lions’ coach also reaffirmed the quality of chances and just playing free, expecting her squad to buy into the resume they’ve built so far.

“(It’s) just about having swagger…play with swagger because you’ve earned it,” Dambach said. You’ve got a body of evidence that shows that you should be playing with swagger… now own it.”

With the confidence required at this juncture, goalkeeper Mackenzie Gress has been a standout all season and made a difference, particularly in the recent game against Rutgers.

“If you’re going to beat good teams, your goalkeeper’s got to make big plays,” Dambach said. “She’s proved she’s one of the best, why she’s considered to be one of the best in the country. But the most important thing is just her presence and our leadership back there, I think, brings a lot of confidence to our team.”

Mindset and goals for this upcoming week

This week, Penn State will play two ranked opponents on the road, with only three games left of conference play; however daunting the task, Dambach and her squad gear up this week to give it their all.

“They’ve been very focused,” Dambach said. “They’ve been very intentional. They are really trying to shrink the target right now, and I think that’s really important at this time in the season.”

With the preparation on the field, the blue and white boss also revealed the mental aspects that go into a squad still vying to make a push for positioning in the Big Ten, giving an ode to a former Penn State coach in the process.

“Something (James) Franklin used to talk about a lot was 1-0. All coaches talk about that, whether they have a mantra or not,” Dambach said. “But really, just staying right here in the moment, staying off of social media, staying off of all of it. Just win the games — You win the games, we’ll be fine.”

Supporting women’s sports

Despite the inevitable pressure that comes with playing in these last few games before there can be a postseason, Dambach highlights how pressure is a privilege for her team.

“Well, one of the things is… you’ll go into Michigan State, they’ll have thousands of people in the stands… Honestly, I don’t even care what comes out of their mouth. It will feel hostile, but for me, it’s more hostile sitting in empty stands,” Dambach said. “This is just an exciting environment and a student section that’s fun and will bring energy to the game. So for us, taking energy from these environments that we’re going into.”

As Penn State prepares for two challenging road matchups, Dambach hopes her team can embrace the crowd's energy. Beyond the competition, she spoke on the importance of fans showing up for women’s sports, reinforcing how much that support means to the athletes and to the game itself.

“I’m so excited to see people supporting women’s sports, supporting women’s soccer. Honestly, I don’t care if they’re for or against,” Dambach said. “They are out there supporting women’s football, and I want the team to feel like that too.”

title: Penn State men’s hockey’s uninspiring start to the season continues, loses to Robert Morris despite late-game surge
author: Chase Fisher | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State defenseman Jackson Smith watched from the blue line as Robert Morris center Patrick Johnson put his head down and glided into the Nittany Lions’ zone.

One second Smith was loading up a slap shot, the next his eyes were glued to Johnson’s stick, which lofted the puck past goaltender Ryder Fetterolf to give the Colonials the lead 20 seconds into Tuesday night’s game. Just when you think the Nittany Lions couldn’t face any more adversity.

In a battle of winless programs, the home team’s late comeback bid was all for nothing, as Penn State lost to Robert Morris 5-2 in a gutting Nittany Lions defeat.

“I feel that the success of this program over the last two years — obviously, we've had two pretty darn good years — I think that there's a feeling that it's just going to come easy, I guess,” coach Guy Gadowsky said Tuesday night. “This is a terrible word to say, but I'm just telling the honest truth of how I feel. I feel it's arrogance. I feel it's arrogance. I feel that we feel we're above what we had to do in the past to get where we got… obviously that's on me because that's a preparation issue, so that's absolutely on me and myself and our staff.”

Here’s how Penn State’s losing skid continued, now at four and nearly matching the worst start to a season in program history.

First period

Penn State was plagued by mistakes early in Tuesday’s contest — a lack of discipline defined the first period.

The Nittany Lions committed four minor infractions, three of which sent Robert Morris to the power play, while the other negated a man-advantage of their own. It was the sloppiest first frame for Penn State all season, featuring several turnovers and preventable mistakes.

The Nittany Lions’ woes led to three first-period goals for Robert Morris.

As mentioned earlier, Smith tried a slap shot early in the frame, which was blocked by Johnson. Johnson skated uncontested in Penn State’s defensive zone shortly after and lifted the puck over Fetterolf’s right blocker to give Robert Morris the early lead.

Nearly 15 minutes later, the Colonials capitalized on another Smith mistake. The highly regarded defenseman turned the puck over in the offensive zone, which sprung a 3-on-1 for Robert Morris. No one was able to get back for the Nittany Lions, as left wing Brennan Faulkner slid a cross-ice pass to Michael Felsing, who snuck the puck into a wide-open net to make it 2-0 for the Colonials.

“Jackson Smith is a great player, and when he plays great, we're a much, much better team,” Gadowsky said.

Shortly after, Robert Morris scored again, this time on the power play. Left wing George Krotiris jammed home a rebound off Fetterolf's pads, extending the Colonials' lead to 3-0.

Second period

Penn State came out of the locker room a bit more disciplined. The Nittany Lions put their foot on the gas, controlling play for most of the period and outshooting Robert Morris 19-6 in the second frame.

Many of those shots came on the power play, as Penn State drew four penalties on the Colonials. The Nittany Lions, who owned the worst man-advantage percentage in the Big Ten (7.69%) through the second period, didn’t convert on any of their chances.

However, they found the back of the net in the latter half of the period.

Right wing Justin Poirier received a soft feed from left wing Justin Larose at the top of the right circle with 5:31 remaining in the frame, before splitting three defenders and backhanding the puck over Robert Morris goaltender Lucas Massie’s right shoulder for his first goal of the season, which cut Penn State’s deficit to 3-1.

Third period

Penn State put its power-play struggles aside early in the third period.

Just five seconds into its sixth man-advantage on Tuesday, Poirier controlled the puck by the left-wing circle and roofed it over Massie, bringing the Nittany Lions within one at the 15:07 mark in the frame.

“His shot is incredible. It's fun to watch,” Gadowsky said. “I like a lot about him. Absolutely love the way he shoots the puck, and I think you guys know he was out, like he had surgery in the off-season. It's been a long road back, and still a little getting there. But you can see every week he's getting a little more and more and more comfortable, and when he gets open he can shoot the puck. I mean, he's as dangerous as any player there is.”

That was all she wrote, however, for Penn State’s late-game surge.

With 3:02 remaining in regulation, Krotiris broke the Nittany Lions blue line and swerved around defenseman Mac Gadowsky. The senior’s nifty move and later shot beat Fetterolf and extended Robert Morris’ advantage to 4-2.

Right wing Jackson Reineke fired a puck into the empty net shortly after, icing the game and delivering the Nittany Lions their fourth straight loss.

Up next

Penn State begins its last non-conference series this weekend at Pegula Ice Arena against Canisius. Puck drop is slated for 7 p.m. Friday.
