title: Penn State women’s volleyball notebook | Katie Schumacher-Cawley discusses 1-1 week, preparation for busy weekend
author: Myles Hannak | The Daily Collegian
description:
One month until tournament play.

The Nittany Lions return to Happy Valley this week for a Dig Pink clash against No. 10 Oregon on Friday before traveling to No. 18 Indiana on Sunday.

With the quickest travel turnaround of the blue and white all season, coach Katie Schumacher-Cawley discussed the upcoming slate and recent results as her squad arrives in this stretch with a 1-1 record, suffering an upset defeat to UCLA and sweeping USC to fall one spot in the AVCA poll to No. 16.

As the schedule begins to ramp up and the postseason looms, here's what Schumacher-Cawley said at her weekly press conference Tuesday.

Grading the Golden Coast

The Nittany Lions started their trip out west slowly, dropping the first set of the road trip against UCLA 25-20, yet that Bruins’ form wouldn’t persist. The blue and white thundered off back-to-back set wins with 10- and eight-point margins, respectively, to go into the driver's seat.

Once Penn State found the momentum, it crumbled, dropping a seven-point advantage in the fourth set, allowing UCLA to force a fifth set and steal the upset victory. In the rubble was Kennedy Martin, who logged a season high of 25 kills and earned her coach’s praise during media.

“I think the positive was that we were able to find a way to win on Saturday after not being able to finish on Friday,” Schumacher-Cawley said. “We start making too many unforced errors and don't do a good job of controlling the ball on our side, and so I think going back, watching film and being able to fix those things in practice this week (to) make sure that we're really mindful about what we're doing.”

Penn State ran away against USC, with a two-point second set as the narrowest finish in the win, as Schumacher-Cawley extended praise in her presser to her outside hitter depth and to her team’s aggression at the end line.

While the boss saw positives, she’ll still use a shortened roster, as Schumacher-Cawley confirmed that star middle blocker Ryla Jones isn’t yet cleared to return from injury, despite being slated to make the trip for this upcoming weekend’s match.

Rankings sandwich

As Schumacher-Cawley gave her statements exactly a week away from the first-ever Big Ten Tournament, the seedings begin to tighten around a blue and white squad that enters a gauntlet of a slate with an Oregon team ranked above it nationally and an Indiana team below.

“Every weekend in the Big Ten is tough, but I think this is a great opportunity to play two really great teams and two teams that are playing really well right now,” Schumacher-Cawley said. “ I think Oregon, they've come a long way and they've gotten better every match they've played in. … it's nice to have them at home and use these days to prepare for not only Oregon but a really, really great IU team.”

The Ducks arrive in Happy Valley on a seven-game win streak that’s propelled them to 16-2 and a perfect 8-0 in Big Ten play. It signals a fast descent for Oregon second-year coach Trent Kersten, who finished with a pedestrian 17-13 in his debut season in Eugene.

“(Kersten is) a great coach. I think he did nice things at his previous school, and I think he gets his players to play hard and compete,” Schumacher-Cawley said. “They have a couple really nice pieces, and they’re playing well together.”

The Hoosiers host Penn State fresh off an upset of then-No. 20 Washington and a five-set thriller with the Ducks, as nine-year Indiana coach Steve Aird guided his squad to the best run of play it’s had so far in its season.

“Steve and his entire staff, I think they do an excellent job with whatever players they have on their team — they get the most out of them,” Schumacher-Cawley said. “I think that's hard to do at times. But I think they're really aggressive on the end line. I think that they play really hard, and that's a tough facility to play at.”

In the new Big Ten postseason format, 15 squads make the bracket. Currently, Oregon sits tied for the No. 2 berth, while Penn State’s 5-4 has it tied with four other schools, all of which are tied for fifth in the conference. Indiana is one of three teams to be 4-4 in the Big Ten, yet it sits comfortably within the window to make the tournament.

Failing to prepare is preparing to fail

A key theme of Schumacher-Cawley’s responses in her presser was what her team can do to succeed down the stretch, both internally and externally, as the boss continued to preach self-confidence.

“They understand that it's a long season and how hard the conference is,” Schumacher-Cawley said. “Every match we need to continue to be prepared and do the things on and off the court that are going to help us be successful. I think some of them are doing a really good job at that and helping themselves a little bit more.”

Schumacher-Cawley continued to open up on her personal match-day preparation, watching film, meeting with coaches, chatting with players and having her coffee, but also how it’s changed with the one-day rest between games. She confirmed that after the game on Friday, Penn State will fly out Saturday, practically only sleeping, eating, practicing and competing.

“I think just using our time wisely,” Schumacher-Cawley said when asked about the preparation for the home-away split. “It’s nice we have a day off in between these upcoming matches, but the focus is one match at a time, but (also) making sure that the staff is preparing the players for both matches as we go through drills and practice.”

title: New Organization Involvement Fair helps students find where they belong
author: Caroline Shaw-Gelman | For the Collegian
description:
As the semester reaches the halfway point, there are several campus organizations that want to get on students’ radar. Newly formed clubs set up booths to give Penn Staters another chance to sign up and learn about organizations they may have missed at the start of the semester in the HUB-Robeson Center from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.

Unlike the previous Involvement Fair on the HUB lawn at the start of the semester, bustling with a wide variety of established clubs, this smaller, more contained version was a relaxed way for students to get to know new organizations. Tables set up throughout the Big TV lounge provided students with information about specific organizations.

Among the groups was the Women of Biomedical Engineering, with Wed Mouazin, 19, events and social chair, who was looking forward to sharing what the club is about with potential new members.

“This was basically my first opportunity to join a club,” Mouazin, a second-year studying biomedical engineering, said. “My entire freshman year, I couldn't find any BME-centered clubs. It was always just a society or biochemistry, never biomed.”

Because of that vacancy, Mouazin aims for this organization to reach women who are specifically interested in the biomedical engineering field. According to Mouazin, Jana Alammari, the president, plans for its first event to be Nov. 13 and hopes to gather people of all backgrounds.

Mouazin said the event is to give people more insight into the club and field of study itself, but also to meet new people who share the same interests.

“We’re so passionate about networking and career development,” Mouazin said.

Even though it can be hard to jump into a club mid-semester, Raya Bhatti, 19, of Clarion, Pennsylvania, said it's important to try new things and challenge yourself in college. As the founder of the Awareness Action Project, she thinks, even if students were intimidated by the grandeur of the fair at the beginning of the semester, they should still give organizations a try now.

“I think the smaller one (fair) is great for students that are intimidated because you get to talk more one-on-one with people,” Bhatti, a second-year studying biomedical engineering, said. “So I think people will be able to connect more with clubs, and they'll even be able to find different ideas from what they saw at the big involvement fair.”

The organization wants to give Penn State students the chance to give back to the State College community.

“Every month is a different national awareness month, so there will be a different project for it,” Bhatti said.

The Awareness Action Project aims to celebrate each national awareness month as the school year progresses, and students involved in the club’s events will be able to bring awareness to different causes and shine light on the disparities in our area.

The Robotic Football Club also attended the event to reach new members and spread awareness of their group. The club was founded at the Penn State York branch campus and was brought to University Park by member Cole Earling, 20, of Shrewsbury, Pennsylvania. Because of this move, the club has a goal to expand membership.

“We want to become something really great because, even today, we had so many people stop by and be like, ‘we didn't even know robot football existed,'" Earling, a third-year studying civil engineering, said. "We have this ability to be this close, tight-knit community."

Earling also said he wanted to embody the spirit of community found at Penn State York and bring that to University Park. In 2020, three years after the club had started at the branch campus, Earling remembered how the league finally took off. Now, robotic football is gaining even more popularity.

“There’s this league starting in America for robot football, and that might be good for us to specialize our robotics in,” Earling said.

The club currently has four different robots with the goal of building a team of eight. They also named each robot after a specific player, or set of players, based on their jersey numbers. Robot number 26 is named after Philadelphia Eagles running back, Saquon Barkley.

As the semester continues, these and many other clubs are welcoming new members who are still looking to find their community on campus.

title: Penn State notebook | Cael Sanderson talks lineups, Levi Haines’ status at local media day
author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian
description:
With 23 days until Penn State opens its season against Bloomsburg, Cael Sanderson took to the podium at Rec Hall on Tuesday for his first media availability of the 2026-27 campaign.

Sanderson and the Nittany Lions open up the season with a home dual against Bloomsburg on Nov. 12. He discussed the lineup, Levi Haines’ eligibility and the growth of Masanosuke Ono.

Here’s what he had to say.

Ready to roll

Coming off of a fifth-consecutive national championship last season, Penn State has returned three wrestlers who won NCAA individual titles.

165-pounder Mitchell Mesenbrink, 197-pounder Josh Barr and 125-pounder Luke Lilledahl will highlight a roster that’ll also feature four wrestlers that placed fourth or higher at the 2026 NCAA Championships.

“I think our culture is going to be really strong, and has been strong,” Sanderson said. “That doesn't mean everything's perfect, but overall, adversity and changes have given us a chance to take our program up a notch.”

Sanderson was hesitant to provide any insight into the lineup that he plans to roll out on Nov. 12 on Tuesday, but is clearly looking forward to getting the season started.

“Obviously, we’ve got several really good wrestlers preparing, but we probably won't announce anything or give any details until our first match,” Sanderson said. “We’re excited, it’s fun to train and prepare, but it’s more fun to compete.”

Could Levi Haines make a return?

At the NCAA Championships in March, 174-pound senior Levi Haines was the fourth Penn State wrestler to win an individual national championship. In June, the NCAA approved a “five-for-five” eligibility model for incoming collegiate athletes.

According to Sanderson, Haines is training in State College for a potential attempt to pursue another season with the Nittany Lions.

“He's preparing just in case he gets that opportunity,” Sanderson said. “We're just waiting to hear the final word. It's been a pretty wild five years of ups and downs and changes and twists and turns. Everyone's in the same boat, and everyone's trying to navigate and figure out what they're doing.”

Haines would be a major re-addition to the squad if he manages to gain eligibility.

The Arendtsville, Pennsylvania native went 26-0 in the 2025-26 season and beat Nebraska’s Christopher Minto in a 2-1 decision to claim his second NCAA title. Currently, Haines is focused on his upcoming trip to Kazakhstan for the Senior World Championships.

“He's preparing, he’s training, he's ready to compete,” Sanderson said. “Obviously, World Championships (are) next week. But if he gets a call back to folkstyle, he's gonna be ready to go.”

Whether or not he’s ruled eligible to wrestle for Penn State this season, Haines’ situation epitomizes the ever-changing landscape of college athletics, something Sanderson has seemingly grown frustrated with.

“You hear different things,” Sanderson said. “I think (it) would really be nice for college sports if at some point the NCAA can enforce rules and have a say in what's going on. It's pretty wild right now, and it's kind of embarrassing.”

Masanosuke Ono’s next steps

Masanosuke Ono is set to begin his second year as a Nittany Lion in 2026 after redshirting last season.

The Matsue City, Japan, native claimed both a U20 World Championship and Senior World Championship at 61 kilograms in 2024, with his resume also featuring gold and silver medals at the Japanese national championships.

Sanderson has seen Ono take major strides in his time in Happy Valley, especially while facing a change of styles.

“He's just a happy, hardworking, competitive guy,” Sanderson said. “He's really excited about folkstyle. The transition from folkstyle to freestyle isn't always an easy transition, [and] it's even more difficult to go from a life of freestyle to folkstyle. But he's gotten really good and he's very disciplined and diligent in his training.”

Off the mat, Ono has also been dedicated to his studies and has set a strong academic example for the rest of the team.

“He’s got one of the best GPAs on our team,” Sanderson said. “He's getting As, and that requires a lot of time from him. Just seeing his devotion and his character, it’s really good for everybody.”

It’s still unclear as to how Ono will slot into Penn State’s lineup this season. He joined the Nittany Lions as a 133-pounder, but could potentially wrestle at 141 pounds in his lone campaign under Sanderson.

The coach didn’t commit to either on Tuesday.

“As far as the weight classes and stuff, I mean, that's something we're still working through. We just have a lot going on. We had, you know, a large group of our guys leave today to go to Kazakhstan for the senior world championships, so we're preparing for the college season, but we're also locked in for what's next.”

title: Centre Film Festival announces festival lineup, local collaborations
author: Colleen Cratty | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Centre Film Festival announced that the 2026 festival will include spotlighting Puerto Rican films, honoring veterans and more.

The 8th annual festival will take place from Nov. 2 to 8, showing movies in a variety of locations over State College and Philipsburg.

3 Dots Downtown was announced as the festival’s new filmmaker lounge, hosting morning short-film screenings and coffee, as well as other special events.

In celebration of the United States’ 250th anniversary, the festival will feature Puerto Rican short films, local music, food and feature films “Extranjera” and “TheyDream.”

On Veterans Day, the festival will play “Jimmy,” a biopic starring KJ Apa, based on actor and military aviator James Stewart. Another biopic celebrating veterans, “I Play Rocky,” will play the next day focusing on actor Sylvester Stallone.

International films selected for Oscar submission will also be featured including “Vértices” from El Salvador and “One Woman One Bra” from Kenya.

The festival is partnering with the Palmer Museum of Art for a free, virtual reality experience on Thursday, Nov 5. Attendees can watch 17 immersive films from around the world during the event.

Other features of the festival include films made in Pennsylvania, stories from the Middle East and screenings celebrating Indigenous Peoples’ Heritage Month.

The festival will culminate in a closing-night celebration recognizing Nashormeh Lindo and Delroy Lindo with the Chandler Living Legacy award and Lifetime Achievement award.

For those who cannot attend the festival, the films will be available to watch on Eventive from Nov. 9 to 16.
